talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK AI Agents As Your Organization's Personal Security Newsroom
talks.teaser: Brett A. investigates #OOTB2025BKK AI Agents As Your Organization's Personal Security Newsroom.
talks.summary:
Speaker and Security Operations Role

Brett Andrews, Anthropic's incidents and intelligence lead, describes his team handling technical investigations, forensic tooling, incident command, and threat-intelligence partnerships across commercial and government channels.

Anthropic Context

Andrews explains Anthropic's public-benefit-corporation status and responsible scaling policy, which can block profitable model releases deemed unsafe. Claude is available via chat and API, enabling programmatic agent architectures.

Threat Intelligence Foundations

He frames threat intelligence as reducing the defender's information asymmetry—illuminating attacker location and capabilities so defenses can be reoriented efficiently, using a fog-of-war metaphor around organizational assets.

Market Limitations

A core problem is commercial threat-intelligence opacity: vendors sell one-size-fits-all feeds that break the tight collector-producer-customer cycle found in government intelligence. The talk proposes exploring agentic AI to build organization-specific intelligence, though the available transcript ends during this problem framing before solution details.

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK - Security Onion: Scaling SIEM
talks.teaser: P. Srisawang explores #OOTB2025BKK - Security Onion: Scaling SIEM.
talks.summary:
Team and Project Context

Thai researchers from a former APP/network lab describe over a year customizing open-source Security Onion 2.3 for enterprise SIEM scale, emphasizing engineering lessons rather than sensitive customer data.

Why Open-Source SIEM

They chose open SIEM for lower license costs, customization freedom, code transparency, community support, and horizontal scaling on Elasticsearch-style stacks as log volume grows.

Tradeoffs and Security Onion Choice

Open platforms demand skilled staff, lack vendor SLAs, and may need custom features. Security Onion was selected for its all-in-one network and endpoint visibility plus active community, with a disclaimer that commercial Security Onion Pro exists.

Enterprise Enhancements

The case study covers performance tuning, custom development to fill enterprise gaps, and ongoing challenges when building production-grade detection on open tooling.

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK Agentic ProbLLMs: Exploiting Al Computer-Use And Coding Agents
talks.teaser: Johann Rehberger analyzes #OOTB2025BKK Agentic ProbLLMs: Exploiting Al Computer-Use And Coding Agents.
talks.summary:
Speaker

Johan (EA red team director; independent researcher) introduces Agentic ProbLLMs, demonstrating LLM brittleness—models misclassifying images and answering 1+1 incorrectly under adversarial conditions.

Threat taxonomy

He layers risks from bad prompting and misalignment through jailbreaking to prompt injection, where third parties control inference inputs (web pages, uploads), impacting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Persistent compromise demo

Building on prior Trust No AI work, he showed ChatGPT memory weaponized via attacker-controlled content: infections persist in long-term memory, poll GitHub for C2 instructions, alter behavior across sessions, invoke tools, and exfiltrate data—partially mitigated recently for image-based exfiltration.

Agents

Defining agents as software that perceives, reasons, decides, and acts autonomously, he links them to Boyd's OODA loop and warns computer-use/coding agents amplify prompt-injection impact when adversaries influence the agent loop.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Johann Rehberger, red team director at Electronic Arts and author of the paper "Trust No AI," presents research on the vulnerability of agentic AI systems, specifically computer-use and autonomous coding agents. The talk investigates how adversaries exploit the reasoning-action (ReAct / OODA) loop using prompt injection delivered via untrusted third-party content like web pages, documents, and GitHub issues. Rehberger demonstrates real-world exploit chains across ChatGPT Operator, Anthropic Claude Computer Use, Devin, and Google Jules that achieve persistent command-and-control, data exfiltration, and unauthorized local command execution.

Key Topics:
- Prompt injection threat hierarchy (bad prompting, misalignment, jailbreaking, third-party prompt injection)
- Persistent LLM command-and-control and data exfiltration via memory and storage bypasses
- Exploiting computer-use agents (ChatGPT Operator, Claude Computer Use) for data theft and command execution
- Attacking autonomous coding agents (Devin, Google Jules) via multi-stage prompt injection and tool invocation

Technical Details:
Rehberger outlines the prompt injection threat spectrum, emphasizing that indirect prompt injection fundamentally compromises confidentiality, integrity, and availability. He demonstrates persistent C2 inside ChatGPT by injecting malicious instructions via a GitHub issue into ChatGPT's long-term memory. Across subsequent user sessions, the poisoned memory instructed the model to fetch fresh commands from an attacker-controlled GitHub repository, update its identity, and execute unauthorized tools like image creation. To exfiltrate sensitive memory data despite OpenAI's URL-safe restrictions, he bypassed domain filters using allowed Azure blob storage domains (windows.net), triggering the model to render images with exfiltrated strings embedded in URL query parameters. Transitioning to computer-use agents, Rehberger targeted OpenAI's ChatGPT Operator. Despite Operator implementing safeguards like inline confirmations and warnings on sensitive websites, he tricked the agent via a malicious GitHub ticket into visiting authenticated user sessions (Hacker News and Booking.com), extracting private account details (email, address, phone number), and pasting them into a form on a deceptive "string combine" site functioning as an attacker keylogger.

The presentation further reveals remote system compromise using Anthropic's Claude Computer Use, Devin, and Google Jules. Pointing Claude to a webpage containing an injected directive to download and run a "support tool," the agent followed the link, downloaded a compiled Sliver C2 implant binary to the local filesystem, located it using bash, made it executable with chmod, and executed it to establish a live reverse shell. Rehberger adapted human social engineering into an "AI ClickFix" attack: a malicious webpage prompted the agent to click an "Are you a computer?" button, which copied an operating system command into the system clipboard via JavaScript; the agent was then directed to locate the terminal icon, paste the clipboard payload, and press Enter to spawn a calculator. In coding agents, Rehberger analyzed Devin's system prompt, noting developer attempts at "prompt begging" (instructing the model not to leak keys). He exploited an automated "expose port" capability (similar to ngrok) through a multi-stage prompt injection payload, causing Devin to expose an internal development port to the internet without human approval and exfiltrate the generated access URL.

Key Takeaways:
Deploying computer-use and coding agents introduces critical attack surfaces that cannot be reliably mitigated through prompt-level defenses or model alignment alone. Sandboxing remains mandatory but insufficient if agents have direct access to local secrets, API keys, source code, or internal network interfaces. Security teams must implement strict human-in-the-loop validation for high-risk actions—such as executing downloaded binaries, opening local network tunnels, and transmitting authenticated session data to third-party endpoints. Organizations must continuously monitor agent terminal commands, browser actions, and outbound network traffic to detect hijacked execution loops.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK - The Power Of Powerlogs
talks.teaser: Sarah Edwards investigates #OOTB2025BKK - The Power Of Powerlogs.
talks.summary:
## Apple Powerlogs Overview

Sarah Edwards of iVerify presents "The Power of Powerlogs" at Hack in the Box Bangkok, exploring Apple's Powerlog database—a rich telemetry source for digital forensics and incident response on macOS, iOS, and related devices. Though her day job focuses on mobile EDR against mercenary spyware like Pegasus, this talk targets DFIR practitioners.

## Where Powerlogs Live

Powerlogs reside under BatteryLife directories on Mac and iOS filesystems. Current logs are actively written; archived copies may appear depending on acquisition method, offering days of historical device-activity data often overlooked in investigations.

## Forensic Value

The database records application usage, screen state, connectivity, and peripheral interactions at granular timestamps. Edwards demonstrates correlating user behavior, background process activity, and system events—material that can substantiate or refute alibis, timeline reconstruction, and compromise indicators on Apple ecosystems.

## Collection Requirements

macOS, iOS, and visionOS support stock-device collection; Apple TV, HomePod, and Apple Watch may need developer profiles installed via paired devices. Edwards references sysdiagnose bundles containing complementary debug artifacts. The database's depth warrants dedicated study beyond a single conference session.

talks.title: #OOTB2025BKK Updates On Public Key Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Covers shorter TLS lifetimes, automation, and certificate transparency for limiting PKI compromise and aiding incident response.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames public-key infrastructure as everyday internet plumbing that still shapes how long a stolen or misissued key can hurt an organization. Historically, multi-year certificate lifetimes meant that a breached certificate authority could keep signing rogue names for months while revocation channels lagged.

The DigiNotar case anchors the argument: a compromised intermediate key led to a wildcard Google certificate, man-in-the-middle use in Iran, and a drawn-out revocation timeline that helped destroy the CA. Industry responses included perfect forward secrecy, free automated issuance through ACME clients such as Certbot and Let's Encrypt, shrinking lifetimes from years toward 90 days, cab-forum movement toward 47 days, and experimental six-day certificates. The speaker argues that lifetimes under about ten days shrink attacker opportunity and reduce dependence on flaky OCSP and CRL workflows when keys are exposed, but only if renewal is automated rather than manual.

Later sections tour operational tooling: modern certificate transparency backends, using CT data to spot forgotten assets, look-alike domains, and vendor-issued names, ACME renewal information for staggered mass revocations, and ACME profiles to mix classic and short-lived policies. Internal PKI guidance stresses visibility, key backup and rotation, cloud or token-based alternatives to traditional hardware security modules, and ACME-friendly internal CAs. Practitioners are urged to treat TLS automation and CT monitoring as core security engineering habits, not optional web admin chores.

talks.title: #HITB2024BKK #COMMSEC D2: BadUSB Attacks on MacOS: Beyond Using the Terminal and Shell Commands
talks.teaser: Shows a macOS BadUSB chain that avoids Terminal, using Script Editor and AppleScript to plant a persistent implant.
talks.summary:
BadUSB devices pose as keyboards and type prewritten keystrokes into unattended computers. Most public macOS examples open Terminal through Spotlight and run shell commands, which can hijack a colleague's open session and is easy for monitoring to flag. The speaker shows an alternative that runs through Script Editor, using AppleScript and its Objective C bridge to run JavaScript for Automation code.

A spoofed Mac keyboard device ID gets past the keyboard restriction prompt on Apple silicon machines, and Spotlight opens Script Editor. A short loader fetches the main payload from a remote host and evaluates it, keeping typed characters to a minimum and letting the payload change without reflashing the device. Native Objective C classes replace curl for the download, and the binary is made executable. A launch agent plist goes into the user's LaunchAgents folder, which may need creating first. The implant is started directly rather than through launchd, so it will not be revived if it dies before the next login. Discarding the draft with a keyboard shortcut closes the editor; the discard shortcut first failed because the key registered as backspace, so it was changed. In the live demo the callback arrived around 12 seconds after the button press.

For defenders, the speaker suggests asking whether Script Editor is needed, and restricting it through device management if not. Alerting on the app launch alone would create many false positives, so detections should target ad hoc signed binaries and file creation in LaunchAgents or other persistence-like locations, filtered to events from Script Editor. Remapping the default Spotlight shortcut could also break attacks that assume Command plus Space.

talks.title: #HITB2024BKK #COMMSEC D2: Exploring Vulnerabilities in Flutter Mobile Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how hardcoded secrets in Flutter Android apps can be pulled out through reverse engineering and used against backends.
talks.summary:
Flutter lets developers write one Dart codebase and ship it to several platforms, which has made it popular for consumer apps. This research focused on Flutter apps on Android. The researcher bulk-downloaded roughly 1,000 apps from a third-party APK site, then flagged the Flutter ones by checking for the Flutter engine library in the native libraries. That left 228 Flutter apps, which were reverse engineered with blutter to recover the Dart assemblies and the static and global data dumps.

The dumps and assemblies were then scanned with gitleaks and with keyword searches for terms such as API key, secret, password, Firebase and HTTP. Across the 228 apps, the work turned up six passwords, four private keys, 61 API keys, 19 access tokens and 121 API endpoints. Four case studies showed how these findings became real access. In a trophy-tracking app, a hardcoded Stripe secret key allowed command-line queries for charges, customer address and card details, and the account balance. In a football coaching app, a private key header was traced through the assemblies to a file in the Flutter assets that held the full key. In a diet tracking app, a JWT led to a Supabase backend, which revealed the data structure and plugins in use. In an IoT device app from a disclosure program, an AWS access key was tied to an encrypted secret file, and the secret was recovered by calling the relevant client function with a Frida script. The key then allowed identity queries and access to the app's S3 bucket.

The main takeaway is that Flutter binaries give up embedded credentials easily once tooling exists to parse them. Developers should keep secrets such as payment keys, cloud credentials and signing keys on the server side rather than shipping them inside the app.

talks.title: #HITB2024BKK #COMMSEC D2: TPMs and the Linux Kernel: A Better Path to Hardware Security
talks.teaser: Explains how Linux kernel keyrings can expose TPM-backed keys to applications without TPM stacks or exposed key material.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why application developers rarely use the TPM, a small, inexpensive security chip found in most laptops and servers. Using it from user space means choosing between incompatible software stacks, working with a resource manager, and dealing with device permissions that block non-root users by default. The speaker then turns to the Linux kernel key retention service, which keeps keys as kernel objects with their own permissions and lifetimes. A live demo showed two users sharing a secret through a keyring. The talk compared key types: user keys expose plaintext to the calling process, logon keys cannot be read back, and TPM-wrapped trusted keys are unwrapped only inside the kernel. Pairing wrapped keys with the kernel crypto API lets a process encrypt data through a socket without seeing the key, a feature available since Linux 6.2 but limited to symmetric keys. Signing support was still pending upstream work at the time of the talk.

Wrapped keys need state kept somewhere, which clashes with stateless or disposable servers. The speaker proposed deriving keys from the TPM's device seed using application-specific input, so the same key can be regenerated after every reboot. A prototype request-key helper plugin derived keys based on the executable path, user ID, or an integrity checksum. The demo showed that deleting and re-requesting a key returned identical material, while moving the binary, running it as another user, or changing one byte produced a different key.

The main takeaway is that the kernel keyring can act as an abstraction layer, so applications avoid TPM libraries and permission setup. The speaker proposed a kernel patch for derived keys and asked the audience whether such a feature would be useful. TPM 1.2 devices are not supported by the kernel resource manager.

talks.title: #HITB2024BKK #COMMSEC D2: Breaking Fake Voice Detection with Speaker-Irrelative Features
talks.teaser: Explains how fake-voice detectors can be fooled by silence and background noise, and how an adversarial attack exploits that.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with how machine-generated speech, from text-to-speech and voice conversion, has become hard for people to tell apart from real voices. The presenters sort existing fake-voice detectors into feature-based, image-based, end-to-end and neural approaches, and report that several published results are hard to reproduce. Their core claim is that detectors rely on speaker-irrelative cues such as leading and trailing silence and background noise rather than on the speech itself.

To test this, they switched the language of test audio, which changed the results of three detectors by more than 15 percent, and removed silence, which changed them sharply. They then present an attack that searches for noise and time perturbations, mixing background noise into a fake clip and padding its start and end with silence, and updates those parameters from the detector's output score. Against four detectors the attack achieved high success rates, and an ablation showed that both perturbation types contribute. Retraining detectors on data with silence or noise removed showed the largest drop when silence was removed.

A live demo generated a clip with a TTS service, showed a detector flagging it as fake, and then showed the perturbed version labelled as real. The takeaway for practitioners is that detectors may be learning dataset artifacts instead of essential differences between genuine and synthetic speech, so robustness tests should include non-speech features. Code and data were said to be available online.

talks.title: #HITB2024BKK #COMMSEC D1: CoralRaider Targets Victims Data and Social Media Accounts
talks.teaser: A threat research briefing details CoralRaider's staged infostealer attacks, credential theft, and social media hijacking.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces CoralRaider, a Vietnam-linked cybercrime group active since 2023 and tracked as UTG-Q007, whose operators steal credentials, financial data, and hijack social media accounts for profit. Victims span Asia and other regions, with infection often starting from customized malicious shortcut files and multi-stage chains that blend PowerShell, HTA loading, and detection evasion tricks such as substituting executable names.

Two campaigns are dissected in depth. The first, from late 2023 into early 2024, chains PowerShell staging, anti-analysis checks, a CurVer registry UAC bypass through fodhelper, and custom payloads including RotBot and XClient stealer. Exfiltration leans on Google-hosted dead drops and Telegram bots, with XClient targeting browsers plus Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok via platform APIs. The second campaign, active into 2024, reuses much of the same flow but adds heavy obfuscation, CDN-hosted downloads, and commodity stealers such as CryptBot, customized Lumma C2, and Remcos loaded through a Python-based BSR injector.

The speakers link both operations to one team through shared infection logic, overlapping decryptor and downloader scripts, and attribution clues from Telegram bots, binary strings, and host indicators tied to Vietnam. They close with case lessons on incident visibility, credential resets after infostealer wins, and the expectation of faster, harder-to-detect credential theft as evasion improves.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 - How I Learned To Stop Reversing And Love The Strings
talks.teaser: Paolo Montesel details #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 - How I Learned To Stop Reversing And Love The Strings.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Paolo (known online as babush) presents "Big Match," a research proof-of-concept developed to identify open-source libraries embedded inside compiled binaries by leveraging extracted strings. Reverse engineers frequently spend days analyzing proprietary binaries only to realize they are analyzing open-source code linked statically into the target. Because manual string searches using standard search engines or code search tools can be noisy, fail due to nested static libraries, or omit parent packages, Big Match automates binary identification by matching binary strings against a massive database of GitHub C/C++ repositories without relying on machine learning.

### Key Topics
- **The Pitfalls of Manual Reverse Engineering:** Relying on ad-hoc string searching often misleads analysts when static linking nests one library inside an outer framework (for instance, identifying libsrtp within a VoIP binary while missing pjsip).
- **Dataset Construction via GHTorrent:** Utilizing GHTorrent dumps (specifically MongoDB exports processed with PyMongo) to access GitHub repository metadata, stars, and commit histories without hitting clone bandwidth limits.
- **Repository Deduplication Challenges:** Filtering forks and duplicate projects across thousands of repositories. The speaker discusses graph traversal edge cases, such as the `octocat/Spoon-Knife` tutorial repository being merged into the commit history of `LibreCAD`.
- **Vector Space Information Retrieval:** Treating extracted string hashes as terms and repositories as documents using TF-IDF weighting and cosine similarity.
- **Clustering Search Results:** Using spectral co-clustering to isolate distinct libraries present together in a single binary instead of returning redundant forks of the first match.

### Technical Details
- **String Extraction & Filtering:** Repositories were scanned using `ripgrep`, followed by custom Python string de-escaping and hashing. Common boilerplate strings degraded matching accuracy; empirical analysis showed that pruning the top 10,000 most frequent strings (such as generic error messages) substantially improved results while preserving useful signatures like `GIF89a`.
- **Data Pipeline:** The ETL pipeline was built largely using Bash scripts and standard Unix utilities, which provided surprisingly fast execution (building the search database in approximately one day).
- **Secondary Deduplication:** To address excessive RAM consumption (averaging 40 KB of RAM per repo and 23,000 strings per repo), repos of similar zip file sizes were unpacked and deduplicated using Jaccard similarity thresholds, stripping thousands of Linux and Android forks.
- **Search Execution:** In the web demo, client-side JavaScript extracts strings from uploaded binaries, hashes them, and submits them to the server. The engine runs a matrix multiplication of query vectors against the repository matrix, followed by spectral co-clustering to display top matching independent libraries.

### Takeaways
- Exact string hash matching provides an effective, privacy-preserving, 0% machine learning mechanism to identify open-source components, as the server only receives string hashes rather than proprietary binary files.
- The approach works reliably when target binaries contain distinctive strings and can be extended to magic numbers, version range detection, monorepo dependency audits, and malware classification.
- Future directions include integrating string matching directly into decompiler plugins (such as rev.ng) to enable function-level string matching and automatic symbol renaming.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 LAB - Automated Incident Response
talks.teaser: Valentine Mairet explores #HITB2023HKT #COMMSEC D1 LAB - Automated Incident Response.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this workshop session at Hack in the Box (HITB), speakers Valentine (Val) and Harjit from the GitLab Security Incident Response Team (SIRT) share how their globally distributed team automates end-to-end incident response workflows. Operating across APAC, EMEA, and Americas regions, the team uses automation to ensure 24/7 service continuity, combat alert fatigue, standardize triage and documentation, and generate operational metrics to justify team headcount.

### Key Topics
- **Broader Scope of IR Automation:** Automation extends far beyond investigation log dives; it encompasses detection engineering, alerting pipelines, incident management, handovers, documentation, and metrics generation.
- **Detection as Code & Deployment Pipelines:** Managing detections in GitLab repositories with review processes, standardized formatting checks via CI/CD pipelines, and automatic deployment to their SIEM (Devo).
- **User Attestation Module (UAM):** Automated outreach via Slack bots to prompt users when high-risk events occur (e.g., Personal Access Token creation). Alerts auto-escalate if unacknowledged within a set timeframe (such as one hour).
- **Shift Handovers with "Hogi":** Maintaining continuity across time zones through automated asynchronous handovers and sync issue creation in GitLab.
- **GUARD Architecture:** The GitLab Universal Automated Response and Detection system, which ties together SIEM alerts, Slack interactions, Tines automation workflows, and a custom metric database (metricDB).

### Technical Details
- **Tool Ecosystem:** GitLab acts as the single source of truth for issues, documentation, and CI/CD pipelines; Devo functions as the SIEM; Slack provides an interactive chat interface for engineers; and Tines serves as the no-code SOAR platform orchestrating actions.
- **Alert Lifecycle in Slack:** When a Devo alert fires into Tines, Tines enriches the event with metricDB data and threat intelligence before presenting an interactive Slack prompt. Engineers can acknowledge, reassign, convert to an incident issue, or close the alert while logging qualitative feedback (sentiment analysis and relevance scores).
- **Practical Lab Execution ("Tokenheimer"):** Participants constructed a workflow integrating a Slack slash command (`/nuke`) via a webhook into Tines. Tines extracted the token parameter from `web_hook.body.text` and executed an HTTP DELETE request against the GitLab API self endpoint (`/personal_access_tokens` / self API) to immediately revoke exposed credentials. In advanced exercises, attendees added GET queries against the `/users` endpoint to determine username and permission scopes before revocation.

### Takeaways
- Standardizing and automating operational workflows allows small, understaffed security teams to scale consistently without manual overhead.
- Capturing metrics directly during alert triage (true/false positive rates, engineer sentiment) provides data necessary to tune noisy detections and justify organizational resources.
- High-risk manual actions can be safely accelerated by blending interactive user attestation with automated fallbacks.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT CLOSING KEYNOTE - Systems Alchemy: The Transmutation Of Hacking - The Grugq
talks.teaser: Explains how attackers scale weak primitives into system-wide disruption by exploiting incentives, fallible sensors, and corporate policy.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the September 2022 Yandex Taxi incident in Moscow, where attackers used a minimal capability—ordering rides—to send hundreds of drivers to one address at once. The speaker argues that debates over whether that was a “real” hack miss the point: the socio-technical taxi network (apps, backend, drivers, penalties for canceling) was manipulated as a whole, turning a lame primitive into large-scale gridlock.

From there the talk generalizes how complex systems fail through limited “sensory organs,” illustrated with fallible facial recognition and retrospective lessons from failed lunar landers and single-sensor aircraft design. It extends to the physics of cyberspace: private firms reshape operational reality through product and corporate policy, citing post-2016 Facebook rule changes, Ukrainian carriers severing links to Russia, and who can realistically pressure hyperscale platforms.

The close examines autonomous vehicles and robotaxis in human environments—crime-scene tape, fire lanes, vomiting passengers, and “coning” that halts cars until staff intervene—plus city complaints and recurring breakdown hotspots. The takeaway is that reality outruns rule sets, systems rarely adapt to people, and defenders and attackers both benefit from thinking in whole-system terms rather than isolated bugs.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Take A Picture Of Your App Code: Android MRI Interpreter
talks.teaser: SungHyoun Song examines #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Take A Picture Of Your App Code: Android MRI Interpreter.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, San, a mobile security researcher at the Financial Security Institute (FSI) in South Korea, introduces the "Android MRI Interpreter"—a customized runtime and kernel-level analysis environment designed to inspect Android application execution and bypass Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) mechanisms without patching app binaries or using detectable user-space hooking tools.

Drawing an analogy to medical imaging, the speaker compares traditional penetration testing tools (like ptrace, Frida, and IDA Pro) to invasive surgery with a scalpel, which triggers application defense mechanisms and requires significant time to bypass. In contrast, the Android MRI Interpreter functions like an MRI scanner, observing internal behavior non-invasively at the operating system and interpreter level.

### Key Topics
- **ART Execution Flow Modification**: Android applications mix Dalvik bytecode, ahead-of-time (AOT) compiled native code, and just-in-time (JIT) compiled code across cold, warm, and hot execution states. Because optimized native code is difficult to reverse-engineer dynamically, the speaker modified the Android Runtime (ART) code flow so that native execution requests are bypassed, forcing all execution through a custom interpreter.
- **Interpreter-Level Inspection**: By replacing standard ART interpreters (the switch interpreter and mterp) with the custom MRI interpreter, the system directly inspects Dalvik instructions, methods, program counters, and virtual register values stored in ART's `ShadowFrame` and `ManagedStack` objects without alerting user-space anti-tamper protections.
- **Taint Analysis and Call Graph Generation**: The interpreter traces target data (such as sensitive strings) across data manipulation and transfer instructions (e.g., `move`). By traversing historical frames on the managed stack, it reconstructs execution call graphs displaying where sensitive data originates (highlighted in red) and where it is subsequently propagated or used (highlighted in green), filtering out duplicate calls and dead code.
- **Stealthy RASP & Integrity Bypass**: To bypass anti-rooting checks, Google SafetyNet, and commercial RASP modules, changes were kept inside a custom kernel rather than modifying standard user-space Android Open Source Project (AOSP) frameworks. The kernel intercepts `/proc/cmdline` to report clean boot state parameters (`verifiedbootstate=green` instead of orange caused by OEM unlocking). A minimalist privilege escalation mechanism was also embedded directly into the kernel's `sys_execve` handler: invoking the standard, unmodified `/system/bin/sh` binary automatically assigns root credentials (`uid 0`, `gid 0`) without installing detectable user-space root binaries.

### Technical Details & Demonstration
To showcase the tool's effectiveness, the speaker analyzed a widely used messaging application ("watch"), focusing on its two-step verification PIN handling. After configuring the target application's UID and the test PIN string in a configuration file (`/data/local/tmp` via BusyBox):
- **Instruction and Register Logging**: Real-time logging captured the function names, Dalvik instructions, and virtual registers when the six-digit PIN was processed.
- **Call Graph Inspection**: Mode 3 graph generation traced the PIN's lifecycle across app restarts, discovering that the PIN was persistently stored and decrypted via Android default decryption functions from `SharedPreferences` upon each app launch.
- **Target Function Tracing**: Using the identified method name, the tool focused execution tracing on specific internal functions, proving unnecessary memory exposure of the credential without triggering the messenger's rooted environment restrictions.

### Takeaways
Instrumenting the runtime interpreter and performing stealthy kernel patches provides deep dynamic visibility while completely evading user-space RASP defenses. When asked how developers can protect sensitive credentials from this level of memory tracing, the speaker recommended avoiding immutable string objects (which persist in memory) in favor of byte arrays or raw pointers that can be explicitly wiped or overwritten immediately after use.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T1 - Hacking Into IOS’s VOLTE Implementation
talks.teaser: Rajanish Pathak details #HITB2023HKT D2T1 - Hacking Into IOS’s VOLTE Implementation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researchers Hardik and Rajneesh detail an architectural and implementation flaw in Apple's Voice over LTE (VoLTE) stack. The vulnerability affected iOS releases prior to 15.1, as well as iPadOS and watchOS, allowing attackers within a cellular carrier's network to directly reach and attack millions of Apple devices without routing through or being logged by standard telecom billing and call-inspection infrastructure.

### Key Topics
- **VoLTE & IMS Architecture**: VoLTE routes voice traffic as data over IP Multimedia Subsystems (IMS) and the Evolved Packet Core (EPC). Handsets establish an Access Point Name (APN) specifically for IMS, initiating registration via SIP over UDP port 5060 before establishing an authenticated IPsec tunnel to the core.
- **3GPP/GSMA Specification Deviation**: Standard 3GPP and GSMA guidelines stipulate that once an IPsec tunnel is negotiated between the User Equipment (UE) and the IMS core (P-CSCF), the UE must terminate or close the listening socket on unencrypted port 5060.
- **Direct Device Exposure**: In iOS's implementation (specifically within the `CommCenter` framework and `libIPTelephony`), port 5060 remained open and listening on interface `pdp_ip1` even after IPsec establishment. Furthermore, lack of strict traffic segregation at the carrier P-CSCF level allowed arbitrary devices to communicate peer-to-peer over the IMS APN.

### Technical Details
- **Test Bed Setup**: The researchers reproduced the issue in a lab environment using Open5GS (simulating RAN/EPC), Kamailio (simulating the IMS SIP server), USRP and BladeRF Software Defined Radios (SDRs) acting as eNodeB/gNodeB base stations, ISIM test cards, Android test devices, and iPhones.
- **Reconnaissance & Enumeration**: By scanning IP ranges allocated to the carrier's IMS APN via tools like Nmap, the researchers found that only iOS devices responded on port 5060, revealing millions of vulnerable endpoints. Testing against Android devices (Samsung, Google Pixel) showed that Android correctly closes port 5060 once the IPsec tunnel is active.
- **Exploitation & Impact**:
  - **Caller ID Spoofing & Ringing**: Unauthenticated, crafted SIP `INVITE` packets sent directly to target IP addresses triggered the native incoming call screen and rang devices without legitimate telecom routing or billing records.
  - **PII Leakage**: Device responses exposed device identities, exact iOS versions, phone numbers (MSISDN), IMEI numbers, and potential IMSI exposure.
  - **Denial of Service (DoS) & Fuzzing**: Direct SIP traffic floods could tie up the telephony daemon, prevent legitimate incoming and outgoing calls, and expose low-level telephony parsing libraries to direct network-level fuzzing.

### Takeaways & Mitigation
Following initial disclosure in March 2021, an early fix attempt by Apple was bypassed, leading to an effective resolution in iOS 15.2 by properly closing socket port 5060 and strictly accepting SIP communication exclusively over the established IPsec tunnel. The researchers emphasized that adhering to core telecom standards is critical, as minor implementation deviations in foundational protocols can leave millions of endpoints exposed to remote, unauthenticated attacks.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Breaking MPC Wallets And Digital Custodians
talks.teaser: Details how flaws in zero-knowledge proofs in TSS libraries let one malicious party extract private keys from MPC wallets.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at threshold signature schemes (TSS) built on the GG18 and GG20 ECDSA protocols, which let several parties jointly produce a signature without any single party rebuilding the private key. The speakers walk through the MtA sub-protocol and the range proofs and discrete-log proofs that protect it, and explain how those proofs can be forged once an implementation is flawed.

They present three attacks on these proofs. Alpha shuffle exploits an ambiguous value encoding that a 2019 audit fix did not fully resolve. C split abuses a larger challenge space used without repeated proof iterations. C gas relies on too few iterations, so a cheating prover can guess the challenge. Each attack lets a single malicious party recover the private key without the protocol aborting. The speakers reported that most of the open-source implementations they examined were affected, and that several were used in production wallets, custodians and bridges. Live demos showed key recovery against a few libraries, including a swap-network test where they estimated 180 million dollars would have been at risk.

The takeaway is that new cryptographic protocols are hard to implement correctly, and optimizations that drop or weaken proofs can silently undermine security. Developers should rely on audited code, since the protocol still lacks a standard library. In the Q&A, the speakers noted that vendors often patch after audits, and that the state of closed-source implementations is unknown.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Breaking ML Services: Finding 0-days In Azure Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Nitesh Surana investigates #HITB2023HKT D2T2 - Breaking ML Services: Finding 0-days In Azure Machine Learning.
talks.summary:
This talk presents security research into Azure Machine Learning (AML) service, discovering multiple critical vulnerabilities in cloud-based ML infrastructure. The speaker, Nes from Trend Micro, structured findings across four chapters of investigation.

**Overview and Motivation**
The research began after observing a pattern of Jupyter Notebook-based service vulnerabilities across major cloud providers. The speaker investigated Azure Machine Learning—a widely-deployed ML-as-a-service platform underlying Microsoft's cognitive and applied AI services—revealing multiple classes of credential exposure and authentication bypass issues.

**Key Vulnerabilities Found**

1. **Credential Logging in Clear Text**: Storage account primary access keys appeared in Azure Batch startup task error logs and authorization logs. These credentials were also stored as environment variables (named PASWD) in agent configuration files, accessible because the default azure-user has sudo privileges without password requirement.

2. **JWT Token Exposure**: User authentication tokens appeared in URL parameters during Jupyter terminal requests and were logged in plain text in nginx access logs. These tokens could be captured via network traffic inspection and belonged to the compute instance owner.

3. **Network-Adjacent Information Disclosure (mlc)**: The DSi Mount Agent running as root exposed an unauthenticated API on port 46802 within virtual networks. Network-adjacent attackers could enumerate installed services and access their logs, including commands executed via sudo that contained embedded credentials for mounting file shares.

4. **Managed Identity Token Extraction from Non-Azure Environments**: The speaker demonstrated that certificate and private key files from compute instances, combined with environment variable configurations, enabled extraction of Azure AD tokens for managed identities from outside Azure environments. This contradicted documented design principles stating only Azure resources should fetch such tokens. Both system-assigned and user-assigned managed identity tokens were obtainable.

5. **Persistent Storage Account Access After Key Rotation**: Even after rotating storage account keys, attackers possessing the certificate, private key, and environment files could continue accessing workspace secrets. The workspace automatically synchronizes new keys, making traditional rotation ineffective against this threat model.

**Technical Architecture Details**
Compute instances are managed Ubuntu VMs in Microsoft subscriptions running multiple agents for mounting, monitoring, and identity management. Authentication flows through Azure Active Directory to generate ARM tokens, subsequently generating AML tokens. Data stores use credential-based authentication (storage account name plus primary key) to mount Azure File Shares across all compute instances by design. The nginx proxy on port 44224 handles incoming requests and forwards them based on the XMS-Target-Port header without logging sensitive information.

**Compromise Chain and Risk Model**
The speaker presented a scenario where a single compute instance breach could expose: other users' notebooks and scripts (stored in shared file shares by design), storage account credentials enabling full workspace access, managed identity tokens for lateral movement, and audit trails that appear identical for legitimate and malicious access patterns.

**Research Attempts Without Finding Exploitable Vulnerabilities**
The speaker also explored container escape in Azure Jobs, cross-tenant scenarios, dependency confusion attacks, and Jupiter implementation misconfigurations (beyond JWT logging) without discovering additional vulnerabilities.

**Microsoft's Remediation**
Addressed issues included masking credentials in logged commands, preventing JWT tokens from reaching compute instances, restricting DSi Mount Agent port exposure through nginx proxy and certificate verification, and implementing additional authentication requirements.

**Key Recommendations**
Deploy through virtual networks and private endpoints, enable comprehensive cloud logging and monitoring, scope managed identities to least privilege principles, monitor for unauthorized certificate usage, implement threat modeling for cloud environments using frameworks like Atlas for AI systems, and follow defense-in-depth strategies acknowledging the shared responsibility model.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D1T1 - Analyzing And Reverse Engineering Antivirus Signatures
talks.teaser: Explains how antivirus byte signatures can be reversed to locate detected matches and break them in red team tools.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how antivirus products decide that a file is malicious. Most signatures are byte strings combined with and/or logic, similar to YARA rules. The speaker explains why this matters to red teams, since common tools such as Mimikatz or Cobalt Strike get removed once detected, and reviews usual workarounds such as recompiling, packing and loader-based encryption.

To study signatures, the speaker presents AV Red, a tool forked from an earlier AV debugger project. It uses a divide-and-conquer reducer that asks an antivirus, reached through AMSI, whether a modified file is still detected, which isolates the matching bytes. A verifier then overwrites each match to classify signatures as dominant, gray or robust. Tests against Defender, AVG and Avira showed wide variation. Many samples had one dominant match that was easy to change, while Cobalt Strike samples were mostly robust. The tool also annotates matches inside PE code and data, .NET methods and Word VBA macros. Roughly half of the PE matches fell in code, while .NET matches were mostly in data. Defender results also depended on cloud-delivered protection, which seemed active only for files downloaded through Chrome or Edge.

The speaker then tried to break signatures without changing behaviour, such as swapping independent instructions or altering the .NET max stack size. This worked for some files but not reliably. The takeaway is that signature quality differs widely between products and tools. Practitioners should expect a dominant match to be simple to alter, while signature authors defending long-lived red team tools should invest in robust signatures.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT D1T2 - Lazarus Group’s Undercover Operations 2022–2023
talks.teaser: Traces a Lazarus watering-hole campaign that abused Korean financial security software and the malware it dropped.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a campaign attributed to the Lazarus group during 2022 and 2023 that targeted a South Korean financial security software developer. The attackers first stole source code from that vendor, then used it to find a zero-day flaw. They set up a watering-hole on a news site that checked visitors' IP addresses against the target's range, so only staff at the victim organization received the exploit. The exploit then triggered a financial security module on their PCs and pulled down a payload.

The presenters described how investigators traced about 60 affected organizations through web-based command-and-control servers and firewall logs. One infected machine sat on a network segment that had been opened to the internet for work needs. Inside the network, the group used a second vulnerability in a security program to spread laterally, kept persistence through registry entries, harvested credentials, and deployed IIS web servers as internal command-and-control points. Privilege escalation relied on a Print Nightmare flaw, and proxies hid the attacker's address.

The malware analysis covered four samples acting as loaders and remote-access tools. Configuration data in the registry had moved from RC5 to AES encryption, and one sample used DLL side-loading. The speakers linked the campaign to earlier clusters, including Operation Book Code and Dream Job, through shared code and infrastructure. The takeaway is that financial software patching lags because of vendor verification, so vulnerable versions can stay on user machines long after a fix exists, and unusual activity from security modules is a useful signal.

talks.title: #HITB2023HKT KEYNOTE - Embracing Failure To Be A Better Hacker (and Human)
talks.teaser: Shares a veteran hardware hacker's missteps, from a missing bypass capacitor to a failed chip rework, and what each taught.
talks.summary:
Joe Grand, a hardware hacker, opens by arguing that talks usually highlight successful exploits, while the stumbles along the way teach more. He traces his path from teenage phone-line experiments to The Loft, a small hacker group that later became a consulting firm. He says the shift to commercial work strained friendships, including the case of a member who was let go after being moved into marketing.

The middle of the talk walks through hardware missteps in roughly chronological order. A medical infusion pump design review exposed a missing bypass capacitor, which senior colleagues helped him fix. A Defcon badge's capacitive buttons failed because he had overlooked a voltage requirement, so he added a second battery holder. A walking robot prototype for a television show was underdesigned and ran over budget, and it stood but never walked. Probing a rental electric car's infotainment unit while it rested on a pillow ended with a torn flex cable. An RFID reader took years to troubleshoot until a single capacitor change reduced antenna noise. Fault injection on a hardware wallet was undermined by a forgotten ground clip, and a package-on-package memory chip shifted during removal, causing shorts, until a specialist reballed it.

His takeaways are to ask questions before joining a project, check basics such as grounding and documentation, trust your instincts, and avoid blaming yourself for every mistake. Mentors and peers who explain problems without ridicule matter. He closes by arguing that learning comes from reflecting on failures rather than avoiding them.

talks.title: #HITB2023AMS #COMMSEC D2 - The Return Of Stack Overflows In The Linux Kernel
talks.teaser: Shows how an nftables stack overflow in the Linux kernel can be turned into a privilege escalation despite modern mitigations.
talks.summary:
The talk examines recent Linux kernel bugs that involve stack overflows and explains why they are hard to exploit. Stack canaries, guard pages between kernel stacks, KASLR, KPTI, SMAP and per-syscall stack offset randomization each close off a simple route. The speaker groups recent vulnerabilities by class and component, noting Netfilter, KVM and BPF as the main components. A TIPC overflow from an earlier conference is used as a starting point, since it is strong but cannot easily overwrite the return address.

The core case study is an nftables bug in Netfilter where a read primitive over register structures leaks kernel addresses. Because nftables hooks run in softirq context, they use a fresh static per-CPU stack, so per-syscall randomization does not apply there. A separate overflow, caused by a VLAN length miscalculation, copies up to 256 bytes into the registers, and the speaker duplicates the payload during that copy to gain room for a ROP chain. The exploit overrides the modprobe path through a user mode helper, avoids a user space payload, and exits softirq context without a panic.

For defenses, the speaker covers a static user mode helper configuration, kernel pointer authentication similar to ARMv8.3 PAC, and a per-softirq stack randomization prototype. The takeaway is that network stack overflows deserve another look, since developers often trust CAP_NET_ADMIN.

talks.title: #HITB2023AMS #COMMSEC D2 Red Wizard - A User-friendly Infrastructure For Red Teams
talks.teaser: Presents an open-source tool that automates deploying redirector and command-and-control infrastructure for red team engagements.
talks.summary:
Ben Brucker of Secura presents Red Wizard, an open-source tool his team released with this talk to automate red team infrastructure. Red team operations rely on command-and-control servers and disposable relays between the target and the backend, so burned relays must be replaced quickly. Building this by hand is slow and error-prone, and existing alternatives are often limited or opaque.

The tool combines Ansible for provisioning, Docker containers on the C2 host for services such as Go Phish and Cobalt Strike, and Python to generate the inventory. Deployment follows four steps: a global team configuration, a campaign configuration, an inventory of servers and components, and the deployment run. Relays link to the backend over OpenVPN, and only requests containing specific secret strings reach the real server; other visitors are redirected elsewhere. Admin access is limited to listed address ranges, and the tool exports key material and DNS settings for SPF, DKIM and DMARC so infrastructure can be rebuilt.

Users supply their own Ubuntu 20.04 servers reachable over SSH, which can be created with Terraform outside the tool. Ben noted the release omits proprietary components, malleable profiles and OPSEC patches. His advice is to prepare spare infrastructure ahead, since a deployment can take 20 to 40 minutes, and to keep a long-term Cobalt Strike callback beside a short-term one.

talks.title: #HITB2023AMS #COMMSEC D1 - Exploring JARM - An Active TLS Fingerprinting Algorithm
talks.teaser: Explains how the JARM active TLS fingerprinting algorithm works, how its hashes are built, and what they reveal about servers.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces JARM, an active TLS server fingerprinting method that Salesforce published in 2022, and contrasts it with passive approaches such as JA3 and JA3S, which the speaker says produce many false positives. Instead of only reading traffic, JARM sends ten crafted TLS client hello messages to a server. Each one varies the cipher suite order, the protocol version, the extensions and the ALPN values, and some include deliberately invalid or reserved values, so the speaker can observe how the server reacts.

The server's replies are parsed for the chosen cipher, the TLS version, the ALPN value and the list of extension types. The cipher and version parts are encoded as fuzzy hashes, the extension list is hashed with SHA-256 and truncated, and the pieces are joined into a 62-character fingerprint. The speaker walks through the encoding step by step and explains how the result can be reversed. He then presents examples: one malware server's fingerprint had no matches on popular sites, while many Cloudflare-fronted WordPress sites shared a single hash, and some widely shared hashes produced large result counts on VirusTotal that suggest false positives. Top-site data also showed weak or insecure cipher choices tied to particular hashes.

The main takeaway is that a JARM hash reflects a server's library, operating system and configuration, so it should be read with context rather than alone, and default setups can be recognised by their hash. The speaker also demonstrated his own C++ reimplementation, which can compute the final fingerprint from raw values and decode a hash back into its intermediate form.

talks.title: #HITB2023AMS #COMMSEC D1 - All You Always Wanted To Know About AntiViruses
talks.teaser: Dissects how antivirus products detect, whitelist, hook, quarantine and update, and why comparing their results can be unfair.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a computer science professor, argues that much criticism of antivirus products misses how they are built, which makes some comparisons unfair. Several products often share one underlying engine, so counting them as independent detectors inflates results. Many products also ship default allowlists that skip scanning certain files before any detection runs. In his signature experiments, roughly 30% to 40% of detections relied on signatures, with the rest coming from other mechanisms, and average signature sizes ranged from a few kilobytes to under 1 MB.

The talk then covered other design trade-offs. UPX detection varied: some products caught only the original samples, most also caught standard UPX builds but not a modified one, and only a few had unpackers built in. Products hook different numbers of functions, trading visibility against overhead. Network inspection via a proxy and a custom certificate was shown, quarantined files were encoded rather than encrypted, and a cache could be abused by a loader. Avast fetched definitions over plain HTTP, and installers lost a race against malware on infected systems. On Android, products mostly check reputation against allowlists.

The takeaways are that vendors should state their threat models, evaluations should cover more than detection rate, and machine learning works best as one layer in a larger pipeline, though it can be evaded. He invited researchers to close these gaps, especially for Android and back-end models.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN Information Collection Of Third-party SDKs - W. Kailong W. Zeyu B. Guangdong & Z. Qing
talks.teaser: Examines third-party mobile SDK privacy risks and delivers scaled taint-analysis methods with verified findings on undeclared data uploads.
talks.summary:
Mobile apps lean heavily on third-party SDKs, yet privacy law and OS permission dashboards still leave unclear what those libraries actually collect and send. The speakers outline why developers, vendors, and auditors each struggle: vague documentation, version drift, reflection and hidden APIs, encryption on the wire, and rules that appear only at runtime.

They compare common SDK audit styles—reverse engineering, network monitoring, policy review, hybrids, and API-call heuristics—and adopt large-scale static taint analysis. Sources are privacy-sensitive API data; sinks are client network send paths. They run Mariana Trench and AppShark over 211 SDKs from Google Play’s SDK index and Chinese stores, extend Mariana Trench for static-variable sources and asynchronous call flows, then manually confirm a subset.

Reported metrics include 92% precision, 88% recall, and an F-score of 0.9 on verified cases. About 19% to 20% of studied SDKs uploaded private data; IMEI and Android ID were especially common, along with IP, Wi‑Fi identifiers, GPS, and serial numbers. Case studies show location or Wi‑Fi data reaching network sinks without matching vendor disclosures, and some vendors with no policy at all. They notified vendors for 40-plus inconsistent SDKs, built a 200-plus SDK dataset, and plan to open-source their Mariana Trench changes.

talks.teaser: Traces ANGLE graphics bugs from WebKit's entry points to a Safari exploit built on a use-after-free.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at ANGLE, the layer that WebKit and Chrome use to translate OpenGL ES and WebGL calls into Direct3D, OpenGL or Metal on each platform. The speaker follows a WebGL drawArrays call from the JavaScript API through WebKit's graphics context into ANGLE's validation step and backend implementation, which is where the bugs of interest sit.

Four one-day vulnerabilities are walked through. A texture storage 3D call lacked checks on width, height and depth, allowing out-of-bounds reads and writes. A multi-draw extension did not check the sum of count and offset, causing a heap buffer overflow. Two use-after-free bugs came from deleted texture and transform feedback buffer objects still being used during drawArrays validation. Some of these also reproduced in Chrome, and the transform feedback case was chosen for a Safari exploit.

The exploit section covers reclaiming the freed object by spraying JavaScriptCore arrays so their butterfly memory lands in the freed slot, then corrupting an array's length to gain out-of-bounds access. From there the speaker builds a valid structure ID, then address-of and fake-object primitives. A live demo showed the primitive working and crashing the renderer, but not a full exploit chain. The takeaway is that GPU-facing browser code is a rich attack surface, since the GPU process needs more privileges and the graphics feature set keeps changing with each standard update.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN Suborner: Windows Bribery For Invisible Persistence
talks.teaser: Shows how writing account data straight into the Windows SAM hive can create hidden local accounts that evade standard creation logs.
talks.summary:
Sebastian Castro presents Suborner, a Windows persistence technique he released at Black Hat. He notes that common identity-manipulation tools can extract credentials, but none can craft a hidden local account. He walks through why the usual routes fail: creating a user with net user logs event 4720 and shows up in the account list, appending a dollar sign still logs the event, and calling the NetUserAdd API with a machine-account flag logs event 4741.

The method avoids the API entirely and writes the account directly into the SAM hive. The username goes into the V value, and the NTLM hash is converted into the SAM-stored form using keys derived from each system, with separate handling for Windows 10 1607 and later, which use AES rather than MD5. The RID in the F value is set to impersonate an existing account, building on his earlier RID hijacking research, and the account control bits mark it as a machine account. In a live demo against a fully updated Windows 11 machine, the new account authenticated and gave a remote high-privilege prompt, yet it did not appear in net user, the user manager, or the event log.

For defenders, he suggests monitoring SAM registry changes for accounts created outside the account APIs. Logons with the account are recorded under the impersonated identity, and machine accounts lack interactive and RDP logon, which reduces its usefulness in some cases. Microsoft treats it as a persistence technique rather than a vulnerability, and it does not apply to domain controllers. The takeaway is that an attacker who already has access can hide accounts from standard tooling, so auditing the SAM for unexpected entries matters.

talks.title: #HITB2022SIN Scripts-behavioral ML Classification Using Windows 10 AMSI-instrumentation
talks.teaser: Maps script and fileless threats to AMSI behavioral ML that stops obfuscated attacks on first execution in Defender.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how initial access has shifted from portable executables toward macros, zipped scripts, and in-memory fileless stages that evade disk-centric defenses. Obfuscated VBA and JavaScript examples, including Trickbot-style payloads, illustrate why static signatures fail when roughly ninety-six percent of script encounters are first-seen variants that change within hours.

AMSI is described as the runtime bridge: PowerShell compile-time scanning, JavaScript and VBScript COM behavior instrumentation, VBA macros, and WMI, with suspicious triggers sending content to the engine while other calls accumulate in a cyclic buffer. Microsoft Defender pairs lightweight on-box models with cloud verdicts fed by global prevalence, fuzzy hashes, and process context. The middle section walks through supervised classification at scale—petabyte telemetry, sandbox detonation, featurization from COM objects, methods, and parameter n-grams, L1-based trimming to about one thousand client features, and meta-labeling across time windows and similar hashes trained with LightGBM before logistic regression on clients and averaged perceptron in the cloud.

A Brazil-focused Trickbot banking chain demonstrates blocking at first sight of the malicious Word document before lateral spread. Practitioners should expect combined client-and-cloud ML, AMSI-aware features, and continuous retraining rather than per-obfuscator rules alone, while recognizing limits when AMSI or cloud reach is disabled.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio: Fireside Chat With Dhillon ‘L33tdawg’ Kannabhiran
talks.teaser: A wrap-up chat reflects on years of hosting the event, its volunteer crew and the community that keeps it going.
talks.summary:
In this closing session of the studio programme, two co-hosts sit down with guest Dhillon Kannabhiran to look back on the event's history. Kannabhiran recalls first crossing paths with the organisers around 2003 and attending events in Bahrain and Dubai in the mid-2000s. He says he keeps coming back because of the energy from volunteers, attendees and a growing number of younger participants.

Much of the conversation centres on hospitality and the people behind the event. Kannabhiran describes how the organisers treated speakers and guests, including a speaker who drove overland from France after flights were cancelled and still made it to the event. He argues that every person who helps, from those running network cables to the speakers themselves, plays a part that deserves respect. He also credits the Dutch and Malaysian crews and the CTF teams who take part, saying their work is what makes the show possible.

The session closes with practical information for remote viewers. Recordings are usually uploaded to the event's YouTube channel one to two weeks after the event ends, and the slides for each presentation are posted on the conference website. Updates are shared on Twitter, and the hosts ask viewers to follow the channels to find the links.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio: Fireside Chat With Nemo & Tim Murck from HackShield
talks.teaser: Explores free youth digital safety education that emphasizes curious mindsets, simple explanations, and tools to resist misinformation.
talks.summary:
A studio fireside conversation follows HackShield founders as they explain why they built Hack in the Class and how the program spreads basic digital protection skills beyond the Netherlands to Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Africa. They argue that parents and schools lack trusted teachers for phishing, passwords, cyberbullying, and the line between legal exploration and crime, while professional trainers often work only with people already in the field.

The middle of the discussion contrasts cramming volatile facts with building durable traits: questioning claims, checking alternatives, and understanding that every message has a source, author, and motive. They describe shielding children from fear narratives that paralyze learning, using approachable storytelling and an augmented-reality quest where players hunt misinformation in a library metaphor and challenge it with verified facts. Penetration-testing anecdotes illustrate how suspicion without guided practice wastes opportunity.

Closing themes urge the security community to stop blaming users and instead demonstrate attacker tricks in trusted settings so learners engage rather than freeze. They also reflect on shrinking privacy, the consequences of joining social platforms, and whether society can choose lighter digital consumption. The through-line is empowering young people to educate families and peers once they feel capable rather than helpless.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio: Fireside Chat With Barry "Fish_" Van Kampen
talks.teaser: Explains how Dutch police steer at-risk young people away from cybercrime using education, games and positive alternatives.
talks.summary:
Barry "Fish_" Van Kampen joins a relaxed studio fireside chat to talk about his work with the Dutch police on keeping young people from drifting into cybercrime. He begins with his background teaching children to use Arduino microcontrollers and running capture-the-flag exercises, and explains how that led to a police offender prevention team. The stated aim is to reduce the number of people who become offenders in the first place, rather than only arresting them afterwards.

The conversation covers how young people end up on criminal paths. Gamers who look for cheats can be approached on gaming forums by criminal groups that want a payment module or other code written. Others lend out their bank cards for quick money, without realising they are taking part in fraud. The speaker also describes finding underage people building phishing panels, who often did not see the harm in what they were doing. On the prevention side, he describes a police game called Frank that confronts possible offenders on their phones with the consequences of their actions, school programmes for primary and secondary pupils, and materials that help children talk with their parents.

The chat ends with the case of a large DDoS-for-hire platform, webstressor, run by a 14-year-old who had been involved for about three years. Once law enforcement worked to find the operators, the team chose to offer the boy an alternative instead of prison. He later built a DDoS mitigation service. The speaker argues that lowering offenders' reputation and profit, and offering real alternatives, can work better than arrests, and that cybercrime needs international cooperation.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio: Fireside Chat With Stefano Zanero and Marco Balduzzi
talks.teaser: Two speakers reflect on decades of security conferences and on how event formats could better foster community.
talks.summary:
This recorded fireside chat closes out a day at the Hack In The Box event. Stefano Zanero and Marco Balduzzi talk with a host about returning to in-person events after the pandemic. They describe how cancelled or virtual conferences left them missing the chance encounters that physical events provide, and how many friendships across continents were built over decades of attending.

The guests trade memories of early editions. One recalls a first trip to Kuala Lumpur in 2008, where a casual conversation on a train turned into a meeting with a friend at the event. Another describes early gatherings where attendees brought their own machines and coded side by side in a hacking arena, with few talks and no capture-the-flag contest. They agree that community spirit has survived the event's growth, and they discuss new formats: a gathering with no fixed programme and a whiteboard for signing up to present, speed-networking tables, multi-day retreats in a seminar castle, shorter lightning talks, and paired academic and industry tracks where attackers and defenders respond to each other's problems.

The session ends with a birthday celebration for a younger guest and a reflection that the spirit of the community carries forward even as formats change. The practical takeaway is that unstructured in-person contact and mixed formats matter for keeping a conference community together.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio: Fireside Chat With Cooper @Ministraitor
talks.teaser: A veteran conference videographer explains rigs, pipelines, and workflows that deliver crisp multi-track recordings at speed.
talks.summary:
The conversation follows Cooper from door-check volunteer to someone who filmed more than forty conferences in a single pre-pandemic year. Early efforts at Steelcon showed how easily focus, storage, and lighting could ruin usable footage, which pushed him to assemble his own hardware and chase the next events that lacked official recording.

He describes a production stack built for reliability and scale: SDI runs with twelve-volt power fed only from the main PC so stage outlets cannot break a take, portrait-mounted cameras cropped into a sharp side column, and a layout that keeps slides visible while the speaker adds presence. OBS assembles inputs; ffmpeg trims by copying libx264 segments instead of re-encoding; Audacity cleans audio from XLR or ceiling condenser mics before tracks are muxed back without recompressing video. Streamlined steps turned multi-week edits into uploads sometimes appearing within about thirteen minutes of a talk ending.

The closing thread is distribution: donations helped grow roughly twenty-one rigs across several countries, with gear left at universities and with UK village organizers to ease Brexit logistics. He wants more local volunteers trained in under fifteen minutes to deploy shared rigs so smaller and library-hosted events can publish talks without rebuilding the whole toolchain from scratch.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 Hack In The Studio Panel: 38°C: Healthcare At A Fever Pitch
talks.teaser: Clinicians and hackers debate how to secure medical devices, hospital networks and vulnerability reporting in healthcare.
talks.summary:
This panel brings together a clinician, a hacker and the executive director of the Biohacking Village to discuss security in healthcare. The panelists describe healthcare as a siloed field, with legacy systems, add-on devices and electronic medical records stitched together over time. They say clinicians and security professionals often talk past each other, and that flat hospital networks let a compromised device reach others.

The discussion turns to who would attack these systems. The panelists say criminals usually want data or money, and patients can be harmed as collateral damage. They outline the Biohacking Village's medical device lab, where manufacturers take part in coordinated vulnerability disclosure through private channels, with a 90-day window mentioned. They also cover regulation, including the FDA's role, an executive order calling for software bills of materials, and government advisories, and they question why medical device flaws rarely appear in them.

The closing takeaways focus on shared responsibility. Speakers call for hackers and hospital staff to learn each other's language, for security to be built into devices by default, and for clinicians to have a clear place to report problems. They suggest borrowing segmentation and control models from industrial control systems, and they call for more joint work across countries.

talks.title: #HITBCW2021 COMMSEC: Military Bioweapons Dev. & Information Warfare
talks.teaser: Surveys chemical, biological and cyber threats in the Gulf region through the speaker's projected conflict scenarios.
talks.summary:
Presented at a Hack In The Box cyber week event in Abu Dhabi, this talk looks at chemical, biological and nuclear weapons in the Gulf Cooperation Council region and how the speaker thinks they could combine with cyber operations in a future conflict. It opens with the regional cyber landscape and a recent destructive malware campaign against Israeli critical infrastructure, which the speaker said had no public attribution. He also notes that personnel records were reportedly taken during that campaign.

The middle section reviews the history of chemical warfare, from gas use in the First World War and the Iran-Iraq war to attacks in Iraq and Syria. It lists nerve agents, toxins and common delivery methods such as missiles, mortars and aircraft. The speaker then profiles several states outside the GCC, including Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Libya, Syria and Iran, and gives a projected list of likely cyber courses of action for each one. For Iran, he focuses on a growing hacking community and a shift in state malware from disruption, as with Stuxnet, toward espionage.

To close, he argues that bioweapon use poses the greatest threat to GCC states and that cooperation across cyber, information and military operations is needed to respond. The conclusions are presented as the speaker's assessments and predictions rather than verified findings. The practical takeaway is that regional defence planning should cover combined cyber and weapons-of-mass-destruction scenarios.
