talks.title: #HITB2021AMS D1T1 - MacOS Security: Escaping The Sandbox & Bypassing TCC
talks.teaser: Examines macOS sandboxing, TCC and SIP, and the third-party and Apple flaws that let attackers get past them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a hypothetical: an attacker has code execution as an unprivileged user on modern macOS and needs root-owned files or access to the camera and microphone. The presenters first walk through the layered defenses, including code signing and entitlements, the App Sandbox, System Integrity Protection, TCC privacy prompts, and the signed system volume that is checked against a seal on every boot.

The second half covers case studies. Privileged updater helpers in third-party software, such as Adobe Acrobat, could be tricked with symlink and hard-link swaps between the signature check and the installation. A sandboxed app could take a snapshot of the open panel to preview files until Apple added an entitlement check. System Preferences could be made to load a third-party preference pane outside the sandbox through a tampered cache file, a path Apple closed in Big Sur. Electron apps and older builds lacking library validation let an attacker reuse the TCC permissions of the original app by swapping code. Finally, generic process injection into Apple applications enabled a sandbox escape, root escalation through a signed installer package, and a SIP bypass, with specifics withheld.

The takeaways are that TCC is a newer layer many developers do not yet understand, that one vulnerable app holding a permission can hand that permission to malware, and that process injection breaks assumptions across the platform. Apple is moving macOS toward iOS-level protection but must balance this against breaking existing software.

talks.title: #HITB2021AMS D1T2 - WoW Hell: Rebuilding Heavens Gate
talks.teaser: Shows how WoW64 internals can be abused to call 64-bit APIs and inject code past antivirus hooks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the problem: endpoint products often hook the 32-bit Windows API inside WoW64 processes, so a 32-bit payload that calls those functions gets noticed. The Heaven's Gate technique switches a 32-bit process into 64-bit mode to call the 64-bit ntdll directly, which is usually left unhooked. The speaker explains why earlier public work was hard to use in practice: 32-bit code struggles with 64-bit calling conventions and data structures, and since Windows 8 the 64-bit ntdll is loaded above the 4 GB boundary.

To get around these limits, the speaker reverse engineers the WoW64 layer. The walkthrough covers how the wow64cpu component saves the thread context, how it dispatches through a function table, and how a translator function converts 32-bit system calls into 64-bit ones. Two techniques follow from this. WoW Grill calls that translator directly with 32-bit system call numbers, avoiding the API paths that security products watch. WoW Injector relies on the predictable placement of the 64-bit TEB and PEB blocks to leak the saved context of a thread and redirect its execution for process injection.

In the demos, a typical injection of a test payload was caught and removed by an antivirus with real-time protection, while the WoW Grill version ran undetected. WoW Injector then injected payloads into system processes such as notepad and cmd, and a Mimikatz payload that was otherwise blocked was able to run. The takeaway is that behavioural protection placed only on 32-bit API entry points can be sidestepped.

talks.title: #HITB2021AMS D1T1 - Should You Be Afraid Of Hands-On Payment Devices?
talks.teaser: Demonstrates code execution on Ingenico and Verifone PIN pads through debug modes, boot loader flaws and firmware bugs.
talks.summary:
Timur Yunusov and Alexey Tyurinikov, both from the Payment Village team, open with the payment ecosystem: card brands, issuing and acquiring banks, merchants, and the PCI standards that set rules for protecting card data on terminals. They separate POS systems, the computers with keyboards and scanners that cashiers use, from PIN pads and terminals where customers enter cards and PINs. The threat model they use covers malicious customers and malicious merchants.

The technical section covers vulnerabilities in PIN pads from two major vendors. On Ingenico Telium 2 devices, a maintenance mode reached through a boot key combination exposed a virtual serial link, an unauthenticated protocol with hardcoded credentials, and a trace debug interface with undocumented commands. Together these allowed memory allocation and injection of code into running tasks. On Verifone VX5 devices, a default service password, a trusted-by-default drive, and a hidden shell led to a buffer overflow in a system call and code execution. The VX boot loader also accepted a crafted update format that let an attacker write arbitrary memory over a physical connection. The Linux-based MX series chained a default password, command injection, privilege escalation and a race condition in role-based access control.

The speakers explain why these findings matter in practice. PIN and track two data can be captured in the main application's memory before encryption, and extracted encryption keys can support a working terminal clone for fraud. They argue that PCI rules leave key deletion on tamper unspecified, so vendors implement it differently, and that proprietary designs have not produced stronger security. They close with open questions about how many vulnerable devices remain in the field and whether firmware can be downgraded.

talks.title: RTV: Privilege Escalation In Da House by Carlos Polop Martin
talks.teaser: Walks through the PEASS enumeration scripts that flag local privilege escalation misconfigurations on Linux, macOS and Windows.
talks.summary:
The talk covers why local privilege escalation matters during penetration tests and red team work. A low-privileged foothold limits what an operator can do, while root or administrator access makes persistence, credential harvesting and lateral movement easier. The speaker also argues defenders need to know these paths to harden their systems.

The main part presents the PEASS suite of enumeration scripts: LinPEAS for Linux, a macOS variant, and WinPEAS for Windows, plus a batch version for hosts without a suitable .NET runtime. Output is colour-coded, with red and yellow marking likely escalation vectors and green marking settings that are already locked down. Demos on a deliberately vulnerable Linux host showed a writable path used by a scheduled job that could be hijacked, and a scan that found an open port on another internal machine. The Windows demo flagged writable services, a DLL hijack opportunity and a Watson hotfix check that the speaker said should be verified by hand.

To close, the speaker outlined planned work: deeper macOS-specific checks, a Metasploit post-exploitation module and HTML report output. Practitioners should review the referenced HackTricks pages before running the scripts, since the output only makes sense alongside the techniques behind each check.

talks.title: RTV: Payload Delivery For Initial Access In Red Team Engagement by Jean Marie Bourbon
talks.teaser: Shows payload delivery for initial access in red team engagements, with AV and AMSI evasion and proxy-aware stagers.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a red team gets its first foothold when the target exposes very little. The speaker recounts a engagement run during the COVID-19 period, where reconnaissance found only a mailbox, a remote access service and a CMS-based website. A phishing campaign harvested credentials that later failed, and the team noticed many accounts used a predictable company-name-plus-year password. Password spraying then produced around 50 valid accounts, and the speaker stresses that the client's response process mattered as much as the technique.

The middle section covers constraints and evasion. Antivirus, AMSI, AppLocker and authenticated proxies all have to be dealt with, and antivirus bypass is presented as a step rather than a goal. A Metasploit staged payload fails behind an authenticated proxy, so a stageless shellcode is preferred. Junk instructions, comments and string concatenation removed detections from the PowerShell template, and hand-customized shellcode, checked in a test virtual machine, kept working. An HTA dropper can be delivered through a browser-hooking framework as a fallback, with attention to user agent, certificate and domain categorization. A live demo against a Windows 10 host with real-time antivirus enabled returned a session.

The closing advice applies to both sides. Red teams should prepare tooling in advance, avoid chasing domain admin when data access is the real goal, and log a full timeline. Blue teams should alert on unusual user agents, monitor PowerShell and AMSI events, avoid investigating with privileged accounts, and assume breach.

talks.title: RTV Panel: Pre-empting Attacks - Relevance Of Red Teaming In Enterprises

talks.title: RTV: Zero Trust Networks: Opportunities And Challenges For Red Team by Dan Levy
talks.teaser: Surveys how zero trust architectures change red team tactics around remote access, cloud, MFA and automation.
talks.summary:
The talk examines zero trust, an approach that stops relying on the network perimeter and instead checks user behaviour inside the network, and asks what it means for red team and penetration testing work. The speaker frames zero trust around three pillars: network architecture, user roles and access, and monitoring. Remote work and cloud adoption make this more pressing, and VPNs, which usually grant broad access once a user is inside, remain a weak point for attackers.

The middle section covers several areas. Solutions that move internal applications to the cloud behind a broker let contractors reach only specific apps, but migrations often leave on-premises remnants, such as a cloud web app that still reads an on-prem database, and misconfigured AWS security groups can expose servers. Behaviour-based two-factor tools that plug into Active Directory and use machine learning make noisy scanning and bulk data extraction easier to flag. The suggested counter is to pace activity slowly over months, match the target user's working hours and time zone, and prefer accounts with predictable behaviour. In cloud environments, the speaker recommends continuous enumeration and multiple persistence paths, since auto-scaling changes the environment quickly. Automated patching and self-healing playbooks shrink the window for attackers, so exploitation has to move faster.

The talk closes by noting that many cloud-based security platforms do not enable two-factor authentication by default, which can produce high-impact findings. The speaker also points to a monitoring tool that was reportedly abused for enumeration in a Kubernetes environment. The overall takeaway is an ongoing back-and-forth between defenders and attackers, in which red teamers must keep adapting their techniques to each environment.

talks.title: RTV: Old Still Cool: Classic SE Formats Merge In Three Peculiar Tales by Daniel Isler
talks.teaser: Walks through three red team social engineering cases, from hand-delivered lures to a fake support call.
talks.summary:
Daniel Isler, team leader of a social engineering unit in Chile, opens by asking where persuasion ends and manipulation begins, arguing that anyone can be a social engineer once the context and triggers are right. He then frames the practical problem for red teams: formal engagements often run only five to ten days, far shorter than the months a real attacker might spend, and client restrictions and mail filters make realistic phishing hard to run at scale. A mock negotiation with a client shows how a phishing lure gets stripped of brands, images and sensitive wording until little remains.

The talk then covers three merged cases. In the first, a physical spear phishing campaign delivered invitations by hand to 13 staff members at an office, offering a cyber security conference workshop with a QR code that led to a fake site asking for corporate credentials. Credentials were captured from 11 of the 13 people, and one employee reported the activity. The second combined an award-event invitation with a pen drive holding a malicious file. A consultant posing as a journalist got past reception and the guards to reach the CEO's office, but the payload failed because it was built for Windows while the target used a Mac. The third case was a vishing attack during the pandemic: the team called the company's published phone number, asked for staff by name, then had an employee log into a fake technical support site and install a remote access tool.

The speaker's takeaway is that strong security controls can make staff over-trust their systems, so they click, download and install without questioning. Practitioners are urged to build scenarios around realistic channels and the interests of each target, and to plan tests that reflect how real attackers operate.

talks.title: RTV: Threat Hunting With Elastic Security by Aravind Putrevu and Haran Kumar
talks.teaser: Presents threat hunting workflows built on Elastic Security in a ten-minute session by two speakers.
talks.summary:
This short session, listed at ten minutes, looks at threat hunting with Elastic Security and is presented by Aravind Putrevu and Haran Kumar. Threat hunting means proactively searching an environment for adversary activity that automated alerts may not flag, and the talk places that practice inside the Elastic Security platform.

Because the slot is brief, it reads best as an overview of the hunting workflow rather than a deep technical walkthrough, and this summary does not attribute specific findings to it.

Security teams that already use Elastic Security can take the session as a prompt to review their own hunting process and the data sources they search. Newcomers to threat hunting will find it a light introduction to both the subject and the platform.

talks.title: RTV: Evolution Of Offensive Security by Jorge Orchilles and Bryson Bort
talks.teaser: Follows a six-week purple team exercise in production, showing how existing tools lifted detection of adversary behaviors.
talks.summary:
Bryson Bort and Jorge Orchilles present a case study of a two-month purple team engagement, with six weeks of hands-on work against a freight-industry organization referred to as Motorhead. The team began with cyber threat intelligence to choose adversaries that had the opportunity, intent and capability to target that organization, then built emulation plans from their documented behaviors rather than from lists of indicators. The baseline showed that nearly all emulated behaviors went unseen, and the organization was using only a small share of its existing security products.

Each week covered a different threat actor, moving from lower to higher sophistication. The team enabled Sysmon telemetry, forwarded it to the Event Sentry SIEM, and wrote and tuned rules by repeating each behavior at every layer until it was logged and alerted. Tuning was the hardest part: a PowerShell rule produced hundreds of alerts because staff used PowerShell without realizing it, so the rule had to separate expected use from suspicious use. Other findings included outbound RDP allowed to any destination, which the staff fixed within minutes, and users who should not have been in the enterprise admin group. A lack of netflow data also limited command and control visibility.

By the end, with no new technology purchased, detection reached 64 percent of the emulated behaviors. The speakers' takeaways were to test in production, expect to tune, repeat techniques until they are caught, and accept that 100 percent is not a realistic goal. They also shared their emulation plans, a Sysmon configuration and the purple team exercise framework with the community.

talks.title: RTV: Visibility In The Clouds by Ilia Rabinovich and Oleg Lerner
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning RTV: Visibility In The Clouds by Ilia Rabinovich and Oleg Lerner.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Ilia Rabinovich and Oleg Lerner from Sygnia present Cloud Scout, an open-source tool designed to map and visualize attack paths across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. As organizations migrate traditional infrastructure to the cloud, threat actors exploit cross-platform connections, hybrid architectures, and expanding attack surfaces to pivot across environments and escalate privileges. The speakers introduce Cloud Scout to overcome visibility limitations inherent in existing siloed security tools by consolidating and correlating identity and asset data across on-premises, Azure, and AWS infrastructures.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Cloud Threat Landscape:** Over the last two years, organizations have accelerated transitions to hybrid and multi-cloud setups, interconnecting multiple cloud vendors, CI/CD pipelines, and microservices. Threat actors exploit this complexity by spinning up malicious cloud applications, targeting CI/CD workflows, developing cloud-dedicated malware, and leveraging cloud attack surfaces to pivot into on-premises networks or other cloud environments.
- **Siloed Tooling Limitations:** Existing open-source tools each address single-environment enumeration: BloodHound (by SpecterOps) focuses on on-premises environments, Stormspotter (by Microsoft) focuses on Azure, and awspx (by F-Secure Labs) focuses on AWS. Because these tools operate in separate databases, security teams previously had to manually consolidate data to identify cross-platform relationships.
- **Cloud Scout Architecture and Capabilities:** Because BloodHound, Stormspotter, and awspx all rely on Neo4j graph databases, Cloud Scout merges their data into a single unified database. It provides three primary functions:
  1. Connecting cross-platform entities (such as users, applications, roles, and services) based on corresponding attributes.
  2. Identifying cross-platform attack paths that threat actors could leverage for lateral movement and privilege escalation.
  3. Visualizing these complex, cross-platform attack paths within a single screen.

### Technical Details
- **Entity Correlation:** Real-world hybrid environments share interconnected entities. For instance, on-premises Active Directory accounts synced to Azure Active Directory can be linked between BloodHound and Stormspotter nodes using their user security identifier (SID). Cloud Scout enriches node data to construct both trivial and complex relationships across platforms.
- **Integration and Installation:** Cloud Scout is packaged as a plugin for BloodHound, downloadable from GitHub. Users install it by running a batch installation script. Once installed, BloodHound's interface displays additional UI buttons that handle the ingestion of data from the different frameworks and execute the logic needed to build cross-platform relations.

### Takeaways
- Visibility into interconnected hybrid and multi-cloud systems is a critical gap for modern security teams.
- Traditional assessment tools provide only fragmented views of specific environments, masking cross-platform lateral movement risks.
- By uniting data from BloodHound, Stormspotter, and awspx into a single Neo4j database, Cloud Scout allows defenders to uncover non-trivial attack paths spanning on-premises networks and multiple cloud providers.

talks.title: #HITBSecTrain: Applied Defense On Docker And Kubernetes
talks.teaser: Shows how to harden Docker and Kubernetes with rootless mode, capability drops, seccomp, AppArmor, RBAC and network policies.
talks.summary:
The workshop walks through defensive hardening of Docker and Kubernetes. It starts with the Docker daemon and explains why running it as root is risky, how rootless mode reduces that exposure, and where it still has limits. The Docker socket, often mounted into containers, grants control of the host, and the TCP socket needs TLS client certificates for remote access.

Next comes container isolation. Namespaces separate host name, processes, network and IPC, and sharing them weakens that boundary. Privileged containers receive every capability, so the speaker recommends dropping all capabilities and adding back only what an application needs. Seccomp and AppArmor profiles restrict system calls and file access, user namespace remapping maps container root to an unprivileged host user, and cgroups cap memory. For images, multistage builds leave out shells and compilers, and a secret deleted in a later layer can still be recovered from earlier layers. Docker Content Trust helps ensure only signed images run.

The Kubernetes section covers control plane components and certificate-based communication, along with service account tokens that attackers often abuse. RBAC roles are tested with auth can-i, and plugins such as who-can, access-matrix and rbac-view help find over-privileged accounts. Secrets are only base64 encoded, so encrypting etcd and using an external secret manager is advised. Security contexts, pod security policies and default-deny network policies round out the hardening, with a reminder to test restrictive policies before production use.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D2 WORKSHOP - CI/CD With SAST And DAST For Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how to test firmware on real embedded hardware in CI/CD, using a Raspberry Pi test rig and static security scans.
talks.summary:
The workshop, presented by Ilia, looks at how to extend a CI/CD pipeline so firmware is deployed onto physical devices and tested there, rather than relying only on over-the-air update tests. The speaker frames the material as experience-based ideas drawn mostly from IoT work, not a fixed recipe, and encourages starting with a simple pipeline and growing it over time.

The hardware section covers a Raspberry Pi used as a test node. It can act as a Wi-Fi router or client, talk to devices through USB serial adapters, and drive relay modules that press buttons or cut power for reliability tests such as repeated power cycling. Practical pitfalls are covered too: power supply sizing, cheap adapter chips with mislabelled wires, cable quality, heat, and radio interference that led to shielded boxes or a sealed enclosure. Software choices include pytest with fixtures and marks, and log monitoring that parses serial output in real time.

The security part shows a pipeline split into separate build and test pipelines, where results change firmware status rather than breaking the build. Scanners run per language in containers, their findings are collected into one report, and custom logic decides pass or fail, starting with critical issues only. In a live GitLab demo on an ESP32 board, Unity tests ran on hardware, and secret detection flagged committed cloud credentials, while a hardcoded Wi-Fi password was missed by the built-in scanner. The takeaway is to evaluate and tune scanners, watch for suppressed findings, and begin small.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 WORKSHOP - Signal Processing With GNURadio And SDRs
talks.teaser: Introduces radio frequency basics, signal processing concepts and hands-on GNU Radio flowgraphs for software defined radio newcomers.
talks.summary:
The workshop opens with the basics of electromagnetic waves and the radio frequency spectrum, then explains how wireless links are built. It covers simplex, half duplex and full duplex communication, the roles of baseband and carrier signals, and modulation schemes including amplitude, frequency and phase modulation, along with digital keying variants. It also introduces sampling, decimation and interpolation, and why time-domain and frequency-domain views of a signal differ.

The practical section moves to GNU Radio Companion, the open-source flowgraph tool. The speaker builds simple flowgraphs that synthesize a sine wave, shows how a low sampling rate distorts it, and uses a throttle block to limit CPU load. He compares two close tones in time and frequency views, and uses a low-pass filter to remove a higher-frequency component from a multiplied signal. He then demonstrates an amplitude-modulated audio transmitter and receiver that run entirely in software, linked over a local TCP connection.

The workshop closes with software defined radio hardware such as RTL-SDR, HackRF, USRP and LimeSDR, comparing their frequency ranges and costs. It outlines a workflow for radio research: choose a frequency band, check local licensing rules, select suitable hardware and prepare the software. The speaker stresses staying lawful and avoiding interference with live communications, shows an SDR spectrum tool and remote SDR access, and points attendees to a repository of example flowgraphs.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 WORKSHOP - How To Train Your Self-Driving (Dragon) Car
talks.teaser: Attendees collect simulator laps, train a convolutional autopilot remotely, and pit models against each other in a timed virtual race.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the Donkey Car open-source stack on Raspberry Pi or Jetson Nano: camera images paired with throttle and steering labels, TensorFlow training, and an optional Google Coral USB accelerator for heavier vision work. Jonathan frames real-world autonomy through Tesla and Waymo examples, SAE-style driving levels, sensor trade-offs including lidar cost, fleet-scale training data, and social questions such as liability during summon features, parking enforcement, and ethical collision choices.

The core loop is collect roughly ten to fifty thousand records (or fewer in the lab), train a pilot, test, and repeat using supervised imitation learning. A mobile controller app drives a Docker-hosted virtual car against a desktop simulator, uploads tubs to a remote trainer, and returns models in minutes. The talk also contrasts reinforcement learning—including a simulator agent that maximizes track time by weaving—and highlights vision hardness for stop signs under varied conditions. Security angles include adversarial speed-limit signage and responsibility when autonomy misbehaves on public roads.

After a Dockerfile review aimed at CommSec attendees, participants install dependencies, record thousands of images, train, and optionally join a community virtual league. The close demos multi-container races: identical models lap together, while a separately trained model attempts overtakes before crashes end the heat.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2 LAB
talks.teaser: Shows how timeless debugging on recorded Windows traces can trace crashes and corrupted data back to their root cause.
talks.summary:
The lab introduces timeless debugging, where a program or a whole virtual machine is recorded once and the frozen execution can then be stepped through backwards and forwards. The instructor surveys related tools, including WinDbg's time travel debugging, rr for Linux processes, and full-system recorders such as PANDA, before presenting Revan, a platform with a GUI, a Python API and data tainting. Participants received hosted virtual machines and worked through Jupyter notebook exercises.

The first exercise used a small Windows program that crashed with a divide error. Participants located the input, searched for symbol calls and memory accesses, and used taint tracking backwards to find where a zero value had come from. The second exercise examined a Windows driver crash caused by malformed IPv6 router advertisement packets. The trace was compared with a patched version to isolate the changed check. The third trace covered a blue screen caused by a buffer overflow, where the corrupted pointer was followed to an allocation whose size calculation overflowed.

The session ended with a short contest built on the third trace. The main takeaway is that a full trace lets an analyst follow data flow from the point of crash back to the code that caused it, which complements static analysis rather than replacing it.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2 LAB

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D1 LAB - A Practical Introduction to BLE Security Without Any Special Hardware
talks.teaser: Walks through hands-on Bluetooth Low Energy hacking with a simulated device lab and an Android phone, no special hardware needed.
talks.summary:
This hands-on lab introduces Bluetooth Low Energy security without special hardware. Participants run a Windows application that simulates real BLE devices and use the nRF Connect app on an Android phone to interact with them. The session opens by explaining why BLE is common in everything from wearables to smart locks, yet rarely understood by security professionals.

Early sections cover advertisements, the public broadcasts that nearby devices send without pairing. Attendees decode raw advertisement data, examine iBeacon packets and clone one with the phone. The talk also shows how Windows and Apple advertisements can be used to track devices, and how Apple continuity messages can carry fragments of hashed phone numbers and email addresses.

Later sections cover connections and GATT services and characteristics. Attendees read a battery level, subscribe to notifications, write commands to a simulated light bulb, and automate writes with macros. A three-digit PIN protecting a hidden mode is then brute-forced at roughly ten attempts per second. The lab closes with real devices, including a smart padlock whose captured traffic can be replayed to unlock it and a smart lock whose password can be reset remotely. The main takeaway is that many BLE devices skip pairing or protect only some characteristics, so anyone in range can interact with them.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D2 - Fuzzing: Finding Your Own Bugs And 0days!
talks.teaser: Walks through building a fuzzer, using it to find bugs, and writing an exploit that gives a shell.
talks.summary:
This talk, given in Portuguese, covers fuzzing as a route to finding your own bugs and zero-days. The speaker, introduced as Rodolfo, lays out how to build a fuzzer, point it at a target and use the results to hunt for vulnerabilities. The aim is to show the whole path from raw input to a working exploit.

Much of the middle section is built around buffer sizes and a POP3 mail protocol, which frame the target as a network service that accepts crafted input. The speaker shows how a fuzzing run can surface a defect, then how that defect is reworked into an exploit that yields a shell. Demonstrations are included to show each stage working.

The closing point is a practical loop of generating inputs, watching for failures, and confirming that a crash is exploitable. Practitioners who want to reproduce this kind of bug hunting on their own targets can take the workflow as a starting point.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D2 - Inside The Mind Of A Threat Actor: Beyond Pentesting
talks.teaser: Explains how red team operations differ from penetration tests and maps a learning path into offensive security.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the speaker's career path, from system administration and network security into application security and consulting penetration testing, and later an internal red team role. It defines offensive security as assessing a target using adversary tactics, techniques and procedures, and splits it into penetration testing, covering networks, applications, cloud, social engineering, physical security and devices, and red teaming.

Next, the talk contrasts the two. Both use exploitation, phishing and malware, but a pentest is restrictive and vulnerability focused, while a red team engagement emulates a real threat actor, avoids detection and has a wider scope. Red team operations draw on open source intelligence about staff, phish for an initial foothold, and use command and control for persistence and lateral movement. They can be mapped to MITRE ATT&CK with a tool called Vector. Purple teaming lets defenders check whether specific techniques are caught.

The closing section covers the path into red teaming, starting with networking, operating systems, Active Directory and scripting, then malware, exploit development, evasion and command and control. It ends with a list of courses, certifications, blogs, C2 frameworks such as Cobalt Strike and Empire, and books, with practice environments like Hack The Box recommended for hacking skills.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D2 - Optimizing The Protection Of IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Presents an open-source tool that ranks attacking IPs into compact blacklists for IoT devices, plus a method to evaluate them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why IP blacklists remain central to threat intelligence feeds, and why they struggle to protect IoT devices that are exposed directly to the internet. The speaker noted that few blacklists target IoT and that no agreed standard exists for judging their efficacy. To test ideas, the team built a lab of 22 devices, including smart cameras, Raspberry Pi boards and NAS storage, and used its captured traffic as a dataset.

The Attacker IP Prioritizer tool ingests lab traffic every 24 hours into Splunk, keeps a database of every IP seen, and scores each address. One model favours IPs that keep attacking, while the other favours newer IPs that attack heavily, and the top-scoring addresses form a compact list. An evaluation method trains a list on one time window and measures how much malicious traffic it would stop in the next. Over a two-month test, the list blocked over 80 percent of malicious bytes and packets while covering under 50 percent of the malicious IPs.

The first version showed that a few features dominated scoring and that aging needed tuning, so version 2.0 normalised inputs, tracked aging per IP, and used a score threshold rather than a fixed 20,000-entry size. Future work adds port and honeypot counts, ASM data and reverse DNS. The speaker shared the tool, the IoT feeds and the methodology openly, and the main takeaway is to measure any blacklist against traffic from the network it protects.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - Adventures in Building a CAN Bus Sniffer
talks.teaser: Shows how an embedded team built its own CAN bus sniffer and the steps for designing, ordering and assembling a first PCB.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts how a small embedded team built its own CAN bus sniffer after commercial and Arduino-based options fell short. Their connected-car telemetry work and car security bug bashes exposed a gap: typical Arduino designs handled a normal bus load of five to ten percent but struggled when dealer diagnostic traffic pushed load to 80 to 95 percent. They also wanted to monitor several buses at once, which is useful when testing security gateways that split a vehicle network into clean and dirty sides.

The speaker then walks through hardware development for a first device. You start with a breadboard prototype, then draw a schematic around a microcontroller, often an STM32, reusing reference designs and open-source boards. Layout follows, covering component placement, short traces, ground pours, separation of analog and fast digital signals, and the fabricator's design rules. Ordering needs Gerber files, a bill of materials and pick-and-place files for assembly. Small batches of ten boards can be inexpensive, though shipping often costs nearly as much.

The talk closes with enclosure options, from food containers and off-the-shelf boxes to 3D-printed custom cases. The team went through six hardware versions over several years, usually needing one or two PCB revisions to fix mistakes. The takeaway is to split the work into small steps and to build your own tools, since making them deepens understanding of what you are investigating.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - Hacking The 0day Marketplace
talks.teaser: A session maps how an offensive R&D hub buys, vets, and fields intelligence-grade zero-days for institutional customers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with sponsorship of a virtual concept track and positions CrowdFence as an independent UAE offensive security research hub serving researchers and a small set of institutional customers. The speaker describes the zero-day market as historically informal, opaque, and inefficient: researchers are often underpaid, demand lacks guarantees, and scams are common, while only a narrow subset of exploits suits intelligence or investigation use.

The middle section explains deliberate efforts to improve that market, including a public zero-day acquisition program launched in 2018 with a ten-million-dollar fund and roughly forty million invested over three years via a vulnerability research hub platform for encrypted submissions and evaluation. Only a small fraction of valid submissions—on the order of five percent—qualifies as reliable, stealthy, and fieldable. The talk covers internal risk indexes, 2019 portfolio statistics on how long exploits remained unpatched and purchasable, and claimed customer return improvements of seventy to two hundred percent when lifecycle management is applied.

Practitioners hear how zero days are scouted, tested, procured, and occasionally replaced after patching, alongside customer vetting, optional weaponization, and defensive tooling informed by offensive work. The close emphasizes partnerships, transparency, and ongoing community event support rather than deep technical exploit mechanics.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - The Work of Cyber in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction
talks.teaser: Malware paleontology and shared-code analysis show how a rare IE validator may bridge Regin and Equation Group development lines.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that defenders gain an edge over time because attackers cannot erase historical telemetry, and that revisiting older intrusions with newer analytic methods—what the speaker calls cyber or malware paleontology—often yields context that was unavailable during the original response. Past projects on Moonlight Maze and collaborative Stuxnet-era activity motivate a broader lens than single-campaign reporting: threat actor genealogy and the idea of a “super threat actor” (STA) as a cooperative umbrella across multiple groups.

The middle of the talk develops that frame using Regin as a semi-coordinated multi-organization platform, then asks why Equation Group does not sit cleanly in the same five-part alliance picture despite shared traits such as the CNE/Wzowski-style host abstraction library. A skeptical interlocutor repeatedly challenges leak-driven conclusions; the speaker agrees technical proof should stand on its own. That leads to retrospective work on an unusual validator sample nicknamed Zerx Fancy Filter (ZXFF), described as Regin-family code tied to rare components such as Hopscotch, piggybacking Internet Explorer as a MIME filter with RC4-protected configuration.

ZXFF is positioned as sharing significant code with Equation-linked NetHandler/MistyVe-style validator behavior and additional overlaps with other Equation toolkit pieces, suggesting shared development rather than mere functional similarity. The closing takeaway is that cooperative, highly automated state-sponsored ecosystems may only become visible when analysts deliberately re-examine aging samples with modern similarity tooling—and that such retrospective links may place Equation Group atop the cooperative Regin picture practitioners have long debated.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - Subverting Bit Locker With One Vulnerability
talks.teaser: Shows how a single firmware flaw in sleep handling lets an attacker reset a TPM and unseal BitLocker keys.
talks.summary:
The talk examines whether BitLocker's trusted platform module protection can be defeated when the TPM alone guards the volume master key. The speaker explains how the key is sealed to measured boot values held in platform configuration registers, and why physical bus attacks were set aside as the approach. The focus instead turns to a flaw in how some firmware handles the S3 sleep state, which can reset the TPM and clear its PCR values without physical access.

After resetting the TPM, a patched kernel module changes the TPM suspend routine so the measurements can be rebuilt. Custom boot loaders captured the event logs, recreated the PCR 7 and 11 values, and used a hash of a Microsoft certificate obtained from other sources. The loader then hooked the firmware TPM protocol to record the commands and parameters used to unseal the key, and the volume master key was pulled from BitLocker metadata. The speaker reports that discrete and firmware TPMs from several vendors were affected, and that TPM-related BIOS code appears to be shared across boards. A prepared demo unlocked a protected partition from a USB drive.

The takeaways are to update firmware, since some products remain vulnerable and older devices past their warranty may never receive a fix. The speaker also recommends adding a PIN to BitLocker so the TPM is not the only factor. A checking tool was published so administrators can test their own systems for the sleep-state issue.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - The Art of Exploiting Logical Flaws in Web Applications
talks.teaser: Demonstrates logic flaws like price tampering, two-factor bypass and role manipulation that automated scanners tend to miss.
talks.summary:
The talk explains logical flaws in web applications, where the application behaves in a way its designers did not intend. The speaker argues that automated scanners rarely find these issues because they depend on understanding how the application's workflow is supposed to run, so testers need to learn the logic before probing it.

The walkthrough covers several cases. In a shopping demo, the server trusted the price and quantity values sent in a purchase request, so editing the price let a jacket be bought for a few cents, and changing the quantity produced multiple items at the tampered price. Another demo shows a two-factor login where the attacker started a login with their own account, swapped the username in the second-step request for the victim's, and then brute-forced the victim's verification code because no rate limit was applied. A role identifier in a request was changed from a regular user value to an administrator value, which opened an admin panel. A real-world case describes a developer who copied a password-reset handler into an admin module without the permission check, letting a user reset the admin password. The last case covers a Facebook account verification flow, where requests from one account were replayed against another to get past the second verification step.

The speaker closes by noting that these flaws can lead to account takeover, fraud, privilege escalation and changes to user data. The practical takeaway is to study how an application's business logic works and test it manually, and the talk encourages researchers to look for logic flaws in bug bounty programs.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek #CommSec D1 - The Journey For Manufacturers To Develop Cyber Resilient IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how a device maker builds threat intelligence from honeypots and internal analysis to make IoT products more resilient.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why device manufacturers need to act on IoT security. The speaker points to rising attack volumes on the internet, with IoT devices such as web cameras heavily targeted, and to IoT malware that spreads from one infected device to others sharing the same vulnerability, turning owners into unwitting attackers. Governments in the United States, Europe, China and Japan are also writing device security rules, and the speaker stresses that suppliers, customers and other stakeholders all share responsibility.

The speaker then describes how the company organizes product security across corporate IT, factory security and product security teams, covering vulnerability intake, analysis, distribution to developers and tiered training. Because waiting for external reports is too slow, the company built an intelligence project using software honeypots and real products deployed in Taiwan and Japan, with plans for more regions. Collected malware targeting MIPS, ARM64, PowerPC and SH4 is analyzed with automation. Sample data from July to September 2020 showed top source addresses launching more than 600,000 attacks, SSH as the most attacked service, and database services such as MySQL and Oracle in the top 20.

Finally, the talk covers storing logs in a log search stack, normalizing data per product line and converting findings into a standard format. The speaker proposes an industry sharing alliance so that, for example, a camera maker's finding about a web service could help a storage vendor using the same service. The takeaway is that manufacturers should gather their own threat data, filter it for their products and share what matters.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2T2 - Industrial Protocol Gateways: A Deep-Dive of Moxa MGate 5105-MB-EIP
talks.teaser: Maps Modbus translation bugs, weak crypto, and manager protocol flaws on a Moxa industrial gateway.
talks.summary:
The session focuses on the Moxa MGate 5105-MB-EIP, a compact gateway that translates between EtherNet/IP and Modbus for Industry 4.0 plant networks. After briefly positioning protocol gateways and prior multi-vendor translation research, the presenter walks through hardware layout, default telnet credentials, and how parser and scanner routines use an IO mapping table to relay changes between industrial buses.

Hands-on segments show inbound fuzzing with an extended Boofuzzer setup and weaknesses on the outbound path: coil writes can disturb holding-register memory outside configured ranges, enabling manipulation of safety-related values such as a critical temperature threshold in an HMI demo. Further work covers decrypting downloaded firmware, gaining root through a semicolon injection on the ping test page, reversing the proprietary MGate Manager UDP/TCP command channel with IDA Pro, replaying authentication because login nonces repeat without proper seeding, and capturing encrypted configuration blobs for offline decryption via vendor libraries built with Crosstool-NG and QEMU. Additional attempts touch boot sequence, event daemons, heap dumping of live session structures, and hardcoded crypto material in configuration stores.

Several ambitious chains fail in practice, including predictable session identifiers blocked by uninitialized stack padding and buffer overflow hunts in printf and UDP handlers. The team reported findings through coordinated disclosure; the vendor addressed issues or offered mitigations. Practitioners gain a concrete picture of how translation logic and management protocols on embedded OT gateways can undermine network segmentation assumptions.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2T1 - Jailbreaks Never Die: Exploiting iOS 13.7
talks.teaser: Walks through an iOS 13 sandbox escape and kernel exploitation chain, from userland bug hunting to kernel read and write.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why escaping the iOS app sandbox and reaching the kernel has become harder over successive iOS releases. It reviews the constraints placed on a process: code signing backed by the trust cache, the default application sandbox, the Unix user model, and entitlements with seatbelt profiles. Using counts of reachable userland services and kernel interfaces from iOS 12.4.1, 13 and 14, the speaker shows the exploitable attack surface shrinking, though not disappearing.

To find a sandbox escape on iOS 13, the speaker filtered the system daemons. Daemons running as root, those using NSXPC (taken as a sign of heavy Objective-C use), and those written in Swift were dropped, leaving a small set of targets. In the chosen daemon, the Objective-C runtime handled a user-controlled selector string in a way that let an attacker-shaped object be deallocated, which gave code execution inside the process. The kernel stage targeted Apple's AppleAVE2 graphics driver, an IOKit driver not reachable from the app sandbox. The exploit used a race on a memory mapping shared between userland and kernel, heap grooming with 40-byte objects to learn a kernel address, and temporary read and write primitives used to build a task port for PID zero.

Later patched versions removed those primitives, so the speaker rebuilt a more stable write primitive by abusing a linked list of client buffers. The main takeaways are that entitlement checks in less-scrutinized userland services can still open a path out of the sandbox, and that incomplete patches can leave older driver bugs reachable for researchers willing to revisit them.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2T2 - RAMN: Resistant Automotive Miniature Network
talks.teaser: Shows a credit-card-sized, low-cost test bed that emulates a four-ECU automotive CAN network for research and learning.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from Toyota Motor Corporation, presents RAMN, a credit-card-sized open-source test bed for automotive network research. The motivation is that existing test beds are costly, hard to reproduce, or built without automotive-grade parts. The talk first explains how automotive electronics differ from consumer ones, covering temperature ranges, vibration, and safety standards that shape which security countermeasures are practical.

The board emulates four ECUs on one CAN or CAN FD bus and can enumerate over USB as a standard CAN adapter on Windows or Linux. Expansion boards add a steering wheel, pedals, a gear shift, a screen, and sockets for JTAG, external memory, TPM chips and ChipWhisperer. A Python tool speaks the microcontroller's built-in boot protocol to dump firmware and check readout protection. The board can also drive the Carla autonomous driving simulator in hardware, and the demos showed bus traffic, a braking command sent over CAN, and a compromised steering wheel affecting the simulated car.

The speaker notes that RAMN uses STM32 L4 or L5 microcontrollers, which offer ECC memory and a wider temperature range, but the design is still not fully automotive grade. The takeaway is that low-cost, replaceable boards let researchers break, modify and test manufacturing variation without risking a real car. The speaker stresses that the bus is terminated on the board, so it cannot connect to a vehicle, and suggests uses in teaching, bug bounties and CTFs.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D2T1 - Trust, but Verify: Maintaining Democracy In Spite of Информационные контрмеры
talks.teaser: Defenders learn to widen election security beyond tabulation to infrastructure, disinformation, and attacks on belief, with paired cases.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that election security cannot be reduced to voter databases, tabulation systems, and polling places alone. Using a voter hierarchy of needs modeled on Maslow’s pyramid, the speaker explains how physiological safety, belonging, and esteem shape whether people vote, and notes that roughly 40% of eligible U.S. citizens do not participate—so suppression and distrust matter even when ballots are counted correctly.

The core analytic model treats election-facing harm across three planes: kinetic infrastructure, false information presented as fact, and attacks on belief and legitimacy. The middle of the talk walks through paired historical and modern cases on each plane—from postwar propaganda and foreign funding scandals to forged social posts, compromised Ukrainian election networks, spoofed polling texts, grid and transit outages, and multifaceted incidents such as Bronze Night in Estonia—to show how combined attacks erode trust faster than narrow technical defenses.

The close returns to defenders: widen the definition of election security to communications, social platforms, transit, and other critical dependencies; run tabletop readiness with government partners; secure personal and organizational systems; maintain channels such as public-private partnerships before crisis day; and counter disinformation patiently as trusted peers rather than shaming sharers. A free white paper is offered for deeper reading.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek KEYNOTE 2: The War for Control of DNS Encryption
talks.teaser: Traces how DNS privacy issues led to a contest over encrypted DNS, and what network operators should do now.
talks.summary:
Paul Vixie opens by arguing that DNS, whose basic architecture dates from the mid-1980s, has become a contested space as commercial interests grew around it. He explains that the recursive resolver sees every name a user looks up, which he treats as personal data. He then walks through how that visibility was exploited: Verisign's wildcard in the .com zone, OpenDNS redirecting failed lookups to advertising, and the EDNS Client Subnet extension, which passed client address information to content delivery networks and often sent full addresses instead of truncated prefixes. Snowden's disclosures and the resulting IETF guidance mark the next stage.

The middle of the talk covers encrypted alternatives. DNS over TLS is easy for network operators to block, while DNS over HTTPS blends into ordinary web traffic, so families and enterprises lose the monitoring and filtering they relied on. He reviews how Firefox, Chrome, Windows and Apple platforms have adopted DoH with different defaults, and raises TLS 1.3 and Encrypted Client Hello as further obstacles to network-level inspection. He also notes that Russia has said it will block such traffic.

He closes with practical advice: run a local recursive resolver where possible, enable DoT and DoH on your servers, and follow Mozilla's trusted recursive resolver rules, which limit data use, require transparency and avoid filtering. He urges engineers to join the relevant working groups and push for better defaults, arguing that complexity and centralised control are the underlying risk.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek D1T2 - Constructing an OS X Cyber Range for Red & Blue Teams
talks.teaser: A macOS cyber range links attack emulation, integrated forensics, and MITRE mapping for structured red-and-blue team exercises.
talks.summary:
As macOS faces more real-world threats, defenders lack mature attack-and-defense playbooks and tooling compared with other platforms. The presenters describe building a macOS cyber range to measure red-team and blue-team performance, grounded in the MITRE ATT&CK matrix for Apple environments.

They introduce an attack–defense association graph that connects malware behaviors to individual techniques, forensic evidence types, and the tools that produce that evidence. On the offense side, the workflow spans open-source remote access tools, repurposed real-world macOS malware controlled by a custom C2, and a Go-based emulator named Gdoor with a full storyline covering initial access, persistence, discovery, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. On the defense side, they compare artifact collectors, unified logging utilities, and process or file monitors, then integrate chosen tools into modular collectors and monitors with unified output.

The range runs samples in virtual machines, filters before-and-after artifacts, labels detections with MITRE technique IDs, and renders results back into the association graph. A live Gdoor run illustrates interactive evaluation. They position the graph as a guide for tool gaps and release the emulation framework, integrations, and labeling pipeline for training, exercises, and product testing.

talks.title: #HITBCyberWeek KEYNOTE 1
talks.teaser: Tackles audience questions on remote work, ransomware, quantum-safe crypto, encryption backdoors and AI bug finding.
talks.summary:
In this keynote, Bruce Schneier answers questions submitted by the audience. He begins with the pandemic, arguing that the biggest change is people working differently from home, on machines and networks that are often insecure, which fraud schemes exploit. For ransomware, he says sound patching and good backups remain the most effective defence, since criminals mainly prey on systems lacking both.

On cryptography, he says quantum computers remain experimental, so standards work such as the US NIST competition for quantum-resistant algorithms is already underway, well ahead of any working machine. On encryption backdoors, he frames the debate as security versus security and argues that weakening widely used platforms harms everyone. On supply chains, he is more concerned about vendors building in kill switches that could degrade infrastructure during hostilities than about covert copying of data.

Looking ahead, he predicts machine learning will automate much vulnerability discovery, though unpatched legacy and IoT devices will keep old bugs alive during the transition. He also argues that surveillance business models may need to be outlawed rather than fixed technically, and urges technologists to take part in policy and public-interest work. His closing advice to graduates is to accept uncertainty, and the overall message is that security must become distributed and borderless.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D2T2 - PEsidious - Create Mutated Evasive Malware Using AI
talks.teaser: Shows how reinforcement learning and GANs can mutate Windows malware to lower its antivirus detection score.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Presidius, a tool that uses AI to mutate Windows PE malware so that it appears benign to antivirus engines, including AI-based ones. The speakers say attackers are increasingly targeting the machine learning models used to block malicious activity, and they wanted to measure how easily such engines could be evaded. Before the tool itself, they explain reinforcement learning with a maze example and generative adversarial networks with deepfake examples.

The pipeline converts each PE file into a binary feature vector built from header, section and import data, using malicious and benign sample sets. A reinforcement learning agent chooses modifications such as adding imports, renaming or adding sections, appending bytes, changing signatures and debug flags, and packing or unpacking with UPX. Its reward comes from changes in VirusTotal detection counts. A GAN, paired with a black-box classifier that imitates common AV models, proposes import and section lists that are more likely to pass as benign. Early versions cut scores sharply but broke the samples, so the team filtered out 64-bit imports, moved file rebuilding from a Python library to C++, and capped modifications at 80.

In the demo, a ransomware-type sample's detections fell from 66 engines to 37 while its sandbox behaviour stayed the same. The speakers note that the tool only handles 32-bit files and plan to add 64-bit support, replace the local classifier with VirusTotal scoring, and use mutated samples to train defensive detectors. The main takeaway is that AI-based detectors can be evaded with modest changes, so defenders should test against mutated variants of known malware.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D2T2 - Quark Engine
talks.teaser: JunWei S. examines #HITBLockdown002 D2T2 - Quark Engine.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Quark Engine is an Android malware scoring and analysis system developed by Kunu Chen and Jin Wei Sung. Rather than relying on existing cybersecurity approaches, the creators derived their methodology from principles of criminal law, resulting in a novel eight-principle scoring system combined with a Dalvik bytecode loader implementation.

## The Eight Principles

The scoring system is built on principles decoded from criminal law:
1. A malware crime consists of action and targets (similar to criminal definitions)
2. Loss of reputation is greater than loss of wealth (reputation is harder to recover than money)
3. Arithmetic sequence for penalty weighting across crimes
4-6. Order theory comprising three sub-principles: later stages indicate greater certainty of crime practice; more evidence increases penalty weight; proportional sequence (e.g., 2^n) reflects escalating severity
7. Crimes are treated as independent events allowing direct penalty addition
8. Threshold generation system to classify threat levels

## Android Malware Crime Order Theory

The core innovation is a five-stage theory mirroring criminal law stages (determination, conspiracy, preparation, start, practice):
- **Stage 1**: Check if malware requests related permissions
- **Stage 2**: Verify if key native APIs are called
- **Stage 3**: Detect specific API combinations
- **Stage 4**: Confirm APIs are called in correct sequence by tracing mutual parent functions
- **Stage 5**: Verify APIs handle the same register through CPU operation simulation

## Technical Implementation

The Dalvik bytecode loader implements all five stages. Stage 4 overcomes obfuscation by tracing function call hierarchies regardless of renamed wrappers. Stage 5 uses a custom "register object" data type storing register name, current value, and which functions access it. The engine simulates CPU operations line-by-line, maintaining a hash table history of register states to track data flow between APIs.

## Real-World Analysis

Two malware cases were demonstrated:
1. Non-obfuscated malware stealing location data via SMS with clear function names (send_message, get_location) containing native APIs get_cell_location and send_text_message
2. Obfuscated malware detecting Wi-Fi hotspots using get_active_network_info and get_cell_location APIs, with intentionally renamed functions (p.a, am.a, etc.) that still traced back to legitimate behavior patterns

## Detection Rule Generation

To scale rule creation beyond human capacity, a seven-step automated strategy was developed:
1. Crawl official Android API documentation
2. Ignore permissions in initial engine scan
3. Generate all possible API combination rules
4. Find first-stage verified rules matching actual malware
5. Add permission context from matched malware
6. Verify second-stage rules and count malware matches
7. Sort and review rules by prevalence

This approach reduces resource consumption versus generating all 1.26×10^13 possible combinations.

## Takeaways

Quark Engine provides malware analysts with structured confidence levels (0-100% based on stage evidence) for behavioral detection, enables rapid analysis of obfuscated code, and automates rule generation. Future work includes handling native libraries (.so files), packed APKs, API version changes across Android versions, and potentially replacing the currently-inactive Andrew Guard core library.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D2T2 - Jackpotting Fortune-500 Treasuries
talks.teaser: Martin Doyhenard explores #HITBLockdown002 D2T2 - Jackpotting Fortune-500 Treasuries.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researchers Gaston Guerra and Martin Oyanarte examine enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems—specifically Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS)—and how attackers can move beyond basic access (such as cryptomining or ransomware) to execute high-impact financial post-exploitation. Organizations rely on ERP financial modules to handle bank accounts, manage vendors, generate checks, and conduct electronic funds transfers (EFT). Despite handling hundreds of millions of dollars, many production ERP systems remain exposed to the internet and unpatched due to concerns that updates might break legacy business operations.

### Key Topics
- **ERP Exposure and Post-Exploitation Gap:** Many internet-facing ERP instances discovered on Shodan run unpatched. While attackers often compromise these systems for low-value goals like Monero mining, understanding ERP financial workflows allows direct monetary theft.
- **Thin Client Framework (TCF) Flaws:** Analysis of the TCF communication protocol, authentication bypass mechanisms via unhandled Java null exceptions, and remote method invocation via proxies.
- **Deserialization to SQL Injection:** Chaining object deserialization in `ServerPostMaster` with gadget services to achieve second-order SQL injection and modify backend database records.
- **EFT Wire Transfer Manipulation:** Intercepting and altering approved payment orders and bank routing details in the database before the automated payment close batch process runs.
- **EBS Payment Module File Upload & Remote Command Execution:** Exploiting the `fileDumpFunction` within `IBATransmitServlet` to write arbitrary files, upload a Perl web shell, and hijack the check printing process.

### Technical Details
Martin details an authentication bypass in EBS's Thin Client Framework (`APBS TCF servlet`). When a handshake request omits the `TCF-Start` header (making it null), calling `.equals("close")` triggers a Java null pointer exception that is not handled properly, allowing the session to persist and returning a valid `JSessionID` cookie without an EBS authentication cookie. Leveraging proxy classes, the researchers identify `ServerPostMaster`, which decompresses a zipped byte array into an `ObjectInputStream` and calls `readObject()`. By crafting a gadget chain utilizing `FNDMessageRequest`/`FNDMessageService` and `ContextBootstrapRequest`/`ContextBootstrapService`, they set the session's display language with a SQL payload. When calling `respond()` on `SingleResponseService`, the injected language variable triggers second-order SQL injection. By declaring a `pragma autonomous_transaction` in the Oracle database, arbitrary insert, update, or delete statements can be run—allowing the takeover of the `sysadmin` account and modification of approved payment records (updating bank accounts, branch numbers, and bank names) while clearing audit logs.

Gaston demonstrates a separate unauthenticated vulnerability in the `IBATransmitServlet` payment module. The servlet processes an HTTP POST request containing XML specifying a class (`fileDumpFunction`) and method (`transmit`), accepting parameters such as `fileDir`, `fileName`, and `transmitRef`. By supplying root (`/`) as `fileDir`, an empty string for `fileName`, and the relative target path in `transmitRef`, an attacker achieves arbitrary file write without path traversal. Gaston overwrites an existing Perl CGI script on the WebLogic server with a Perl web shell. Using a reverse shell connection to the reports directory, he locates a cached check file (`check.out`), modifies the payee and payment data to his own details, and executes `lp` to send the modified check file to the remote check printing queue, physically printing an unauthorized check.

### Takeaways
1. **Functional Controls Are Ineffective When the Core Platform Falls:** Once attackers obtain underlying database or operating system access, business logic validation and multi-tier approval workflows are completely bypassed.
2. **Blind Trust in ERP Integrity:** Banks and business operators inherently trust batch-generated EFT files and check spoolers because the payments were already approved by authorized personnel.
3. **Deserialization and Legacy Codebases:** Decades-old enterprise frameworks built with Java EE, reflection, and remote method invocation introduce severe modern attack vectors such as deserialization.
4. **Post-Exploitation Risk:** The security community and enterprises must realize that attackers will eventually focus on business logic and financial post-exploitation rather than commodity malware.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D1T2 - Operation SemiChimera
talks.teaser: Follows a targeted APT campaign against Taiwanese semiconductor vendors and the blended tools used to steal data.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Operation SemiChimera, a targeted APT campaign against Taiwanese semiconductor vendors observed in 2018 and 2019. The attackers reached subsidiaries, competitors and supply-chain partners, aiming to steal intellectual property such as documents, source code and SDKs for chip projects.

The first case concerned a long-term partner whose environment the researchers had monitored over time. Attackers disguised a Cobalt Strike beacon as a Google update and launched it through scheduled tasks timed before working hours. They ran WMIC and scheduled-task commands across endpoints, then collected registry hives and the NTDS.dit file from a domain controller. The trail led to a VPN host that was itself compromised. The second case was a one-time response at another company, where an intrusion dating to 2018 had gone unnoticed. A graph of the environment exposed compromised domain controllers, and a new injector deployed in late 2019 had extended the attackers' reach.

The tool analysis covered a Cobalt Strike beacon hidden in a hybrid PE file, and a WinRAR build whose binary differed by a small byte change, which can defeat hash matching. The standout tool, a skeleton key injector, merged Dumpert and Mimikatz code and used direct system calls to slip past hooks. It planted a backdoor password on domain controllers, letting attackers log in as any user with few traces, and it is hard to remove without rebooting every controller. The speakers advised against relying on a single security service and urged regular threat hunting and faster detection and response.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D2T1 - Exploring Deficiencies in Automatic Vuln Mining Technology
talks.teaser: Shows where fuzzers and hybrid tools miss bugs behind hard constraints, and proposes backward constraint propagation as a fix.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at where automated vulnerability mining falls short. The speaker explains that fuzzers such as AFL and libFuzzer, and hybrid tools, rely on preparation like dictionaries and seed files and still stall on hard checks. A small example guarded a null pointer dereference behind a pair of four-byte integers whose product had to match a fixed value, and the fuzzers could not produce an input that reached it.

Next the speaker covers how these tools gain feedback. Compiler instrumentation exposes branch coverage and comparison operands, and distance measures such as Hamming and absolute distance rank inputs by how close they come to a comparison. The speaker argues these distances approximate poorly for many functions, and that symbolic execution suffers from path explosion. The proposed alternative starts from a constraint that is sufficient to trigger the bug, such as a flag variable equal to 0xff, and works backward through assignments in LLVM bitcode before a solver checks the result. A demo on the example produced an input that reaches the null pointer access.

The speaker frames the method as automating manual code review in four steps: set initial constraints with sanitizers and assertions, collect concrete paths with fuzzers, bound the depth of back propagation, and use approximation techniques when the solver stalls. In Q&A, the speaker said grammar-based fuzzing still requires reading the target code, and that no white paper was planned.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 VIRTUAL LAB: Qiling Framework: Build a Fuzzer Based on a 1day Bug
talks.teaser: Walks through emulating IoT firmware with an emulation framework and building an AFL++ fuzzer around a known 1-day bug.
talks.summary:
The lab starts from a problem familiar to IoT researchers: vendor firmware is hard to run outside the device. The speaker recounts earlier attempts, including extracting a camera image from flash and booting it under QEMU, and explains why a CPU-only emulation library, Unicorn, was chosen as the base for a cross-platform framework. The framework loads PE, ELF, Mach-O and UEFI files, supports x86, ARM, ARM64 and MIPS, and offers hooks, syscall replacement and file mapping for binaries that expect real files such as NVRAM data.

Attendees then followed a hands-on exercise in a Linux environment, installing AFL++ with Unicorn support and running a provided script against a D-Link DIR-815 CGI handler with a known bug. The script sets environment variables, uses a memory search hook to locate the target input in the emulated filesystem, and rewrites that input on each iteration to check whether the binary crashes. Later exercises covered a Tenda web server overflow as homework and a NETGEAR case that used a file system mapper to return fake data to the binary.

The main takeaway is a workflow: trace what the firmware needs at runtime, fake those resources, then fuzz from a bug that is already known. The speaker also noted that throughput can be raised by running several fuzzing instances and by snapshotting emulator state so that only the code under test is executed. Practitioners should expect to implement missing system behaviour by hand, since the emulator does not model the kernel.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D1T2 - MemoryRanger Comes to the Rescue Again
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows kernel file and token structures can be hijacked, and how a hypervisor enclave stops the attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how kernel-mode drivers can read and overwrite Windows kernel memory without hardware restrictions, so data such as file contents and process privileges can be altered without tripping built-in defenses. The speaker frames the problem around a researcher who keeps a formula in a file opened without shared access, and an attacker who wants to read or change it.

Three attacks are presented. Two target exclusively opened files: handle hijacking, which overwrites the object pointer in the kernel handle table, and NTFS data structure hijacking, which copies structures from the secret file into the attacker's file and must patch a thread ID before each access. The third is token stealing, which copies a privileged process's token structure to elevate privileges; in the demo it was used to disable Windows Defender. In the demos, PatchGuard did not react to any of these changes.

The speaker's tool, MemoryRanger, is a hypervisor-based project that moves newly loaded drivers into isolated enclaves, hooks ZwCreateFile to restrict access to file structures, and places token structures in a data-only enclave. The demos showed the attacks blocked. The speaker noted a performance cost from trapping memory access, which suits rarely accessed data more than frequently used data. The takeaway is that isolating drivers limits what an exploited bug can reach, even when not every vulnerability can be found.

talks.title: #HITBLockdown002 D1 VIRTUAL LAB - Car Hacking
talks.teaser: Walks beginners through CAN bus basics and a simulated car, showing how to find and inject the messages that control it.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how a modern car's internal network is organised, where sensors and control units exchange messages over several bus protocols. The speakers focus on CAN, explaining the frame layout, the identifier that indicates what a message controls, and the data field of up to eight bytes. They also note the CAN FD extension, which allows more data per frame, and describe differential signalling as a way to resist interference.

Next, the tools are introduced: candump logs traffic, canplayer replays a captured log, cansend injects a single frame, and cangen produces random traffic for fuzzing. The attendees then set up the ICSim instrument cluster simulator on a virtual CAN interface and use a controller to accelerate, brake, lock doors and signal. Watching cansniffer, the presenters map arbitration ID 244 to acceleration, 188 to turn signals and 19b to door locks by spotting which bytes change.

Crafting frames with cansend, the speakers push the simulated speedometer past its 220 mph limit, hold both turn signals on and open doors, showing that injected messages can override the controls. They point out that the simulator has harder levels that randomise the IDs, and they explain the evening CTF on physical and virtual benches. The main takeaway is that CAN carries no sender identity, so anyone with bus access can send any message.
