talks.title: #HITB2018DXB D2T1: DHCP Is Hard
talks.teaser: Walks through several DHCP client and server bugs, from stack overflows to a heap exploit chain on Linux.
talks.summary:
Felix Wilhelm, a security engineer on Google's product security team, presents vulnerabilities he found in popular DHCP software. Although DHCP looks like a small, harmless protocol, its type-length-value options are decoded by many type-specific routines, which makes them error-prone. The focus is on client and server bugs that lead to code execution, since a client flaw can be reached from a rogue access point or a compromised neighbour on the same network.

Several cases are covered. In dnsmasq, an option length is copied into a fixed stack buffer. In the ISC DHCP code, a reference counter is not decremented on an error path, so repeated malformed packets eventually wrap it and cause a use-after-free. A Red Hat helper script calls read without the raw flag, letting a malicious server inject shell commands for remote root on affected systems. In systemd-networkd, a length check that ignores the header size causes an underflow and heap overflow, and a missing position check enables an info leak.

The systemd-networkd chain is demonstrated end to end: the leak reveals a libc pointer that defeats ASLR, the heap overflow becomes an arbitrary write through tcache poisoning, and the free hook is pointed at system. A live demo shows a shell running as the systemd-networkd user, not root. The takeaways are that backward compatibility and default-enabled features widen attack surfaces, and that new network daemons should be written in a memory-safe language rather than C.

talks.title: #HITB2018DXB KEYNOTE 2: Cyber Arms Race
talks.teaser: Surveys how IoT expansion, crypto-focused crime and state cyber operations are reshaping the threat landscape for defenders.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the shift from isolated computers to networked ones and argues that connectivity is now spreading to ordinary appliances. The speaker expects even basic devices to join the internet because manufacturers want the data they generate, and points to industrial control panels and factory systems found exposed online, some with no password at all. Changing network configurations, such as a reconfigured router or a newly added remote link, are presented as a common way for once-isolated systems to become reachable.

The middle section turns to attacks. Mirai is described as a botnet that spread through IoT devices by scanning for Telnet services and trying default credentials, and it was used in a large denial-of-service attack on a major DNS provider in December 2016. The speaker also covers how criminals struggle to convert stolen data into spendable cash, which pushes them toward cryptocurrency exchanges and wallets. A 2017 Petya outbreak is cited as a state-linked attack that entered through a Ukrainian accounting package and then spread to companies worldwide.

The closing argument is that organisations cannot keep every intruder out and should assume a breach. The speaker recommends building a baseline of normal network traffic so unusual activity stands out, while acknowledging that false alarms will occur and that a baseline is unreliable if the network is already infected. Keeping attackers out remains worthwhile, but defenders should plan for failure as well.

talks.title: #HITB2018DXB KEYNOTE 1: Crouching Tiger, Sudden Keynote
talks.teaser: Examines why bug bounties and vulnerability markets fall short without internal labor, triage and patching capacity.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how vulnerability reporting moved from hired penetration testing to paid bug bounty programs, and why that shift has not fixed basic patching problems. The speaker draws on her years at Microsoft, where she helped start its bounty program, and on later work with governments. She argues that vulnerability disclosure is a process that works without cash rewards, and that bounties are only one tool within it.

Several cases anchor the argument. An Internet Explorer 11 beta bounty drew a burst of reports only after the beta ended, showing how timing and recognition shape what researchers send. The Uber breach, where a bounty payout was used to cover up stolen records, led to a $148 million penalty from the Federal Trade Commission, and the same hackers were later indicted after trying it on another organisation. A capped Hack the Pentagon pilot produced a better signal-to-noise ratio than a larger one. She also described a labour market of only a few thousand top researchers worldwide, active for about seven years, and said outbidding the black market is not the answer.

Her practical advice is to clear easy issues with internal tools first, define scope clearly, and build the triage and patching capacity needed before opening a bounty. Universities should also require security in computer science courses. Bounties work best as a supplement to skilled internal teams and professional testing, not as a replacement.

talks.title: BSides Dubai 2018: My Experience Of Running CTF Competitions In 7 Arab Countries
talks.teaser: Shares five insights from running more than 50 capture-the-flag contests across the MENA region and how they feed hiring.
talks.summary:
The speaker, the chief executive of the CyberTalents platform, reviews what the company has learned from more than 50 capture-the-flag competitions held in recent years across the Middle East and North Africa. The platform ranks participants and helps place them in part-time or full-time security roles. He frames the work around a shortage of cybersecurity professionals and argues that contests both surface talent and give practitioners peer recognition that salary alone does not.

The data covers roughly 9,000 members. About 88% were men and 12% women, although women often attended orientation sessions and then did not show up to live competitions, which led to a planned women-only contest. Around 90% of participants were aged 18 to 34, and about half were students or recent graduates. Egypt accounted for 36% of members, the UAE for 6.5% and Morocco for 4.5%; Saudi Arabia was excluded because no contest had yet been run there. The most common skill was web security, followed by digital forensics and then malware analysis. Language was a barrier because challenges were in English, so some players translated them locally. Ethical conduct and communication skills also varied, and the speaker suggested bug bounty work suits some people better than corporate roles.

The talk closes with beginner bootcamps, where each day covers a different domain, and the speaker said 80 to 85% of attendees went on to join competitions. Planned follow-ups include school-level contests and the women's event. In the Q&A, he explained that weekly public challenges test skills at graduated difficulty, and employers can filter candidates by the challenge categories they solved before interviews.

talks.title: #HITB2018DXB: Hacking Into Broadband And Broadcast TV Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how a smart TV's broadcast-delivered apps and browser can be abused to attack the TV and pivot into a home or office network.
talks.summary:
Smart TVs are increasingly used as projectors in offices and critical facilities, yet they add network interfaces, web-based applications and broadcast features that can open new routes into corporate networks. The speakers built an open-source test bed to assess one such set, pairing a DVB-T transmitter with the HbbTV test suite so that crafted broadcast streams could be sent to the TV. They first mapped its attack surface: an outdated Opera-based browser whose user agent claimed to be Chrome, bundled JavaScript libraries, the electronic program guide, and the XML AIT signalling used to install applications without authentication or user interaction. They also showed a fake-news overlay injected through the video stream and an application that survived a channel change, which suggested persistence.

The second part looked at the TV as a relay into the local network. Scripts running on the TV could scan internal ranges and services through JavaScript and WebSockets, and a crafted HbbTV application could be used to flood a remote website. The team then triggered a zero-day against an IP camera from the TV, and wrote JavaScript exploits for several routers, all delivered over the broadcast signal. Three zero-days were reported to the vendor, which asked for a six-month delay before publication.

The takeaway for practitioners is that these devices are often far behind current browser and platform security and leave few logs, so they can quietly become an entry point. The speakers recommended disabling unused interfaces such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and HbbTV where the option exists, assessing any device before it joins a sensitive network, and weighing the business benefit against what connecting it could expose.

talks.title: #HITB2018DXB: Building Security Beyond The Genesis Block
talks.teaser: Ryan Shepherd examines #HITB2018DXB: Building Security Beyond The Genesis Block.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at HITB2018DXB, the speaker examines cybersecurity within the blockchain sector through the lens of detection, response, and purple teaming. As an active detection and response investigator at Hunter [Hanna] Sept (an MWR company), the speaker argues that despite the academic hype around blockchain, real-world compromises in the space are technically very similar to conventional cyber attacks in other industries. The primary differences lie in the sector's low security maturity, immense financial incentives, and specific attacker objectives focused on rapid monetization.

### Key Topics
- **History of Major Exchange Hacks**: An analysis of high-profile incidents including Mt. Gox (unencrypted wallet files in 2011 and internal transaction system manipulation in 2014), Bitstamp (phishing via email and internal Skype pivoting), Bitfinex (flawed multi-signature validation implementation with third-party BitGo), Gatecoin (the DAO smart contract recursive call flaw), Bithumb (social engineering targeting an employee to steal 30,000 customer records), Coincheck (lack of cold storage and missing multi-signature controls for NEM hot wallets), and Binance (exploitation of API trading bot keys).
- **Attack Techniques and Delivery**: Common initial footholds rely on classic methods like phishing documents, clipboard stealers targeting pasted wallet addresses, social engineering, and compromised credentials/private keys. Rather than developing novel exploits against underlying cryptography, attackers repurpose existing tools because the sector's low defense maturity makes it a lucrative, low-risk target.
- **Detection, Threat Hunting, and Response**: The investigation of crypto-mining incidents using endpoint telemetry (process arguments and PowerShell execution) to uncover stages of execution, enumeration, persistence, and external connections to centralized mining pools. It highlights how defenders can extract hard-coded wallet addresses and node configs from payloads to perform on-chain intelligence.
- **Evaluating Blockchain Use Cases**: A critical assessment of whether a blockchain is truly needed (referencing a decision flow-chart paper by Wüst and Gervais). The speaker critiques marketing-driven implementations and examines the security trade-offs of private/permissioned ledgers (centralization vulnerabilities at validating master nodes) and the 'garbage in, garbage out' problem of bridging physical sensor data into an immutable ledger.

### Technical Details
- **Exchange Transaction Mechanics**: Cryptocurrency exchanges maintain order books and execute high-speed customer transactions off-chain within standard relational databases. On-chain blockchain transactions only occur when users deposit or withdraw funds. Consequently, attackers focus on compromising exchange backend databases or administrator/user accounts to trigger on-chain withdrawal transactions.
- **Forensic Visibility and Chain Analysis**: The transparency of public ledgers aids defensive investigations. Defenders can perform chain analysis to trace stolen funds across wallet hops until they reach an exchange or off-ramp. While ransomware operators previously accepted Bitcoin, increased tracing visibility has driven some towards privacy coins.
- **Payload Dissection**: In the examined cryptominer case study, malicious commands fetched payloads over FTP, ran PowerShell commands to identify the host operating system, downloaded secondary architectures, and beaconed to mining pool endpoints, exposing hard-coded configuration credentials.

### Takeaways
- Blockchain security failures are overwhelmingly traditional IT and application security failures: phishing, poor access management, unencrypted keys, software bugs, and social engineering.
- Immutability is a double-edged sword: once malicious or erroneous transactions are validated on-chain, they cannot be reversed without extreme measures such as hard forks (e.g., Ethereum and Ethereum Classic after the DAO).
- Organizations must critically question the necessity of a blockchain before adopting it, ensure security is integrated during development rather than treated as a marketing afterthought, and leverage endpoint detection combined with chain analysis for incident response.

talks.title: BSides Dubai 2018: Adversarial Attacks on Autonomous Cars - The Missed Gap
talks.teaser: Dr. Hoda Alkhzaimi details BSides Dubai 2018: Adversarial Attacks on Autonomous Cars - The Missed Gap.
talks.summary:
Rudolph Azeemi, Director of the Center for Cybersecurity at NYU Abu Dhabi, presents research on adversarial attacks targeting autonomous vehicle object detection systems. He contextualizes autonomous vehicle development from DARPA challenges in the 1970s–1980s to contemporary prototypes by Tesla and Uber, noting that by 2025, over $3.7 billion in semiconductor industry investment is expected. However, a critical security awareness gap exists: at the Dubai Autonomous World Challenge (350–400 submissions), fewer than 10% of entries addressed cybersecurity issues. Real-world failures underscore the risk—an Uber autonomous vehicle fatality in September 2018 when a pedestrian was struck, and Tesla incidents where object detection failed to identify obstacles.

The research team developed an object detector using YOLO (You Only Look Once), selected for efficiency and speed, paired with a generator to attack detection via adversarial examples—minimally modified images that fool deep learning models. The team experimented with one-pixel, three-pixel, and four-pixel attacks using differential evolution, testing on Udacity and CARLA simulators. The methodology mirrors physical attacks (such as UC Berkeley's work manipulating traffic signs) but uses algorithmic perturbations. By iteratively modifying pixels, the team generated adversarial samples barely perceptible to human eyes yet causing misclassification of road signs and objects.

The adversarial examples successfully altered the steering angle and trajectory of the simulated autonomous vehicle. Tiny pixel modifications created significant changes in classifier output, with the team demonstrating modified steering commands that shifted vehicle routes. They successfully fooled the Udacity classifier through one-pixel attacks, changing central and right-side camera images. Throttle control remained unmodified.

Azeemi emphasizes that autonomous vehicle security requires a holistic, multi-stakeholder approach involving academia, industry, and government. Testing must extend beyond lab environments to real-world scenarios. Current security algorithms lag behind autonomous vehicle deployment pace. The speaker advocates for bridging research-industry gaps, establishing measurable security models, and raising cybersecurity awareness among manufacturers. The presentation concludes with demonstrations at a car hacking village and announcements of an autonomous vehicle racing challenge for audience participation.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 CLOSING KEYNOTE: Rethinking The Cyber Kill Chain
talks.teaser: Reframes the cyber kill chain as a defender's framework, linking attack paths like pass-the-hash to layered controls and testing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks back at how security priorities shifted over about eight years, from availability attacks and firewall-era defenses, to data breaches and detection tooling, and now to resilience and integrity attacks that are harder to detect. The speaker argues that defenders must model their attack surface, avoid overpromising machine learning, and break down security silos through cross-team collaboration.

The core of the talk reworks the kill chain into a defender's framework. Using a pass-the-hash path from a compromised workstation to domain admin as the running example, the speaker maps each attacker step to techniques and then pairs them with candidate controls. Those controls are sorted by tactical versus strategic effort, and by whether a response is instinctive or informed, illustrated with a Batman and Wonder Woman comparison. Testing comes next, with tools such as BloodHound and a detection lab used to check whether controls actually hold, and the talk closes with a blue team view that maps controls to each stage.

The closing takeaways are to model the attack surface, engineer controls, test the attack path, and bring the results into operations so the cycle is complete. The speaker notes that defense is hard, manual work that tools cannot fully replace, and says collaboration is the piece that has been missing. Known attack paths should be covered before worrying about the unknown.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 D1: God Mode Unlocked: Hardware Backdoors In x86 CPUs
talks.teaser: Shows how an undocumented control register on a VIA C3 processor exposes a hidden core that bypasses x86 privilege rings.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the idea of hardware backdoors in processors through a case study on an older VIA C3 x86 chip. It opens with a demo in which an obscure instruction sequence lets an unprivileged process become root. The research started from patents that hinted at undocumented control registers, and because no developer manual existed for this chip, the work treated it as a black box. Enumerating about 1,300 model specific registers and using a timing side channel to group functionally similar ones narrowed the search to a small set of candidates.

Automated bit toggling on a rig of power-cycled test machines identified one global configuration bit that enabled a launch instruction. That instruction switched execution to a separate, non-x86 core. A modified fuzzer then found a bound instruction that forwards a 32-bit value to that core as a command. Around three weeks of fuzzing produced large logs of register state changes, which an automated tool used to recover the alternate instruction set. The recovered instructions were assembled into a payload that reads and writes kernel structures to grant root from ring 3.

The speaker noted that the enabling bit was already set by default on the tested system, so the ring 0 requirement offered little real protection there. An old datasheet, found later, mentioned the alternate instruction set only briefly and pointed to the vendor for access. The speaker concluded that the feature looked like a poorly implemented capability rather than a deliberate backdoor. The broader takeaway is that undocumented processor features should be treated as red flags, and that black-box analysis can expose them even without vendor documentation.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 D1: A Year Of Purple
talks.teaser: Ryan Shepherd analyzes #HITBGSEC 2018 D1: A Year Of Purple.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Hack in the Box GSEC 2018, Ryan Sheppard, a Detection and Response Investigator at Countercept (an MWR InfoSecurity company acquired by F-Secure), shares insights from his experiences bridging offensive and defensive security under the concept of purple teaming. Sheppard argues that skilled practitioners drive defensive technology rather than the reverse. He explores real-world case studies contrasting offline versus online investigation methods, discusses modern Incident Response (IR) collaboration alongside real-time attack detection during a major banking heist, and advocates for building isolated attack and defense simulation environments to safely cross-train security personnel.

### Key Topics
- **People Over Technology**: Emphasizing that analyst experience and methodology outweigh tool limitations, especially when critical telemetry or endpoint agents are unavailable.
- **The Time Factor in Investigations**: Comparing attacker dwell time and defensive urgency across low-level opportunistic malware versus long-duration Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs).
- **Attack Detection vs. Incident Response**: Evolving traditional IR from post-incident cleanup to proactive, real-time collaboration with detection teams during active intrusions.
- **Limitations of Red Team Engagements**: Understanding how artificial scope constraints limit what defenders can learn compared to unrestricted real-world adversaries.
- **Purple Team Simulation Labs**: Utilizing automated, isolated lab environments (such as DetectionLab) to safely mirror production estates, run attacks, and build detection pipelines.

### Technical Details
Sheppard details a case study where the same malware infection was analyzed by two different teams within one week:
- **First Team (Offline Host)**: Investigating historical data without active endpoint agent access, analysts identified suspicious PowerShell activity downloading a payload from an IP address. They retrieved the payload over Tor, revealing an obfuscated PowerShell script referencing open-source GitLab code designed for reflective DLL loading. Analyzing historical telemetry uncovered a phishing email vector delivering an `.scr` file disguised as a PDF via Outlook and Internet Explorer. Execution involved AutoIt scripting binaries (`fkqf.exe`) and `regsvcs.exe` (a .NET utility capable of registering COM objects and running code across privilege boundaries). Forensic clues included Windows UserAssist ROT13-encoded entries.
- **Second Team (Online Host)**: With endpoint agents active, analysts detected the reflective load directly into `regsvcs.exe`, captured memory thread mappings, gathered live network traces, and extracted process dumps. When the host went offline mid-investigation, analysts leveraged the Master File Table (MFT) to reconstruct file write timestamps back to the original Outlook download.

A secondary case study reviewed a $40 million bank heist where attackers bypassed standard credit card switch targets to access the generic transaction switch. Over a three-month reconnaissance and testing period, the adversaries reverse-engineered a custom switch application to issue automatic transaction authorization loops, enabling mules to withdraw funds with blank cards encoded only with target IBAN numbers. By analyzing attacker enumeration paths using BloodHound graph analysis, the defense team mapped relationship paths, closed critical privilege escalation routes, and detected the adversary's re-entry before initial users were compromised.

### Takeaways
- Purple teaming creates a direct feedback loop: offensive knowledge enhances threat hunting, threat hunting sharpens live attack detection, and attack detection empowers incident response.
- Long-running APT attacks offer defenders substantial time windows to identify anomalous reconnaissance or lateral movement before the final objective is executed.
- To overcome the risks of testing in production and the scope limitations of red teams, organizations should deploy standalone simulation labs utilizing tools like Sysmon, Windows Event Forwarding (WEF), Bro/Zeek, and the Elastic Stack (referencing open-source work by Chris Long).

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: Learning How To Smurf With Honeypots
talks.teaser: Shows how honeypot projects with students build blue team skills in threat intelligence, game theory and IoT.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that honeypots are most valuable as a learning tool for blue team skills, not only as a detection or deception device. The speaker describes a honeypot as any resource with no production role that exists to be attacked. Running one pushes people to think through architecture, data collection, analytics, forensics and operations.

Several student projects are used as examples. One applied threat intelligence, agreeing on a definition of intelligence before using a framework of objective, artifacts and data sources to design a honeynet. Another applied game theory by changing honeynet configurations to observe attacker reactions, limited to one strategy. A third mapped about 42 of 280 tactics onto a seven-step kill chain to predict attacker moves. A fourth built an IoT honeypot that diverted suspicious home traffic using a TensorFlow classifier, and honeyclients that collected data on malicious servers.

The speaker's main point is that these projects build domain knowledge: protocols, browsers, the threat landscape and attack chains must be understood before a useful honeypot can be built. Some projects proved costly to maintain, and one network was taken down. Practitioners are encouraged to use honeypots as a flexible way to test new blue team ideas and carry those skills back into their organisation's operations.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: Internet Of Things: Battle Of The Bots
talks.teaser: Tracks how Mirai botnet variants changed their encryption, exploits and monetization across a year of honeypot-collected samples.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at the Mirai IoT botnet, whose source code was published in 2016 and has since been reused by many copycat groups. The speaker walks through Mirai's parts: a command and control server, a report server, a loader and the bot itself. The bot carries attack, killer and scanner functions and spreads by scanning for Telnet devices that still use default credentials. Its configuration table is XOR-encoded, and many variants altered the UPX header so standard unpacking fails. The researchers restored the headers and automated decryption of the configuration to extract command and control details.

Over a year of monitoring, the team ran a low-interaction honeypot behind a FortiGate that routed Telnet traffic to a test network. They collected about 21,000 samples, roughly 15,000 of them Mirai-related, and identified around 120 variants, with 127 active by August. They counted about 47 XOR keys across variants, and some samples left their configuration unencrypted. They also detected 28 exploits, 16 of them unauthenticated and 14 dating from 2017 and 2018.

The talk closes with case studies. Satori, also called Okiru, targeted ARC processors and used exploits including a remote code execution flaw in Huawei devices and Realtek SDK issues, and one version swapped cryptocurrency mining wallets. OMG turned infected devices into proxy servers using brute force. Sora, Wicked and Omni, likely written by the same author, used a cross compiler and chose exploits by scanning specific ports, and one replaced the login page of vulnerable devices with a message mocking a well-known security journalist. The takeaway is that unpatched IoT devices and predictable encryption keep the botnet ecosystem growing.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: Cognitive Automation With Machine Learning In Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Rishi Kant explores #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: Cognitive Automation With Machine Learning In Cybersecurity.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC, the talk explores how cognitive automation and machine learning (ML) transform cybersecurity operations and risk management. The speaker, a security professional with over eleven years of experience across banking and defense projects, outlines the shift from legacy cryptographic protections to modern defense mechanisms required to counter dynamic infrastructure threats, zero-days, and complex attacks.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Cyber Threats:** The cybersecurity landscape historically focused on mathematical cryptography, hashing, and password brute-forcing in the 1980s and 1990s. Post-2000, threats expanded to viruses, worms, infrastructure attacks, and distributed denial of service (DDoS), rendering manual controls insufficient.
- **Cognitive Automation & Machine Learning Workflow:** Cognitive automation combines adaptive learning, natural language processing, speech recognition, and regular expressions to automate repetitive processes, reduce human error, and lower costs. The high-level ML pipeline involves data collection, categorization and clustering based on permissions and rules, feature selection (such as payloads or timing metrics), dataset creation, and continuous training with real-world data.
- **Operational Cybersecurity Applications:** ML enhances several frontline operations, including spam mitigation (e.g., Gmail and Outlook inbox categorization), anti-phishing, user identity theft detection, and data loss prevention (DLP) via automated data classification and labeling.

### Technical Details
- **Incident and Fraud Detection:** Traditional fraud detection relied heavily on manual verification and user notifications, resulting in medium processing speeds and medium accuracy due to human error. ML models enable real-time anomaly detection, achieving low human intervention, high speed, and approximately 98% accuracy. For external incident detection (such as brute-force attempts), timing metrics at the microsecond or nanosecond scale are analyzed to distinguish automated scripts from human users.
- **Event-Based Cyber Risk Architecture:** The speaker illustrates an architecture for event-based analysis using proxies, SIEM platforms, and network monitoring. Network flows from endpoints, servers, and data centers pass through a proxy server and feed into two analytical tracks: a forensic SIEM (handling incident verification, severity determination, event reconstruction, and post-event root cause analysis) and a real-time SIEM (providing real-time alerting, threat correlation, and enterprise log management). 
- **Data Standardization & Control Prediction:** Because disparate tools generate divergent reports, a common frame connector is required to normalize data into standardized event datasets. These aggregated datasets feed an analytical engine that performs deep packet analysis, NetFlow inspection, threat intelligence matching, and behavioral monitoring to predict required information security controls and evaluate organizational risk appetite.

### Takeaways
Machine learning and cognitive automation provide the adaptive, self-updating mechanisms necessary to match evolving cyber threats. By automating routine analysis, correlating real-time events, and continuously updating detection rules, organizations can decrease risk impact, optimize network defenses, and maintain consistent regulatory compliance across different geographic regions.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: SayaKenaHack: Breach Notification In Malaysia
talks.teaser: Walks through building a Malaysian breach-lookup site from a leaked phone-number dataset and the regulatory block that followed.
talks.summary:
Keith Rozario, an IT architect who says he has no security background, tells the story of a breach notification website he built for Malaysians. The trigger was a late 2017 forum post offering personal data on millions of people, including a set of 46.2 million mobile phone number records from 2014. He explains how the data surfaced first as a sample, then as a full file protected by a password that doubled as a link back to the seller's hidden service.

He then describes building the site. Visitors enter an IC number and get back their phone number with most digits masked, keeping only the last two visible, so they can confirm a match without the site exposing the full record. The design was serverless on AWS: a static front end on S3, an API, and a Lambda function that reads one masked row at a time from a database. The site drew more than a thousand users on its first day, then about 100,000 in a single day after newspaper coverage.

Trouble followed on the day of that coverage. Regulators blocked access after a complaint, arguing the site broke national law, and the speaker shut it down rather than risk legal action, changing the response to return an HTTP 451 status. He describes his fear of legal consequences and a meeting with the personal data protection commissioner, and says the project is still unfinished. Total AWS costs stayed under $60, mostly for loading the data into DynamoDB. The takeaway is that the legal and regulatory side of breach disclosure can matter as much as the engineering.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: The Trails Of WINDSHIFT APT
talks.teaser: Profiles the WINDSHIFT espionage group's targeting of individuals, its macOS malware, and its phishing tactics.
talks.summary:
The talk profiles WINDSHIFT, a cyber-espionage group that targets individuals rather than companies, particularly in the Middle East. The speaker argues that an APT is only as advanced as its target and suggests judging actors by operational security, success and detection. The group runs fake personas, sends tracking emails over long periods, and hosts short-lived phishing pages on free domains with free certificates. Its phishing and command-and-control servers are kept separate.

The malware section covers several samples. One signed macOS implant is launched through a crafted web page that abuses a custom URL scheme, showing that a registered handler can start a program without admin rights, unlike on Windows. A macOS screenshot tool sends captures to its server in clear text, and another sample reuses code from a 2012 surveillance tool. A Windows dropper shares that server, and its string decryption was recovered by emulating the routine with Unicorn driven from Binary Ninja instead of rewriting the algorithm. Overlaps with the Bahamut group are noted.

The speaker closes with the group's patience, budget and mistakes, such as a typo in the URL scheme, and reports that two command-and-control domains were taken down. Personal devices, which often lack endpoint protection, are a key blind spot. Planned follow-ups include detection rules and a MacBook lockdown guide.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC: Breaking Full Disk Encryption
talks.teaser: Shows how remote analysts examine disks behind proprietary full disk encryption using a bootable Linux live CD.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses forensic analysts who must examine a remote machine protected by proprietary full disk encryption that common open-source tools cannot read. The speaker presents BitScout, an open-source live CD that boots Linux, opens a VPN, and gives the analyst SSH access into a container. The machine's owner maps the physical drive into that container as a read-only block device, and all work happens in RAM so the host disk stays unchanged, which matters for forensically sound acquisition.

The demonstrations covered three cases. On a Windows 10 machine, the encrypted volume could not be read from the container, so the analyst ran a virtual machine on a write-protected disk overlay, used Volatility on a memory image to give a command shell SYSTEM privileges, and decoded a PowerShell payload that revealed a command-and-control address. Where no login was available, a saved snapshot's registry was edited to swap an accessibility executable for a command shell, and the decrypted disk was exported over a network block device. When Windows would not boot, a debugger attached to the hypervisor let the speaker patch a small implant into the boot code after the password prompt, read sectors over a serial pipe, and expose the decrypted disk through a FUSE driver.

The closing segment described writing to the decrypted drive to clean an infected system, but this was not demonstrated. The main takeaway is that the method works without reverse engineering the vendor's encryption product, so it can apply to proprietary tools that offer no forensic support.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 COMMSEC - Demystifying The Definitions Of Dark
talks.teaser: Untangles the terms surface web, deep web, dark web and darknet using everyday examples and the Tor network.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out to clear up how people use the terms surface web, deep web, dark web and darknet, which are often treated as if they meant the same thing. The surface web is content that search engines index. The deep web is everything they cannot reach, such as a webmail inbox behind a login, protected databases, password-protected forums and private social media posts, while some databases are exposed by misconfiguration and can still be found with search operators.

The dark web is presented as a small subset of the deep web, made up of onion services that can only be reached through the Tor browser. The speaker points to a marketplace administrator who was arrested and sentenced, and to a 2017 Singapore case involving illegal financial accounts bought there. He cites researcher counts of about 30,000 onion websites in 2016 and 50,000 in 2017. The darknet term is traced to an older Microsoft-authored paper that described file-sharing networks such as eDonkey and LimeWire, and to a later academic definition built around encryption and anonymous participation, covering Tor, Freenet, I2P and ZeroNet.

The practical takeaway is that using Tor does not by itself put you on the dark web. Loading ordinary sites through Tor keeps you on the surface web, and only onion addresses count as dark web. The speaker argues that news coverage should say dark web when it means onion sites, and that the iceberg picture shows how much content sits beyond what a search engine can reach.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2018 - COMMSEC: Welcome Address
talks.teaser: A zero-day broker describes modernizing exploit sales, major bounties, and a confidential web platform for researchers and lawful agencies.
talks.summary:
The welcome address opens with a fast overview of a Dubai-based firm founded in 2017 and publicly launched in April 2018. The speaker explains a mission to modernize the zero-day market, which still reflects habits from the last fifteen to twenty years even as nation-states and agencies treat these capabilities as strategic tools for intelligence and investigations.

The company buys and refines vulnerabilities for information-gathering customers, including law enforcement and intelligence agencies, while declining offers aimed at critical infrastructure, ICS, SCADA, IoT, healthcare, and similar targets it does not want to arm as cyber weapons. It cites a ten-million-dollar bounty program, published interest lists, and lab work that tests, documents, and polishes researcher code so buyers get reliable deliverables instead of scams or rough proofs. Payment examples include iOS chains priced far above public vendor programs.

The centerpiece is an upcoming vulnerability research platform meant to standardize submission, discussion, pricing, and purchase over encrypted channels, with contracts and digital signing built in. Practitioners hear how voluntary community participation, filtering of unacceptable targets, and higher quality bar align seller speed and buyer expectations in a lawful, confidential workflow.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CLOSING KEYNOTE - Security is What We Make of It - Blockchain and Beyond
talks.teaser: Argues that blockchain should be treated as an information security product, and weighs its privacy and governance trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who had just left a blockchain programme leadership role at a major bank, opens by arguing that blockchain is fundamentally an information security product and should be assessed as one. He notes that the technology is often misunderstood, that a plain database is often enough, and that public chains struggle with consensus speed, settlement finality and contested governance. He sorts the field into public networks, enterprise distributed ledgers and a likely hybrid model, and explains the trade-off between openness, resilience, privacy and performance.

The middle section covers privacy and geopolitics. Public chains are effectively world-readable, and tracing tools can deanonymise participants, so enterprise adoption needs confidential transactions. He describes state-backed cryptocurrency projects in several countries, the risk of fractured networks, and the open question of who controls private keys for identity systems. He argues that the security model shifts from perimeter defence toward integrated controls, and that gaps remain in smart contract tooling, identity and access management, oracle veracity, and threat modelling.

He closes by calling for people beyond cryptographers and blockchain specialists, including usability experts, red and blue teamers, risk managers, and policy and economics people, to shape these systems before they mature. His takeaway is to treat blockchain with the same rigour as any production infrastructure, since its security and privacy properties are not yet settled.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D2T1 - Expanding Your WMI Lateral Movement Arsenal
talks.teaser: Shows new WMI-based lateral movement methods that avoid the service, task and process artifacts defenders usually watch for.
talks.summary:
Lateral movement, as defined here, means running code on another Windows machine with stolen credentials through features built for remote execution. Because those features have legitimate uses, they are rarely patched. The familiar options, such as PsExec-style service creation and remote task scheduling, are easy to spot, so the talk looks at Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) as an alternative, since it works remotely over DCOM.

Several methods are demonstrated. Deriving a new subclass of Win32_Process hides the parent class name, but the underlying create call still appears in provider events. Service classes mirror sc.exe, and their network traffic looks like generic WMI calls rather than service operations. Scheduled-task classes can replace at.exe on older systems, while the newer task class only works from Windows 8 onward. A Win32_Product install can run an MSI payload without creating services or tasks. The speaker also registers a custom WMI provider whose COM local server runs an arbitrary command as SYSTEM, using a hosting model that avoids a noisy event log entry. Finally, the boot configuration store is altered to replace the boot loader, shown with calc.exe.

For detection, the WMI activity ETW provider and WMI's own event introspection reveal most of these techniques, although ETW does not expose method arguments. The main takeaway is that few teams watch WMI closely, so defenders should know which classes and providers exist on their systems and monitor activity around them.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D2T1 - Backdooring & Remotely Controlling Cars
talks.teaser: Sheila A. Berta details #HITB2018AMS D2T1 - Backdooring & Remotely Controlling Cars.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At HITB2018AMS, Claudio and Sheila from ElevenPaths (the cybersecurity unit of Telefónica in Argentina) presented their research on backdooring and remotely controlling cars that lack native internet or cellular connectivity. While prior prominent car hacking research focused on modern connected vehicles equipped with built-in GPS or Wi-Fi, older or emerging-market vehicles—such as many in Argentina—lack factory connectivity. To address this, the presenters designed a custom hardware implant and software framework to inject CAN bus messages remotely via GSM/SMS.

### Key Topics
- **Physical and Safety Challenges**: Hacking vehicle networks carries physical risks. Errant frame injection can trigger engine protections and disable vehicle functionality, requiring diagnostic resets or battery disconnects.
- **CAN Bus Fundamentals**: The Controller Area Network (CAN) operates as a broadcast bus using differential signaling (CAN High and CAN Low) and inverted logic (dominant 0, recessive 1). Frame arbitration prioritizes lower IDs (such as engine communications), but frames carry no source or destination addresses or explicit content identifiers.
- **Reverse Engineering CAN Frames**: Identifying specific actions (e.g., turning on headlights or accelerating) requires systematically triggering actions and inspecting changing bytes using tools like oscilloscopes or CAN analyzers.
- **The "El Vicho" Implant**: To overcome latency and physical range limits of Bluetooth or software-based injectors, the researchers developed custom hardware called "El Vicho" to inject high-frequency frames directly via an OBD-II port connection.
- **Open-Source Ecosystem**: The project includes the hardware implant, a desktop configuration interface, and "Open CANdb", a crowdsourced online repository for sharing vehicle-specific CAN frame IDs.

### Technical Details
- **Vehicle Interfacing**: Communication relies on OBD-II pins 6 (CAN High) and 14 (CAN Low).
- **Hardware Evolution**:
  - *Version 1*: Built on a Microchip PIC18F (PIC18F2585/PIC18F2685) microcontroller with CAN transceiver and firmware written in assembly to achieve high-frequency injection to beat legitimate node chatter. Paired with a SIM900 GSM module to receive SMS trigger commands, but required hardcoding frame data directly in firmware.
  - *Version 2*: Added a USB interface, a physical toggle switch between Programming Mode (via PC) and Hacking Mode (vehicle deployment), and expanded firmware supporting configurable triggers and sender phone number whitelisting.
  - *Version 3*: Mini-USB hardware iteration with refined firmware features.
- **Payloads and Attack Scenarios**:
  - **SMS Control**: Injects preconfigured CAN frames when specific text messages are received (demonstrated by remotely actuating brake lights and accelerator pedal).
  - **GPS Geofencing**: Automatically executes frame injection payloads when entering specific coordinates.
  - **CAN Condition Triggers**: Monitors the bus and triggers an attack (such as actuating brakes) when a specific frame (such as turning on the air conditioner) is observed.
  - **Sheila-Kill (Bus Denial-of-Service)**: Floods the CAN bus with the lowest ID frames (mostly zeros), seizing bus arbitration priority and causing vehicle ECUs to stop functioning.

### Takeaways
- CAN bus architectures lack inherent encryption, authentication, or granular logging within ECUs, allowing injected high-rate frames to override legitimate ECUs.
- Older and non-connected cars can be transformed into remotely controlled vehicles using low-cost hardware backdoors placed via social engineering, valet services, or car washes.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D2T2 - Over The Edge: Pwning The Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Rancho Han analyzes #HITB2018AMS D2T2 - Over The Edge: Pwning The Windows Kernel.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at HITB 2018 Amsterdam, Ran Chen from Tencent Security Xuanwu Lab discusses methods for auditing, fuzzing, and exploiting the Windows kernel to escape the Microsoft Edge sandbox. The talk covers techniques for discovering vulnerabilities within the win32k subsystem and DirectX graphics kernel driver, as well as breaking sandbox boundaries using both win32k system call filtering bypasses and driver vulnerabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Win32k Subsystem Analysis and Fuzzing**: Overview of win32k architecture, focusing on User and GDI objects, tracking object allocations (`HMAllocObject`, `AllocateObject`), and fuzzing object relationships and state changes.
- **Unconventional Win32k Attack Surfaces**: Exploring deprecated/moved system calls in function tables (`gapfnMessageCall`, `apfnSimpleCall`), hooking user-mode callback mechanisms via the Process Environment Block (`PEB->KernelCallbackTable`), and auditing public GDI objects with owner PID 0.
- **Edge Sandbox Mitigation & Bypasses**: Bypassing Edge's win32k system call filter by abusing Chakra JavaScript engine's out-of-process JIT server handle permissions, and transitioning to DirectX graphics drivers due to increased kernel mitigations like Type Isolation.

### Technical Details
- **CVE-2017-8465 (Cursor Use-After-Free)**: Discovered in win32k's cursor linking mechanism (`UnlinkCursor`). Linking two cursors forms a doubly-linked list. By altering the head pointer and destroying the cursors in sequence, a dangling pointer in the first cursor is freed twice. The freed cursor memory is reclaimed using accelerator table objects, manipulating pointer references to achieve an arbitrary bit modification via `HMMarkObjectDestroy` and abusing palette primitives to gain full kernel object access.
- **Chakra Out-of-Process JIT Handle Duplicate Issue**: In Edge builds with out-of-process JIT (introduced around Windows 10 Insider Build 15048), win32k filtering was not applied to the JIT server process. The Edge content process held a communication handle to the JIT server with duplicate handle permissions. An attacker could duplicate a full-access process handle from the JIT server, inject shellcode into the JIT process, and bypass win32k system call filtering completely.
- **CVE-2017-8580 (Palette Use-After-Free)**: The `EngDeletePalette` function passed a shared lock count parameter that could free a palette object with a non-zero reference count. When creating a Device-Independent Bitmap (DIB), win32k creates a public palette with a shared count of 1. After querying the GDI shared handle table to locate and delete the palette, its memory was reclaimed with magnifier objects. Calling `GreSetDIBColorTable` copied data over the freed palette, achieving arbitrary read/write.
- **CVE-2018-0977 (DirectX Driver Vulnerability)**: With Windows 10 RS4 introducing Type Isolation (separating metadata from GDI object headers and breaking traditional bitmap/palette exploitation primitives), focus shifted to the DirectX graphics driver. An untrusted command submitted to the driver triggered execution in a system process worker thread. By controlling `rdi` and `rax` registers without kernel CFG checks, the speaker used named pipes (`NPFS`) to spray and lay out kernel data, leveraged an unpatched kernel info leak for address calculations, and executed a ROP chain to achieve arbitrary read/write and elevation of privilege.

### Takeaways
As win32k mitigations such as system call filtering and Type Isolation continue to mature, traditional GDI exploitation primitives are largely eliminated. Attackers and researchers must identify architectural flaws (such as IPC and handle management in multi-process architectures like Chakra JIT) or pivot to alternative attack surfaces like the DirectX kernel subsystem to achieve full system compromise.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS KEYNOTE 2 - A Risk Assessment of Logo Disclosures
talks.teaser: Examines how security marketing can create harm through hype, logos and early disclosure, and suggests standards to fix it.
talks.summary:
Jennifer Leggio, a security marketer, argues that people who promote security work share responsibility for reducing harm alongside the researchers and engineers who produce it. She says the marketing and technical sides have long been divided, and that each needs the other to fix the problems in the field.

She then walks through cases where communication went wrong. The Heartbleed name and logo, created by a marketing team, branded the flaw and drew attention from executives and boards, which pulled security teams into upward reporting instead of fixing systems. She also describes a firm that announced AMD processor flaws by press release with little notice, a move criticised as breaking coordinated disclosure. A third case involved publicising a ransomware weakness in a way that could help the malware's authors close it.

To close, she offers a rough decision tree for marketers: check whether coordinated disclosure has happened, whether the message is scary or spun, and whether researchers are credited. She proposes a standards review desk like those at news organisations, urges peers to give constructive feedback, and says a company without a disclosure policy should build one. In questions, she advised framing risk in terms of reputation for marketers who are not motivated by security, and distinguished quiet sharing within trusted communities from public marketing campaigns.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D1T2 - Rooting Android 8 with a Kernel Space Mirroring Attack
talks.teaser: Explains how a media codec bug and a kernel space mirroring technique lead to root on Android 8 devices.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how root remains reachable on Android 8 despite newer kernel and memory mitigations. The first route starts with a malformed MP4 file that crashes a media codec process. The speakers traced the crash to a stack buffer overflow, where width and height fields in the file control how much pixel data gets written. They overwrite a function pointer on the stack to hijack control flow, then hook the default OMX decoder selection so their code runs inside the media server, which lacks the codec's sandbox.

The second route is a kernel use-after-free in the notification subsystem, where a race between two calls leaves a stale object that attacker data can refill. Heap spraying and carefully sized allocations give them a kernel pointer leak to defeat address randomization, then arbitrary read. Page-table protections still block direct use of kernel memory from user mode, so they introduce kernel space mirroring attack. By editing level 1 page table entries, a kernel data region also gets a user-accessible mapping, letting them overwrite process credentials and spawn a root shell. A phone demo ran with the mitigations enabled.

The takeaway is that the mitigations make rooting Android harder but not impossible. Kernel bugs in drivers and media components remain the weak point, and page-table protections must hold against an attacker who can write to memory. The codec bug used in the first route had been fixed only days before the talk.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D1T1 - How to Analyze and Find Bugs in MacOS and iOS Kernel Drivers
talks.teaser: Shows how kernel drivers on macOS and iOS are analyzed for bugs, covering two vulnerabilities and a new reversing tool.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the case for kernel drivers as attack surface on macOS and iOS. Drivers run inside the kernel's space, so a bug in one can give full kernel control. They are reached from user space through IOKit user clients, and some remain callable from sandboxed apps on iOS. The speakers walk through how drivers are located, how their entry points such as external methods and shared memory work, and why they have been used in real jailbreaks.

The middle of the talk covers two vulnerabilities found in Apple drivers. The first is an information leak in which an output buffer was never initialized and an out-of-memory path returned its stale contents, exposing a kernel pointer that defeated address randomization. The second is a race condition in another driver where one thread freed a buffer while another still used it, a use-after-free that gave control of the program counter. To reach root, the chain used a ROP sequence and a property-reading path. Newer macOS versions lacked classic gadgets, so the speakers located replacement gadgets. Apple issued two CVEs and fixed the issues in macOS 10.13.4.

The speakers then describe the analysis obstacles: driver binaries lack symbols, and C++ class metadata and vtables are hard to follow. To address this they present Ryoga, a plugin for IDA Pro that recovers classes from initialization functions, reconstructs vtables, names virtual functions and resolves object types so call graphs can be built. The practical takeaway is that kernel drivers are often weaker than the core kernel and that better tooling makes them easier to audit. The tool has been released as open source on GitHub.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D1T2 - Pwning KNX & ZigBee Networks
talks.teaser: HuiYu Wu explores #HITB2018AMS D1T2 - Pwning KNX & ZigBee Networks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Hack in the Box Amsterdam 2018 (HITB2018AMS), researchers Nikki and Allen from Tencent's security team examine vulnerabilities in intelligent building management systems. Highlighting a relative lack of public security research despite increasing IoT adoption in modern buildings, the speakers target two of the most ubiquitous building automation and home automation protocols: ZigBee and KNX. They showcase practical attacks, culminating in a demonstration of controlling smart lighting systems remotely, including via a drone, and attacking room controls in a luxury hotel.

### Key Topics
- **Intelligent Building Architecture**: Systems for lighting control, fire detection, and access control spanning home automation and industrial building automation.
- **ZigBee Network Vulnerabilities**: Examination of ZigBee topologies (cluster tree, star, mesh) and device types (coordinator, router, end device), noting weaknesses in key distribution, storage, and replay counter mechanisms.
- **Automated ZigBee Attack Tool (Zombie)**: Development of a multi-transceiver attack platform built on a Raspberry Pi 3B to overcome radio coverage limitations and scan across multiple ZigBee channels simultaneously.
- **KNX Architecture and Protocol Analysis**: Structure of KNX networks over twisted pair (TP) and IP (KNXnet/IP), detailing group objects, physical addressing, couplers, and default group filtering configurations.
- **KNX Security Exploitation**: Practical attack scenarios against unisolated LANs and physically accessed twisted-pair buses in a hotel, including default key exploitation and group filter table reconfiguration.
- **Security Recommendations**: Countermeasures for both ZigBee and KNX deployments to mitigate unauthorized interception and command injection.

### Technical Details
- **ZigBee Attacks & "Zombie" Tool**: 
  - ZigBee utilizes 128-bit AES symmetric cryptography with link keys, network keys, and master keys across distributed or centralized security models. Common failure modes include well-known default keys (such as ZigBee Alliance default link keys), insecure over-the-air key transmission during node joining or rejoining, insecure storage in flash/firmware, and bypassable replay protection once network keys are sniffed.
  - To resolve channel-hopping and signal-range constraints during automated building auditing, the researchers built "Zombie," a multi-radio device powered by a Raspberry Pi 3B and multiple CC2531 USB dongles. Zombie spins up virtual network devices with randomized addresses and initial sequence numbers to broadcast attack payloads with valid PAN IDs across multiple channels.
- **KNX Attacks & Hotel Case Study**: 
  - KNX transmits Common External Message Interface (cEMI) frames over UDP port 3671 for KNXnet/IP. While "KNX Secure" (Data Secure and IP Secure) exists in modern specifications, legacy deployments lack encryption and authentication.
  - In a tested 300-meter-high hotel featuring 340 rooms with KNX-controlled lighting, thermostats, TVs, and curtains, the KNX network was isolated from external ethernet/Wi-Fi. The researchers gained physical access to the room's locked utility closet, tapped the twisted-pair bus using a USB interface, and mapped out individual room addresses and group objects.
  - By identifying that IP router couplers shared between adjacent rooms were protected only by default factory authorization keys (`0xFFFF`), they used ETS software to rewrite router group filter tables. This enabled injection of malicious telegrams from one guest room into another, allowing arbitrary control over devices in neighboring rooms.

### Takeaways
To defend ZigBee deployments, organizations must routinely update network keys, avoid well-known default pre-configured keys, and consider higher-layer application encryption. For KNX networks, operators must physically protect bus cables, segment and isolate networks per room, avoid exposing KNXnet/IP to public or untrusted Wi-Fi networks, update to modern ETS versions supporting KNX Secure, and immediately replace default authorization keys (`0xFFFF`) on routers and couplers.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D1T2 - Smashing Ethereum Smart Contracts for Fun and ACTUAL Profit
talks.teaser: Walks through Ethereum smart contract flaws, using Mythril and symbolic execution to find bugs and generate exploits with Z3.
talks.summary:
Ethereum runs state changes through smart contracts executed in the Ethereum Virtual Machine. Its instruction set is Turing-complete, which allows flexible use cases but also opens room for bugs. The talk reviews recent incidents in which flaws in contract code led to hundreds of millions of dollars in Ether being stolen or locked permanently, and it sorts the common kinds of flaws found in these contracts. The Parity exploit is among the cases referenced.

The middle of the talk focuses on tooling. The speaker uses Mythril, described as an nmap-like tool for Ethereum, to explore the blockchain and reverse engineer contract bytecode. Symbolic analysis is then applied to detect several vulnerability types, including those that arise from calls between contracts. Walkthroughs show how execution paths and the conditions needed to reach a vulnerable point can be examined this way.

The final section shows how to generate exploits automatically with the Z3 solver, so that the constraints on a path produce an input that triggers the flaw. The main takeaway for practitioners is that contract code can be analysed with symbolic tools before deployment, since problems in deployed contracts are difficult to fix.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS D1T1 - Real World Attacks Against Secure Elements
talks.teaser: Shows how Apple's MFi secure element provisioning for Wi-Fi accessories can be abused to obtain network keys.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher Don analyzes the fundamental architectural limitations of secure elements deployed at scale, focusing specifically on Apple's Wireless Accessory Configuration (WAC) and Made for iPhone (MFI) chip ecosystem. Drawing an analogy to Capgras syndrome—where a person believes a familiar entity has been replaced by an impostor—the speaker demonstrates how IoT provisioning mechanisms fail to establish a trusted chain of identity between an accessory's application processor, the external secure element, and the configuring mobile device.

### Key Topics
- **IoT Identity and Secure Elements at Scale**: The challenge of provisioning millions of embedded devices securely without ballooning manufacturing complexity and cost.
- **Apple WAC and MFI Architecture**: How iOS configures Wi-Fi and network credentials on IoT accessories using MFI authentication chips.
- **Threat Models of Secure Elements**: An analysis of three standard architectural models: the flash/no-SE model, the external secure element model (e.g., Apple MFI, Ledger Nano S), and the internal element/ARM TrustZone model.
- **Man-in-the-Middle Provisioning Exploits**: Spoofing WAC beacons and relaying authentication traffic to coerce devices into leaking Wi-Fi provisioning credentials.

### Technical Details
Apple's WAC protocol allows an iOS device to discover an unconfigured accessory via Wi-Fi beacons and provision credentials over HTTP to an embedded MFI chip. The MFI chip securely signs authentication challenges to verify itself as a legitimate Apple-authorized accessory. However, because the accessory's application processor (typically a low-cost microcontroller such as an ARM Cortex-M0+) lives in an insecure world and ultimately requires the Wi-Fi credentials to join the network, the credentials held in escrow by the MFI chip must eventually be handed off across an unauthenticated physical bus.

The speaker exploits this architectural gap using a test harness consisting of:
- **hostapd**: Configured with a Wi-Fi vendor-specific element (Type `0xDD`) containing Apple’s OUI (`00:0A:F5` / `00:0a:f0`) to advertise a rogue access point as a WAC-compatible accessory.
- **mDNS Forwarding (`fling` and `moops`)**: Because iOS looks for MFI configuration over multicast DNS, the speaker used custom Python tooling (`moops` / My Object-Oriented Packet Spoofer and a relay script named `fling`) to rewrite and bridge multicast frames across distinct network interfaces.
- **Instrumented Target Accessory**: By flashing custom firmware onto a compromised MFI-bearing accessory (or communicating over a serial UART interface), the attacker acts as a man-in-the-middle between iOS and the real MFI chip. When iOS attempts to configure the device, the setup requests are relayed to the MFI chip, authenticating the exchange and prompting iOS to transmit network provisioning keys to the attacker.

The speaker compares this to Salim Rashid's attack on the Ledger Nano S, where the application processor tricks the external secure element by manipulating flash memory mappings during validation. Both illustrate that external secure elements cannot reliably attest to the integrity or identity of the application processors communicating with them.

### Takeaways
The speaker highlights that the core failure in external secure element architectures is the lack of mutual attestation between the application processor and the secure element: the SE only authenticates its own silicon, not the surrounding host system. While internal hardware security architectures like ARM TrustZone mitigate bus sniffing, they introduce proprietary black-box implementations and often leave external DDR RAM buses unencrypted. Remediating these vulnerabilities across large-scale ecosystems requires coordinated protocol updates, application specification redesigns, and costly per-device manufacturing key injection. Consequently, these architectural gaps persist across consumer IoT ecosystems.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS KEYNOTE 1: The Future, The Past, and … Wait, Where the Hell are We Now?
talks.teaser: Traces a researcher's shift from antivirus detection to CPU microarchitecture research and a women-only reverse engineering bootcamp.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who now works as a security engineer at Intel, opens with a career path that runs from antivirus signature work through advanced threat protection, reverse engineering tools and incident response. The central argument is that pattern-based detection, whether signatures, indicators of compromise or machine learning, always chases threats that are already known. The talk also argues that static analysis tooling is underfunded, because the open-source developers who build it often cannot make a living from it.

The middle section draws on several experiences. At a security expo booth, customers asked about scaling, update workflows and data formats rather than detection quality. At a European policy conference, officials focused on cyber norms and diplomacy rather than binaries. The speaker also reviews nation-state malware analysis, noting that many advanced samples are less sophisticated than commercial software and that analysts rarely understand the political motives behind them. Incident response on large networks is presented as a recurring problem: defenders often cannot trace how an intrusion entered, and a hospital case is used to illustrate unmanaged admin accounts and internet-exposed legacy servers.

The closing section covers the speaker's move into CPU microarchitecture research and the value of returning to basics, such as writing a first hello-world program in an unfamiliar domain. It then describes a free reverse engineering bootcamp for women that has run for three editions, with attendance growing each year and alumni moving into new research areas and teaching spin-off events. The takeaway for practitioners is to accept discomfort when learning a new field and to make technical spaces more welcoming to newcomers.

talks.teaser: Michel van Eeten explores #HITB2018AMS Welcome Address: Improving Incentives for Cybersecurity.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Smart Contract (In)Security
talks.teaser: Ben Schmidt explores #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Smart Contract (In)Security.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Hacking a Hospital for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Shows how a red team reached domain admin and exposed unsecured medical devices, PLCs and imaging systems in a hospital network.
talks.summary:
The team, working with a hospital client, set out to test how well a medical facility's network and devices were protected. Their physical walk-through began in the cafeteria, where an open Wi-Fi network turned out to bridge into the internal LAN, and wall jacks in public waiting areas gave them valid internal addresses. A Windows 7 kiosk used for patient check-in had a logged-in user with local administrator rights and domain membership, which gave them a path to domain admin within hours. The network was largely flat with no segmentation, and the antivirus was out of date.

The middle of the talk covered the medical equipment. DICOM traffic between imaging devices and the PACS server was unencrypted, so a simple man-in-the-middle position exposed patient images. A portable CT unit ran an unauthenticated VNC server and stored historical exams with patient names and IDs locally. PLCs controlling operating room air conditioning and medical gas pumps were reachable over plain HTTP, and their technician configuration was protected only by a trivial default passcode. An EKG device had default FTP credentials and a command injection flaw in its proprietary telnet-style CLI, which let the team run their own ARM code on it.

The closing point was that these devices receive functionality updates but rarely security patches, leaving them years behind current IoT security practice. The speakers argued that hospitals must treat medical devices as part of their threat model, since tampered results or altered equipment could directly affect patient care.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - PyREBox: Making Dynamic Instrumentation Great Again
talks.teaser: Presents PyREBox, a QEMU-based tool for Python-scripted instrumentation, and shows its use in malware analysis.
talks.summary:
PyREBox is an open-source reverse engineering tool built atop the QEMU emulator that gives analysts dynamic instrumentation and debugging of a running virtual machine. The talk starts with why the speaker chose full-system emulation over alternatives such as KVM-based approaches, which tie guest and host architectures together, and over existing QEMU-based frameworks that require plugins written in C or C++. Because the tool keeps its changes to QEMU small, the Python layer stays decoupled and is easier to upgrade.

The design section covers how the Python layer is attached to QEMU and how Volatility is used for virtual machine introspection, recovering processes, DLLs, handles and symbols from raw guest memory. To keep Python overhead manageable for frequent events such as instruction execution, the tool uses small compiled trigger snippets that decide whether a callback reaches a Python handler. A live demo shows an interactive shell for listing processes, setting breakpoints in a guest process and writing scripts, with an optional guest agent used only for file transfer and automation.

The final part presents Malware Monitor, a set of scripts covering API tracing, memory dumping, code coverage and memory event logging, all configured through JSON. A demo follows a sample that injects code into a service host process, where the logs point to an injected buffer and the memory dump is taken at a file creation call. The results are then imported into IDA Pro to colour basic blocks and annotate API calls. The speaker closes with a roadmap that includes ARM and MIPS support and integration with other frameworks.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - ProdSec: A Technical Approach
talks.teaser: Jeremy Brown analyzes #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - ProdSec: A Technical Approach.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Automatic Generation of ROP Chains
talks.teaser: A tool builds ROP chains from specified operations and evaluates gadget availability across Windows releases.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames memory corruption and control-flow hijacking, then explains how return-oriented programming sidesteps write-or-execute and data execution prevention by chaining gadgets already present in executable pages. The speakers tie that idea to a random-access-machine model: if each primitive operation has at least one gadget, an attacker can approximate arbitrary computation, though their conditional-branch definitions remain incomplete.

They introduce an open Python 3 utility integrated with Capstone that accepts a binary plus a text description of desired operations, including user-defined primitives via XML, and emits matching gadget addresses. Evaluation scans common Windows system DLLs across versions from XP through 10 in 32- and 64-bit builds inside virtual machines, reporting that combinations such as ntdll with shell-related libraries usually supply full RAM sets except branches. A case study walks through CVE-2010-3333 in Microsoft Office RTF parsing, building a chain that calls SetProcessDEPPolicy and demonstrating calculator launch from Word with DEP enabled on Windows 7.

Practitioners gain a concrete automation path for DEP-aware exploit development, empirical gadget coverage tables for Windows targets, and limits to watch—branching semantics, gadget side effects, and weaker 64-bit gadget density compared with 32-bit environments.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Hiding Tasks via Hardware Task Switching
talks.teaser: Kyeong Joo Jung examines #HITB2018AMS CommSec D2 - Hiding Tasks via Hardware Task Switching.
