talks.teaser: Stephen Hilt explores #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Attacking IoT Speakers.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - A Deep Dive Into Malicious Documents
talks.teaser: Surveys how malicious Office documents hide macro code, embedded shellcode and staged payloads, and how analysts extract them.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys techniques seen in malicious Office documents over the past year, focusing on features built into the suite rather than new exploits. Social engineering is the key step, since a user must open the file and enable macros. Lures include a fake message claiming the file is incompatible and needs content enabled, a password-protected attachment, and a polished fake shipping notice. Macros usually act as a first stage that leads to PowerShell, scripts, shellcode, or DLLs.

Analysis starts with dumping OLE streams using a Python script to list and decompress macro code, then moves to the Office developer tools, where user forms can be opened and macros stepped through with breakpoints and watches. Each case differs. One document hid a Windows executable as decimal text in a user form, and macro code converted it back to binary. Another passed shellcode to the EnumDateFormats API as a callback, and breakpoints revealed the memory base and entry offset. A third ran a base64-encoded PowerShell script hidden among interleaved bytes. A macro-free file embedded VBScript that dropped files with certutil, and a Mac variant opened a reverse shell through MacScript.

Obfuscation such as string concatenation, junk variables, pointless loops, and aliased API imports slows manual reading. The speaker also notes that a document password can stop automated sandboxes from reaching the payload. The takeaway is that the IDE and selective debugging can expose hidden code faster than tracing it by hand.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Faster, Wider, Greater: Modern Pentest Tricks
talks.teaser: Thomas Debize examines #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Faster, Wider, Greater: Modern Pentest Tricks.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - How to Find and Exploit Bugs in IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how JTAG, UART and chip-off access exposed open debug ports and plaintext secrets on consumer IoT devices.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a digital forensics investigator, starts from the observation that most IoT research targets Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, SDR or NFC, while hardware routes get little attention. He presents physical access as a way to reach device memory when software paths are closed. The main options he covers are JTAG, which needs as few as four test points on small devices compared with about nine for phones; UART serial consoles; ISP clips that attach very thin wires to the lines of nearby memory chips; and chip-off, where a package is heated with infrared rework equipment and read on a BGA adapter.

For the demonstration he used a Linksys router of about twenty years old. Connecting a JTAG debugger and the open-source OpenOCD tool identified the CPU and revealed a Telnet service on port 4444 that accepted connections without a password, giving him control of the device, the ability to reset its watchdog, and root-level actions. Dumping the memory produced images in which the admin password, a private key, and HTTP, PPPoE and dynamic DNS credentials were stored in plain text. He also described reading an Amazon Alexa through ISP access and a Google Home Mini through chip removal, noting that the Google device exposed no debug pads at all.

He explained the plaintext storage by pointing to the limited memory and processing power of small IoT parts, which leaves little room for encryption, and to cheap designs that are easier to build. The main takeaways are that raw hardware dumps are valuable evidence for investigators and analysts, and that hidden debug pads do not reliably prevent access to a device's stored secrets.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Keynterceptor: Press Any Key to Continue
talks.teaser: Niels van Dijkhuizen examines #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Keynterceptor: Press Any Key to Continue.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - An Isolated Data Center Security Policy Model Using SmartNICs
talks.teaser: Ofir Arkin investigates #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - An Isolated Data Center Security Policy Model Using SmartNICs.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Behaviors and Patterns of Rogue Hosting Providers
talks.teaser: Examines how bulletproof hosting providers in the Netherlands operate, using ASN graphs and offshore registration patterns.
talks.summary:
The speakers set out to map how hosting providers in the Netherlands are abused, separating ordinary providers that get misused from bulletproof hosts that knowingly serve criminals. They framed the work as a threat intelligence cycle, moving from defining requirements to collecting large-scale DNS resolver telemetry and routing data, then processing, analysing and disseminating findings to stakeholders such as hosting operators, law enforcement and policy makers.

The analysis looked beyond individual IP addresses. Stub autonomous systems that rely only on upstream providers let operators shift infrastructure quickly when pressured. Graphs of upstream and downstream relationships revealed chains of networks, for example a Dutch colocation provider feeding smaller hosts registered in the UAE, Bulgaria, Belize or Panama, several of them tied to pirated content or dump shops. Offshore company registrations, anonymous payment options and vague terms of service were other recurring signs. The speakers also described a low-cost recipe for setting up such a provider and how the same steps repeat across different countries.

For defenders, the main takeaway was to study tactics and business models rather than only reacting to indicators, and to share intelligence across the community. The speakers noted that takedown requests involving offshore providers take a long time, and they proposed a code of conduct for hosters, closer scrutiny of colocation and peering relationships, and checks on who requests autonomous system numbers.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - Steganography Ante Portas
talks.teaser: Surveys decades of network steganography research and condenses hundreds of covert channel techniques into reusable hiding patterns.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on steganography, the practice of concealing a message inside an innocuous cover object so that it blends in. It contrasts this with covert channels, using the classic prisoners' problem to show how two parties might hide an escape plan from a warden who inspects their messages. Historical examples run from tattoos on skin to digital image and audio files, and the speaker notes that malware already uses network steganography in the wild.

The core of the session is a taxonomy of network information hiding. After surveying publications from the late 1980s onward, the researchers grouped the many techniques into a small set of patterns, split by whether they manipulate timing or stored data, and by whether they touch metadata or payload. Examples include encoding bits in packet sizes, reordering HTTP header lines, toggling letter case in a request, using unused header fields, and varying inter-arrival times. Redundancy and value-modulation patterns appear most often in the literature, while retransmission appears rarely. Advanced variants such as micro-protocols, pattern combination and pattern hopping are also discussed.

The final part covers cyber-physical systems, where hidden bits were stored in smart building devices by slightly altering actuator set points or unused registers. Capacity was limited to roughly 350 to 1,500 bits, so a 128-bit key needed about 30 actuators. The speaker closes by urging attendees to find new patterns and to build countermeasures against whole pattern families rather than single techniques.

talks.title: #HITB2018AMS CommSec D1 - The Life & Death of Kernel Object Abuse
talks.teaser: Walks through Windows kernel GDI object abuse for privilege escalation, then Microsoft's type isolation mitigation against it.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how memory corruption bugs such as use-after-free and integer overflows can be turned into arbitrary kernel read and write on Windows, and why those primitives matter for privilege escalation. The first speaker walks through GDI objects commonly abused for this purpose: window objects, bitmaps (surface objects) and palettes. For each, the approach is to corrupt one object's size or pointer so it can reach a neighbouring object, then use that neighbour to read and write arbitrary memory. A live demo shows a low-privileged process triggering an overflow, overwriting a palette's data pointer, and copying the system process token into its own process to get a shell with system rights.

The second speaker covers the defensive side. Use-after-free bugs make up a large share of the kernel vulnerabilities in Microsoft's historical case data, so the team chose to target them. Their type isolation mitigation moves the fixed-size part of selected GDI objects into a separate heap, so attacker-controlled variable-size data cannot overlap it. Freed slots are zeroed, so a stale pointer lands on empty memory and typically crashes rather than giving a usable primitive. The speaker compares this to similar heap partitioning used by Adobe Flash, Google, Internet Explorer and WebKit.

The main takeaway is that patching individual bugs is a constant game of whack-a-mole, so mitigations that control memory layout raise the cost of exploiting an entire bug class. Protection for bitmaps and palettes had already reached insider builds, and further object types were planned.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 CLOSING KEYNOTE - A Spin Around The Block: 13 Years Of Infosec Challenges
talks.teaser: Reflects on thirteen years of security work, with lessons on legacy systems, vendor disclosure and building trust.
talks.summary:
Kelly Lum closes the conference by looking back on thirteen years of information security work, moving between government, finance, a stock exchange, a media company and a healthcare data firm. The talk is a light-hearted set of anecdotes rather than a technical presentation, and the stories are grouped around problems that recur across very different organizations.

Early on, a vulnerability research role for the army showed how a flaw found in a network appliance that processed classified data became classified itself, so it could not be reported to the vendor unless staff held matching clearances. In a later engagement, an office was still running Windows XP and Lotus Notes, where old systems were hard to secure and staff were reluctant to change long-standing habits. The speaker also described buying security products as a quick fix that added more systems to patch and maintain, and an acquisition that brought in an application full of unfixed flaws.

The middle of the talk turns to vendor disclosure. While evaluating a product for an organization, the speaker found vulnerabilities, could not find a security contact, and then received a cease-and-desist letter after reporting them. The closing advice is for vendors to offer an easy way to report flaws, for security staff to act as partners rather than critics, to put frameworks in place and record decisions, and to choose work that is enjoyed.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D2 - Neuralfuzz: Neural Networks For Fuzzing Web Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how recurrent neural networks can generate web attack payloads to widen fuzzing coverage against HTTP parameters.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at fuzzing web applications, where the space of possible HTTP inputs is too large to brute force, and asks how neural networks can help choose payloads that a scanner would not otherwise try. The speaker splits the problem into three parts: where to place a payload in a request, what the payload should look like, and how to recognise that it caused a problem. Most of the talk focuses on the second part. A proxy captures requests produced by existing functional tests and substitutes generated payloads into them, which avoids crawling single-page applications.

To build the generator, a character-level recurrent network is trained on public payload collections and on traffic from a deliberately vulnerable application scanned with sqlmap. In a local file inclusion example, output moved from unreadable strings to plausible paths and then to realistic file names as training progressed. Other cases included a null-byte input that produced new variants against an nginx target, URL fragments for a server-side request forgery in a method field, and newline-led shell or XML inputs that produced memcached-style injections. A JSON injection in a bug bounty target, which the speaker had missed by hand, was also surfaced by the model.

The takeaway is that learned generators can reach contexts that manual intuition misses, particularly for complex syntaxes such as SQL and XSS. Response analysis and false-positive filtering remain open problems, and the speaker plans to automate the workflow in a proxy tool and feed responses back into the model. Pre-trained models and the training tool were announced for release on GitHub.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D2 - Rootten Apples: Vulnerability Heaven In The iOS Sandbox
talks.teaser: Details an iOS kernel exploit chain built on IOKit bugs in the Apple AV driver, bypassing PAN and PXN.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at IOKit, the C++ driver framework in Apple's kernel, and why its user client interface, which dispatches requests through external methods, has drawn so much attention from jailbreak developers. The focus is the hardware video encoding driver in iOS, which had no public documentation or source code, so the research began by reverse engineering its external method table.

The research uncovered eight kernel bugs, mostly in the driver and the IOSurface shared-memory component. One let user input stand in for an IOSurface kernel pointer, giving an arbitrary-object primitive; another leaked kernel pointers for any IOSurface ID; and a mapped buffer could be changed while the kernel processed it, giving a controlled read. Leaking the IOSurface vtable and then an IOFence object defeated kASLR. Storing fake objects in IOSurface property dictionaries let the attacker spray kernel heap data persistently and read it back. Chained gadgets then let copyin overwrite sysctl handlers, giving deterministic kernel read and write past PAN and PXN.

The speaker argues that kernel-based jailbreaks rest on an aging design, and that user-mode methods with a task-port sandbox escape are a better path. The bugs were reported to Apple in March 2017 and patched in May. The exploit was withheld at Apple's request until more fixes landed, and the speaker praised the vendor's responsiveness and its mitigations.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D2 - XFLTReaT: A New Dimension In Tunnelling
talks.teaser: Presents a modular open-source framework that tunnels traffic over TCP, UDP, ICMP and DNS to bypass restricted networks.
talks.summary:
Balazs Bucsay presents XFLTReaT, an open-source, modular tunnelling framework written in Python. He starts from the gaps he hit while travelling: restricted networks often leave only one protocol open, and the existing tunnelling tools each need separate installation, configuration syntax and language, and many are no longer maintained.

The framework separates transport modules, such as TCP, UDP, ICMP, DNS, HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS, from encryption and authentication, so a new protocol needs only a small module that inherits shared code. A check function probes every module against the server to show which paths are open. In a live demo, the speaker ran a tunnel over ICMP at around five megabytes per second, then switched to DNS, which was slower. He also covered protocol details: ICMP tunnels must track identifiers and sequence numbers, and DNS payload size depends on the record type used, with fragmentation still limited.

The takeaways cut both ways. Attackers can use the tool to reach the internet from locked-down networks, while defenders can run it from outside their own network to test whether egress filtering and staff detection catch the traffic. Recommended controls include forcing clients through authenticated proxies, allowing DNS resolution only through internal servers, keeping an accurate asset inventory and baselining flows with NetFlow or Bro.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 KEYNOTE D2 - The State Of Cyber
talks.teaser: George Kurtz examines #HITBGSEC 2017 KEYNOTE D2 - The State Of Cyber.
talks.summary:
## Overview

This HITB 2017 keynote examines how sophisticated attack techniques pioneered by nation-states are rapidly commoditizing and trickling down to cybercriminal groups, making advanced attacks accessible to actors with minimal resources. Drawing on CrowdStrike's telemetry from 60 billion daily events across 176 countries, the speaker illustrates an emerging convergence where the lines between state-sponsored and e-crime operations blur, with criminal groups now operating as formal organizations complete with help desks and HR departments.

## Attack Landscape Evolution

The threat landscape has evolved from basic network exploration to intellectual property theft (exemplified by design theft for military equipment), election interference and data manipulation, and weaponization of breached information. The speaker discusses CrowdStrike's 2016 DNC breach investigation, identifying Russian actors involved in both theft and influence operations that combined data leaks with disinformation campaigns. Nation-states like North Korea have increasingly turned to cybercrime and wire fraud as revenue streams, while data breaches are now weaponized for extortion, public embarrassment, stock manipulation, and political influence.

## The Trickle-Down Effect and Commoditization

A central thesis is that previously expensive, state-level attack capabilities are becoming commoditized. The Shadow Brokers' leak of NSA exploits—particularly EternalBlue—exemplifies this; once-classified tools are now freely available and rapidly integrated into e-crime operations. Underground markets now offer ransomware-as-a-service kits (listing products like Dragon, Bricker, Jigsaw), delivery Trojans, exploit kits, and bulletproof hosting for hundreds of dollars monthly. This economic accessibility has eliminated the skill barrier; sophisticated campaigns incorporating EternalBlue and PowerShell techniques are now accessible to minimally-trained operators.

## Malware-Free and Living-Off-The-Land Tactics

A critical observation is industry overemphasis on malware signatures. Adversaries increasingly avoid creating detectable malware, instead exploiting legitimate Windows tools. Sandbox proliferation drove this shift; attackers now abuse built-in utilities like PowerShell, Windows utilities from the Microsoft Resource Kit, and administrator tools—techniques documented in "Hacking Exposed" (1999) but remain highly effective when properly chained.

## Technical Attack Vectors

**Link File Exploitation:** Windows .lnk files are created with base64-encoded PowerShell payloads appended to the binary, disguised with Word icons. Clicking executes the embedded code as a dropper, bypassing file-based detection.

**UAC Bypass:** Base64-encoded PowerShell impersonates explorer.exe (a whitelisted process), using UAC bypass techniques to gain administrative privileges without user prompts or authentication.

**OneDrive Persistence:** In a real incident, adversaries embedded PowerShell in VB startup scripts that dumped credentials via mimikatz, encrypted them over SSL using OneDrive with burner accounts, and exfiltrated them. Despite password resets, the backdoor persisted in startup scripts, evading login-based detection.

**BITS Service Abuse:** Word macros abuse Microsoft's Background Intelligent Transfer Service (legitimately whitelisted for Windows updates) to download and execute arbitrary payloads, bypassing firewall restrictions.

**Chopper Web Shell:** A 72-byte ASP file provides full code execution, file operations, and command access on web servers. It generates no malware signatures yet enables complete system compromise.

**Sticky Keys Backdoor:** Registry modifications redirect the Windows accessibility sticky keys feature (Shift pressed 5 times) to launch cmd.exe with system privileges, creating a pre-login backdoor requiring no credentials.

## E-Crime Market and Ransomware Trends

Criminal organizations operate as legitimate businesses with hierarchies, help desks, and multilingual victim support including Bitcoin purchase tutorials and payment facilitation. Ransomware-as-a-service pricing and market dynamics are fluid and accessible. WannaCry and NotPetya exemplify how leaked state exploits enable mass campaigns. The speaker discusses CrowdStrike's technical achievement in partially decrypting NotPetya's master file table using Salsa20 cryptography analysis and known plaintext attacks.

## Defensive Strategies

**Graph-Based Detection:** Rather than signature-based detection, mapping discrete events (file execution, enumeration, backup deletion, encryption calls) into graph databases enables behavior-based detection independent of malware variants. Attack sequences remain consistent even when payloads change.

**Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning:** Drawing analogy to AI reconstructing a Rembrandt painting by extracting features from known works, ML can classify good/bad behavior by analyzing multidimensional feature spaces in both supervised (known malware) and unsupervised (anomaly detection) modes.

## Key Takeaways

Three pillars support modern defense: (1) cloud-based threat intelligence processing massive telemetry to understand adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs); (2) threat intelligence sharing to distinguish targeted attacks from commodity malware, fundamentally affecting response scope; (3) dedicated threat hunting teams proactively searching for adversaries already on networks to prevent breaches from becoming catastrophes. The core message: defenders must shift from malware-focused approaches to behavioral analysis, leverage cloud scale, and adopt AI-driven prediction to counter an increasingly commoditized yet sophisticated threat ecosystem.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 SG Conf D1 - A New Era Of SSRF - Exploiting Url Parsers
talks.teaser: Shows how mismatched URL parsers and protocol smuggling turn server-side request forgery into remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits server-side request forgery, where an attacker tricks a server into sending requests to internal networks. Its central claim is that many SSRF defenses break because the URL validator and the HTTP client read the same string differently. The speaker walked through parser mismatches across PHP, Perl, Java, Python and curl, including cases where special characters in the authority section changed which host was checked versus which host was fetched. Further quirks covered Unicode and IDNA handling, and resolver functions that tolerated trailing junk after an IP address.

Protocol smuggling was the second theme. Carriage return and line feed characters injected into a host name let an attacker add extra requests to a plain HTTP call, and a similar trick reached SMTP over a TLS handshake through the SNI field. The case studies applied these ideas to real products. A WordPress protection was bypassed by combining a DNS answer that changed between validation and fetch with curl's handling of internationalized domain names. In GitHub Enterprise, a webhook SSRF was chained through an internal graphite service and a memcached write that stored a serialized Ruby object, which ran commands when the cache was later read.

The takeaway for developers is to resolve the hostname once, connect only to the validated IP address, avoid reusing user-supplied URLs in later requests, and enforce network policies that block internal traffic from application servers.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D1 - How We Broke Intel Amt
talks.teaser: Shows how an authentication flaw in Intel AMT's remote management server exposes many Intel systems to remote takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Intel Management Engine, a privileged subsystem built into Intel-based systems that has its own network access and keeps running when a machine is switched off. The focus is Intel Active Management Technology, which runs on that engine for remote administration. The speakers walk through the engine's firmware layout on SPI flash, the difficulty of reverse engineering its compressed modules, and how they used a disassembler and scripts to locate the AMT web server's digest authentication code.

They describe a flaw in that code: the length used when comparing the computed digest response came from the user-supplied value, so an empty response string passed the check. In a demo, routing requests through a local proxy that blanked the response field gave administrative access without the password. The team reported the issue through Intel's bug bounty program, and it was tracked as CVE-2017-5689. They covered vendor firmware patches, the fact that many systems would not update automatically, and a downgrade scenario where flash protections were weak. They also showed that AMT could be activated on non-vPro boards by sending undocumented messages over the host embedded controller interface, using a Windows-only tool that supported 6 to 9 series chipsets.

Near the end, they explained that a 1.5 MB Management Engine image could be swapped for the 5 MB version with an SPI programmer or, on some systems with unlocked flash regions, from software with administrator rights. They noted that malware had already used AMT serial-over-LAN as a channel that sits outside the operating system. The practical takeaways are to check whether AMT is enabled and patched on managed machines, and to treat the management engine as a remote attack surface that a firmware update alone may not close.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D1 - Get To The Money: Hacking PoS And PoP Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how unauthenticated back-end services in SAP and Oracle Micros POS systems allow price changes and remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at point-of-sale systems, which combine hardware and software to record transactions. The speakers argue that earlier research mostly targeted payment terminals rather than the store servers and back-office software behind them. They chose SAP POS, a client-server retail product, and walked through its architecture: POS clients at the checkout, a store server, a store manager application, and a head-office configurator that pushes settings out as files.

Analysis of the store server's text-based service showed it accepted commands without authentication. Among the undocumented methods, the speakers found a function that reset cashier passwords and file functions that could read, write and delete files on the server. Settings could be planted through a trigger file that the server checked every 30 seconds. Combined with a payload the server executes on Windows, this gave remote code execution. A live demonstration showed a MacBook Pro priced near $900 sold for $3, with altered receipt content and unmasked card data. They also described weak encryption levels on some stored fields and plaintext exposure in memory. The vendor's patches reduced some exposure, but the speakers found a way around the IP check. For Oracle Micros, they reported search-engine exposure, arbitrary file reads and default accounts.

The conclusion is that missing authorization checks in supporting POS infrastructure create significant fraud risk and put customer data at risk. Their overall message is that the security of this back-end infrastructure is weaker than it should be, and that it deserves the same scrutiny as the terminals at the counter.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 Conf D1 - Spy Vs Spy: A Modern Study Of Microphone Bugs
talks.teaser: Shows how hidden microphone bugs work and how the Salamandra SDR tool detects and locates them.
talks.summary:
The talk covers covert microphones, the hidden audio bugs used for eavesdropping. The presenters review older cases, including a microphone reportedly found in artist Ai Weiwei's studio after about four years of use, and a device hidden in a Moscow embassy seal for seven years that had no battery and drew power remotely. They also describe transistor-era and modular bugs, and a 1970s bug that took power from nearby electrical wiring.

To test modern devices, the team bought stationary FM and GSM bugs and a baby monitor from online marketplaces. Their field tests showed advertised ranges were unreliable: audio stayed clear at distance with line of sight and degraded behind buildings. A GSM unit could be called from anywhere but left SIM and carrier traces. They then built Salamandra, a free software-defined radio tool that spots the energy a live bug produces and counts peaks above a threshold. Against a commercial handheld detector, a tuned setting produced zero false positives but caught only 33% of microphones.

In hide-and-seek exercises, a hidden microphone was usually flagged within seconds to minutes, but pinpointing it took far longer, sometimes around 40 minutes. The takeaway is that detection is quick and location is slow, and that hiding a bug well requires knowing the target and a power source. For high-risk situations, the presenters advise professional sweeps.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 KEYNOTE 1 - Finding Vulns And Malware In Open Source Code At Scale
talks.teaser: Explains how malicious and vulnerable open source dependencies spread, and demos a query language for hunting them at scale.
talks.summary:
Open source libraries now make up most of the code in a typical application, yet the dependencies that package managers pull in are rarely checked. The talk argues that public registries such as npm and Maven Central offer little malware screening, known vulnerable versions stay available, and publisher accounts can be compromised or sold. A live demo showed a backdoored library added to a Spring web application. When a sign-up triggered the library, it copied database contents, deleted the tables and left a ransom note.

The speaker then argues that matching CVE identifiers to library names misses most issues, since it ignores whether the vulnerable code is actually reached. The proposed approach builds a global dependency graph and call graph across library versions, stored in a graph database and queried through a security graph language that compiles to Gremlin. Demonstrated queries found copies of vulnerable classes through bytecode similarity, vulnerabilities inherited through transitive dependencies, calls to risky methods such as runtime exec, and XML parser usage that lacked protections against XXE. One broad query reported more than 6,500 Java libraries affected by known vulnerabilities, about three times the number listed in CVE data.

The practical takeaway is to analyse packages as they are published upstream, before downstream projects consume them, and to mine commit histories for fixes that were never reported. The speaker said the query language specification would be released as open source later in the year, alongside a researcher program for invited participants.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 CommSec D2 - 2FAssassin: Bypass 2FA, Stealing Private Keys, And More
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen SSH keys, client certificates and one-time passwords get abused to move through networks and impersonate sites.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how attackers get past two-factor authentication and how they take private keys from servers and users. It starts with ways to obtain one-time passwords: social engineering against mail account recovery, Android malware that intercepts codes and diverts voice calls, devices that sniff SMS, and IMSI catchers that force phones onto weaker 2G service. It then moves to private keys, which are often passphrase-protected but can still be cracked, pulled from SSH agent memory, or found on USB tokens and shared network drives.

The demonstration starts with network enumeration to build a list of live hosts and open services, then checks which hosts accept public key authentication. A brute-force SSH attack against weak passwords succeeds, and the tooling downloads keys and authorized_keys data from each host. Next, a PKCS#12 client certificate is analysed and its passphrase cracked, after which the private and public key are extracted. The real domain name is recovered by testing candidate top-level domains and matching key fingerprints. With the server key in hand, the speaker builds a phishing copy of a certificate-protected site, uses DNS spoofing to send a Windows client to it, and obtains a reverse shell. Persistence through added public keys and a chained SSH tunnel for moving files out of a network are also shown.

The main point is that a private key never leaves its machine, so the risk lies in how keys are stored, reused and trusted. Suggested defences include disabling password authentication, not leaving passphrases on disk, avoiding shared keys across hosts, keeping authorized_keys files small and reviewed, shortening DNS TTLs, pinning critical IP addresses in hosts files, and revoking a certificate through the issuing CA if a key may be stolen.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 CommSec D2 - Intelligence And Counterintelligence Techniques
talks.teaser: Frames classic intelligence and counterintelligence methods as a practical model for red and blue teams in cyber operations.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works in cyber network operations and digital forensics, argues that security teams can reuse established intelligence and counterintelligence methods from state practice rather than chasing new buzzword frameworks. The talk treats an organization as something like a nation with secrets to protect, and walks through the classic intelligence cycle of tasking, collection, processing, analysis and dissemination. It separates signals, open-source and human intelligence, and maps each one to familiar work such as network monitoring, reconnaissance and interviews.

The middle section applies that cycle to two cases. In an offensive example, a team moves from open-source research to on-site Wi-Fi capture and account access, and each stage feeds findings back to decision-makers. In a defensive example, a threat hunting team investigates suspicious updates by collecting host and network data, reducing noise, and passing findings to forensic and reverse engineering staff, whose results feed back into the next hunt. The counterintelligence section covers deterrence, detection, deception and disruption, including a data center scenario where a red team got in and out without being noticed by physical security.

The closing message is that red and blue teams should swap roles, know their own assets well, and share what they learn with the wider community so others do not repeat the same work. The practical takeaway is to reframe existing tools and processes through an intelligence lens rather than buying new feeds.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 CommSec D1 - The Original Elevat0r: History Of A Private Jailbreak
talks.teaser: Traces one iOS kernel bug through several failed patches and the exploit changes each iOS release forced.
talks.summary:
The talk traces a private iOS jailbreak the speaker called the elevator, a codename that started as a joke about a broken elevator in his building and then stuck to his own private exploits. It centres on one kernel memory corruption bug in the setattrlist system call. A volume name offset taken from a user-supplied attribute buffer was signed, so it could point in front of the buffer and write a single zero byte into kernel heap memory.

The bug existed from early iOS releases up to iOS 8. On iOS 5 there were no kernel mitigations, so the speaker overwrote an object's vtable pointer to redirect execution into user memory. Apple's iOS 6 patch checked for negative offsets, but on 32-bit systems the offset could wrap around the address space and the bug stayed reachable. A later fix for zero-length attributes was harmless on little-endian devices. Each release forced a different exploit. iOS 6 introduced kernel mitigations, so the speaker leaked kernel and heap pointers through I/O Kit objects combined with heap grooming. iOS 7 added unprotected doubly linked list metadata to the heap, which allowed a single unlink to write arbitrary kernel memory without grooming. iOS 8 removed that unlink.

The closing lessons were that Apple's fixes were often declared complete when they were not, that architecture changes between releases can make exploitation much easier or harder, and that persistent jailbreaks became rare as repeated fixes and high exploit prices reduced the incentive to release them for free.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2017 CommSec D1 - Hacking Robots Before Skynet
talks.teaser: Shows how home and industrial robots can be taken over through network flaws, weak updates and software-only safety controls.
talks.summary:
Lucas Apa and Cesar Cerrudo describe how robots are spreading into stores, hospitals, homes and factories, and argue that a robot is a computer with arms, legs and wheels. Their research covered twelve robots across home, business, research and industrial lines. They gathered public firmware and documentation, then reverse engineered the applications and services to map how each robot connects to the local network, the vendor cloud and mobile apps.

Findings included mDNS advertisements that make units easy to locate, unauthenticated control ports, and a web console whose basic authentication covered only one script file, leaving other resources reachable directly. Traffic to vendor clouds was often unencrypted and exposed personal data, and one robot sent its speech-to-text output over the local network. For a home robot, the action protocol could be driven remotely, shown in a live demo. For an industrial collaborative arm, the safety limits lived in software. The team chained a path disclosure with a buffer overflow in a network service to gain root, then altered the safety file and used a short checksum collision to hide the change. An emulator demo showed the arm running with its safety planes disabled. Unverified updates, cloud account binding and research framework code moved into products added further risk.

Vendor responses ranged from no action to promised fixes that did not arrive. The speakers urged vendors to design security in from the start, disable features by default, verify updates, isolate safety functions from other components and invest in security as heavily as in marketing, since robots will soon be everywhere.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS CLOSING KEYNOTE - The ECMA And The Chakra
talks.teaser: Walks through how Chakra's JavaScript engine design, from array memory layouts to proxies, led to type confusion and overflow bugs.
talks.summary:
This closing keynote presents research into Microsoft Edge's JavaScript engine, Chakra. After years away from browser work, the speaker code-reviewed the engine and reported about 13 bugs, all since fixed. The talk starts by placing Chakra within ECMAScript, the standard that other engines such as ActionScript and QtScript also implement, and notes how quickly the language keeps growing.

The middle of the talk explains why arrays and objects are hard to implement safely. Chakra moves arrays between several memory layouts as their contents change, and it splits work into fast paths for normal cases and slow paths for everything else. Each optimisation adds conditions that must be checked, and exotic features such as accessors on array indexes, prototype chains, proxies and array species create unexpected states. The examples include an information leak when a getter changed an array's layout during a join call, a stack overflow reached through the spread operator, a segmentation fault in reverse, and type confusion in filter and shift. A type confusion in internationalization code, which trusted a property that user code could override, and a fall-through to an uninitialized variable rounded out the cases.

The closing lessons are that many obscure language features add bug surface, so engine designers should ask whether they are worth including. Implementation choices also determine which bug classes appear. For bug hunters, understanding how an engine is built makes it easier to find these flaws, and for developers it helps them know what to avoid.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D2T1 - Hunting For Vulnerabilities In Signal
talks.teaser: Walks through vulnerabilities found in the Signal messenger, from an attachment MAC bypass to a session replay attack.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at HITB 2017 Amsterdam, Markus Vervier (along with co-researcher JP Aumasson / Jean-Philippe Aumasson) presents security research into the Signal messaging app and protocol. The researchers set out to evaluate Signal’s code base, attack surface, protocol mechanics, and implementation specifics, primarily focusing on the Android client, the Chrome desktop extension, and the underlying C/Java libraries.

### Key Topics
- **Signal Architecture and Attack Surface**: While Signal guarantees end-to-end encryption using the Double Ratchet and X3DH protocols (licensed and used in WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Google Allo), the actual application attack surface is massive. The Android client encompasses hundreds of thousands of lines of code, third-party libraries (such as WebRTC and OpenSSL), and system media decoders with no privilege separation or sandboxing between media parsers and core messaging logic.
- **Threat Models**: The researchers evaluated two primary attack scenarios: a classical active/passive network attacker (or compromised Signal server) and a malicious communicating peer who holds valid encryption keys and can deliver arbitrary media payloads directly to parsing components.
- **Manual Audit Approach**: Rather than relying on rigorous formal verification or automated tooling, the researchers performed manual code analysis focusing on data flows, edge cases, language-specific bug classes, and protocol boundary handling.

### Technical Details
- **Attachment Integrity MAC Bypass**: An integer overflow vulnerability was identified in the Android attachment validation logic. When calculating remaining attachment data to authenticate with HMAC, the length of the MAC is subtracted from the file length using a 32-bit signed integer. By appending 4 GB of padding (compressed via HTTP content encoding down to 2–4 MB during transit), the integer wraps around. As a result, only the initial bytes are checked by the MAC, while remaining manipulated bytes are processed. Combined with AES-CBC malleability, this allows block duplication and plaintext alteration without triggering integrity check failures.
- **Cryptographic Quirks**: Setting the public key to zero results in a shared secret of zero in Signal's implementation, producing predictable secrets and undermining break-in recovery properties. Furthermore, example C code provided with the Signal library contained flaws including type confusions and integer/heap overflows.
- **Denial of Service and Parsing Issues**: In the RTP calling code, missing bounds checks on packet headers caused an underflow leading to out-of-bounds reads and remote crashes. In Android, feeding malformed media triggered crashes in `libskia` that caused continuous reboot-crash loops on devices like the Nexus 7. In the Chrome extension, a crafted SVG image could crash the renderer process via out-of-memory errors.
- **Protocol Message Replay Attack**: Signal handles asynchronous communication using pre-keys, including a persistent 'last resort' medium-term key. Bundled messages contain an encrypted ciphertext alongside unauthenticated key exchange metadata. Because the key exchange parameters are not MAC-protected and the client only tracks 40 concurrent session states, an active man-in-the-middle attacker can inject modified key exchange parameters across 40 messages to evict legitimate sessions from the session store. Once the original session state is purged, the attacker can replay a previously recorded message using the last resort pre-key, causing the recipient to accept and decrypt the replayed message again.
- **Localhost HTTP Audio Streaming**: On Android, incoming audio attachments were written out and streamed unencrypted via a local HTTP server on `localhost` over a random port to the Android media player, potentially exposing audio data if the ephemeral URI is leaked.

### Takeaways
Secure messaging relies heavily on more than cryptographic design. The large code footprint, lack of sandboxing for third-party media parsers, and implementation bugs in protocol handling expose trusted applications to memory corruption, denial of service, and message replay attacks.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T1 - I Got 99 Trends And A # Is All Of Them! Steven Seeley and Roberto Suggi Liverani
talks.teaser: The session maps how repeated enterprise product testing yielded 200-plus unauthenticated RCE issues across Trend Micro suites.
talks.summary:
Enterprise security appliances often sit at high privilege with large attack surfaces, yet receive less scrutiny than consumer antivirus. The presenters explain that tweets about remote code execution in Trend Micro offerings sparked a long campaign aimed at fully compromising server-side products without user interaction, prioritizing command injection, authentication bypasses, and RCE over lower-impact bug classes.

They describe shifting from black-box installs of downloadable trial software to white-box review of binaries and source, reusing malware-analysis habits such as traffic capture, API hooking, and protocol decoding. Shared web gateways and recycled libraries across products enabled pattern-based hunting and partial automation to enumerate hidden API methods. Pitfalls included trial license limits, incomplete lab environments without Active Directory or Exchange, and over-focusing on a single vulnerability class.

Case studies span Smart Protection Server PHP command injection, Data Loss Prevention unauthenticated Java deserialization and agent impersonation, KeyView file-parser fuzzing, Control Manager blind SQL injection chained with pass-the-hash login, InterScan Struts REST command execution as root, and Threat Discovery Appliance chains that delete configuration to force default credentials after reboot plus zip symlink uploads. They release unpublished exploit material for some appliances and note cooperative vendor disclosure.

Practitioners should treat security products as privileged infrastructure, map unreleased server APIs, and assume one authentication bypass can unlock many post-auth flaws.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T1 - Drammer: The Making Of
talks.teaser: Researchers recount how ARM Rowhammer became the Drammer Android root chain, from dead ends in cache maintenance to ION heap grooming.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through how a PhD effort to bring Rowhammer from cloud Flip Feng Shui scenarios onto everyday ARM Android phones turned into the Drammer work. Early momentum came from hammering in a loadable kernel module on a Nexus 5, including debugging assembly mistakes, before the real goal became flipping bits from ordinary app context without privileged cache-flush instructions.

Most of a month went into techniques that work on x86 but fail on ARM and stock Linux: repeated cacheflush syscalls, pointer-chasing with throttled flushes, custom versus kernel flush implementations, and the distinction between point of unification and point of coherence that kept kernel flushes from returning traffic to DRAM. Instruction-cache–driven hammer loops showed promise only with a careful implementation. The path that shipped was Android’s ION allocator, which exposes physically contiguous buffers suitable for hammering from userspace.

With placement solved, collaborators shaped PHYSICAL Feng Shui: exhausting and reallocating ION heaps so a page table lands beside a known flip, flipping a PTE bit to redirect mappings, and using that to reach kernel structures and root. Device testing showed huge spread in flip rates across nominally identical hardware. The team disclosed to Google, received a bounty, and notes that disabling the contiguous ION heap complicates but may not fully kill the idea, while flawed DRAM itself has no software cure on the phone in your pocket.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T1 - A New RISC
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a RISC-V supervisor-to-machine escalation via page tables, then covers hardware fixes and debug authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces RISC-V, an open instruction set the speaker presents as a low-cost alternative to proprietary processor designs for IoT and mobile devices. He walks through its privilege levels, from user mode through supervisor to machine mode, and explains why the machine layer should sit beyond the reach of the operating system kernel.

The core is a proof of concept run in the QEMU emulator. A supervisor-level Linux kernel is shown escaping its privilege by mapping the physical DRAM region that holds machine-mode code into its own page tables, since the supervisor is allowed to edit those tables. The attacker overwrites the handler for a shutdown call that is never needed, then triggers that trap so injected instructions run in machine mode. The proposed physical memory protection extension would stop supervisor code from reaching that region, a fix that needs only a small silicon change. The speaker also covers tagged memory, which can block return-address overwrites, and a debug authentication design that uses two registers as a serial channel to check signed messages rather than a static password.

The closing argument is that an open architecture avoids up-front licensing fees and per-chip royalties, so stronger security becomes affordable on cheap devices. Practitioners should study existing documentation and known weaknesses before implementing a design, and should authenticate debug access rather than disable it. In the Q&A, he said the specification does not currently require verifying that instructions execute correctly.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T2 - The Secret Of Chakracore: 10 Ways To Go Beyond The Edge
talks.teaser: Shows how ChakraCore, the JavaScript engine behind Edge, yielded exploitable bugs, heap tricks and control-flow guard bypasses.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how hard it is to find remote code execution in the Microsoft Edge browser, and the speakers answer by focusing on the ChakraCore JavaScript engine at the core of Edge. Because the engine is open source, the researchers audited its code by hand. They report more than twenty exploitable vulnerabilities and over ten working exploits against 64-bit Edge on Windows 10. The first part describes engine characteristics that create exploitable bugs, especially those that differ from the older Internet Explorer JavaScript engine.

The talk then moves from bugs to exploitation. The speakers describe exploit techniques built on ChakraCore's own features and show how they arrange heap layout to make exploitation reliable. They also present control flow guard bypass methods that had not been published before and that earned a Microsoft mitigation bypass bounty reward. A further segment demonstrates how the return flow guard mitigation added in a Windows RS2 preview can be bypassed.

To close, the presenters go through details of several real 64-bit Edge exploits, including the one used to win PwnFest 2016. The takeaway for practitioners is that a browser's script engine remains a major attack surface even when the browser is built with security as a design goal, and that exploit work against such engines depends on the specific mitigations and heap behaviour of each release.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T2 - Can't Touch This: Cloning Any Android HCE Contactless Card
talks.teaser: Shows how Android host card emulation payment credentials can be copied to another phone and used for contactless transactions.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how mobile contactless payments built on Android host card emulation (HCE) can be attacked once the secure element hardware is removed. The speaker explains that the card number is tokenized, but the EMV cryptographic keys must live on the phone, so an attacker who copies the app's private data can recover them. He demonstrates a live clone: a rooted victim device has its application data copied to a second phone, which then completes a contactless payment accepted by a terminal.

The clone must pass device provisioning, which binds keys to hardware identifiers. The speaker shows that spoofing identifiers such as the Android ID with an Xposed module can satisfy this check without identical hardware. Root detection such as SafetyNet can be hidden, and for transactions above the floor limit he patches an app to advertise cardholder verification method support so the terminal skips the PIN. Across eight applications built on seven libraries, he reports that all tested apps could be cloned, though the difficulty varied with root detection and integrity checks.

To close, he suggests defenses: deeper native root detection, device characteristics that are harder to spoof, app integrity protection, and backend fraud scoring in place of duplicate-card checks, which miss a clone used for a few low-value transactions. He concludes that cloning cannot currently be prevented, only made harder, so issuers should plan for it.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS D1T1 - Hacking Customer Information Control System
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can abuse CICS on IBM mainframes, from escaping business apps to running code and escalating privileges.
talks.summary:
Mainframes are often dismissed as legacy, but the talk argues they are actively maintained and run critical workloads for banks, insurers, airlines and governments, yet receive little security testing. The speaker, a penetration tester, found almost no public research or tooling for them and set out to change that. CICS is presented as the transaction middleware that hosts business applications and handles concurrency and file access for them.

The attack path starts at a green-screen banking application reached through a 3270 terminal emulator. The speaker shows how to leave the application's context for the CICS terminal, enumerate four-character transaction IDs, and bypass the login program. Default administration transactions then expose transactions, files and system details, and can disable an application. A default program that runs CICS API calls allows reading customer files. For code execution, a spool file submitted to the internal reader runs jobs, and a transient data queue can serve the same role when spools are disabled. Redirecting a transaction to a restricted program reaches the file API, and the resulting shell inherits the trusted attributes of the CICS user.

For privilege escalation, the talk explains that programs in authorized program facility libraries run with kernel privileges. Where those libraries are writable, an attacker can load an assembler program that sets the special-privilege bit in its address space's accessor environment, then elevates the user. The takeaways are to lock down APF libraries and CICS administrative transactions, and to include mainframes in audit and penetration test scope.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS COMMSEC D2 - Unauthorized Erlang: A Demonstration
talks.teaser: Explores how Erlang's atom handling and predictable cookie generation enable stealthy remote guessing of cluster secrets in minutes.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting Erlang's reputation for eliminating common programming flaws with the BEAM virtual machine's blunt security model: anyone who can join the node mesh with a valid cookie can run code in the interpreter and often on the host. Prior work on difficult VM bugs is noted, but in typical deployments the practical remote path is obtaining that shared secret.

The core finding ties cookie creation to guessable monotonic timers and a tiny pseudo-random component on many cloud hosts, shrinking the search space to roughly a megabyte. An attacker can register remote node names that resemble cookie strings and use timing differences when names are converted into permanent atoms to learn which strings already exist, iterating across many nodes in parallel. The technique is described as silent under normal logging, abusable against recommended auto-generated cookies in products such as RabbitMQ, and difficult for the vendor to change without breaking remote naming.

Internet-wide scanning reportedly found on the order of a quarter-million reachable Erlang endpoints, with a substantial fraction deemed operationally sensitive. Filling the atom table can crash nodes and disrupt admin processes, while core dumps may leak attack material unless deliberately obscured. The closing guidance stresses never exposing Erlang to the public Internet, setting long custom cookies instead of default generation, and treating lateral movement inside telco or mesh environments as a serious risk even when vendors treat exposure as an operational mistake rather than a code defect.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS COMMSEC D2 - IoT Hacking Simplified
talks.teaser: Presents a console framework for IoT penetration testing and demos weak CoAP, MQTT and cloud data checks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at HITB2017AMS CommSec, the speaker addresses the growing security challenges within the Internet of Things (IoT) landscape and introduces "ExploitI" (exploitI), an open-source framework designed specifically for IoT penetration testing and exploitation. The talk outlines how IoT vendors—driven by speed-to-market pressures and low security awareness—frequently bypass basic functional testing, misconfigure protocols, hardcode encryption keys, and leave critical interfaces exposed. It highlights why security testers need dedicated, modular tooling rather than juggling fragmented or immature open-source scripts across hardware, firmware, mobile, and cloud layers.

### Key Topics
- **IoT Attack Surface**: The IoT ecosystem encompasses the device itself (embedded Linux, external storage/USB, exposed hardware like UART, unencrypted firmware), the mobile application (data storage, communication channels, firmware delivery via Bluetooth), and the cloud backend.
- **Common Vendor Pitfalls**: Startups and hardware vendors often adopt protocols without understanding their security models, deploy debug libraries into production apps, hardcode static encryption keys across product lines, or rely entirely on default, unvetted hardware modules.
- **Penetration Testing Tooling Gaps**: Testing IoT environments currently requires cobbling together disparate tools (SDR tools like HackRF/BladeRF, firmware unpackers, serial terminal emulators). The absence of mature, commercial IoT pen-testing suites led to the creation of ExploitI.
- **The ExploitI Framework**: A modular penetration testing tool where all operations (scanning, service discovery, attacks) are treated as test cases managed by a test suite engine and controlled via a console interface.

### Technical Details
- **UART Baud Rate Identification**: Hardware assessments commonly require connecting to serial UART interfaces using tools like Minicom, Screen, or Tera Term. ExploitI incorporates a `baud_scan` module—adapted from `devttys0`'s `baudrate.py`—which cycles through standard baud rates (e.g., 115200) until valid data is parsed from a target board (demonstrated using a custom test board called "DEVA").
- **CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) Discovery**: CoAP is a lightweight, UDP-based RESTful protocol derived from HTTP using binary options instead of text headers. The speaker demonstrates RFC 6690 service discovery against an Eclipse Californium test server (`californium.eclipse.org`), revealing exposed resource endpoints (`/.well-known/core`) that can be tested for unauthorized `GET`, `PUT`, `POST`, or `DELETE` requests.
- **MQTT Client Disconnection (Denial of Service)**: Using the Mosquitto MQTT broker (`mosquitto.org`), the speaker shows how the protocol's requirement for unique client IDs can lead to denial of service. When an attacker connects to the broker using an active client's identifier (such as `foobar`), the broker automatically disconnects the previously connected legitimate client. Additionally, brokers often expose administrative topics containing system information or logs.
- **Cloud Injection via Sensor Telemetry**: Because cloud platforms frequently treat incoming sensor telemetry as trusted, unvalidated data streams can compromise backends. The speaker demonstrates injecting an XSS payload in place of standard temperature values over an MQTT topic, showing how malicious payloads render directly in monitoring web applications.

### Takeaways
Hardware hacking is only one facet of IoT security; the cloud backend represents the single largest threat vector because compromising the cloud can compromise an entire product fleet. Security testers must validate end-to-end trust boundaries, particularly by treating sensor telemetry as untrusted input. The ExploitI framework aims to unify protocol-level testing (CoAP, MQTT), hardware interfacing, and exploit modules, with planned roadmap additions for Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), hardware breakout boards, ZigBee (via KillerBee), and community-contributed exploits.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS COMMSEC D2 - Intel DCI Secrets
talks.teaser: A walkthrough covers Intel DCI, the public x86 hardware-debug stack, and practical use over a ordinary USB 3 link.
talks.summary:
Software debuggers share the same privilege domain as the code they inspect, which limits kernel, hypervisor, system management mode, and firmware work. The speakers introduce Intel’s Direct Connection Interface as a newly accessible path to genuine hardware-assisted debugging on x86, after long-standing cost and confidentiality barriers kept such tooling away from most researchers.

They walk through the validation stack behind the capability: design-for-test and design-for-debug mechanisms, Silicon View and embedded DCI bridges, the platform controller hub DCI aggregator, and how this ties to industry JTAG-style standards and the debug abstraction layer. Connection can use a standard USB 3 back cable; OpenDAL-style Python CLI and GUI tooling expose a hierarchy of physical and logical debug targets. Capabilities discussed include tracing and halting deep in the silicon model, sideband register access, and reaching internal platform devices without going through the operating system firmware path in the usual way.

From Skylake-era parts onward they describe unhiding the P2SB device via a control register to reach fuller sideband interfaces, and outline the DCI packet protocol over USB with authorization semantics. Practitioners should treat the interface as extraordinarily powerful for embedded and firmware security research, while noting that board support varies and not every platform exposes CPU JTAG fully.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS COMMSEC D1 - Exploiting Windows Automatic Wireless Association
talks.teaser: Shows how forged Wi-Fi beacons can fool Windows location services into automatically joining a rogue network without user action.
talks.summary:
The talk covers automatic Wi-Fi association on Windows 10 and Windows Phone 8.1, a class of attacks that can place a device in a man-in-the-middle position without any user interaction. The speaker recaps the Karma attack and explains why Windows stopped adding open networks to its preferred list and moved to beacon-based discovery. He then describes Wi-Fi Sense, a feature that automatically connects devices to crowd-sourced hotspots Microsoft considers high quality, with the list of hotspots pushed to each device according to its area.

The attack abuses the location service. Windows sends the MAC addresses of nearby access points to Microsoft's positioning server, and because 802.11 management frames are unprotected, an attacker can forge beacons that make a device appear to be somewhere else. The attacker then sends deauthentication frames to drop the victim from its current network, broadcasts beacons that copy the name of a nearby Wi-Fi Sense hotspot, and the victim joins the rogue access point automatically. A video demonstration showed the victim's apparent location shifting before the spoofed network appeared and connected. Forcing the preferred network out of the scan list through router denial of service or jamming was presented as an alternative.

The speaker reported the issue to Microsoft, which considered it an accepted risk with no patch planned. Devices using default Express settings are affected, and the recommended mitigation is to turn off the Wi-Fi Sense open hotspot suggestion setting. The talk closes by pointing to the Wi-Fi Visser rogue access point tool, whose new version implements the technique. The takeaway is that convenience features enabled by default can widen exposure to wireless interception.

talks.title: #HITB2017AMS COMMSEC D1 - Breaking Apple's iCloud Keychain
talks.teaser: Explains how forensic examiners can reach passwords, call logs and backups stored in Apple's iCloud and keychain.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how forensic examiners obtain smartphone data, arguing that cloud acquisition is becoming the most practical route as devices encrypt local storage more strongly. The speaker compares what Apple, Google and Microsoft store in the cloud: backups, continuous sync of contacts and calendars, call logs, mail, browsing history and media. Apple syncs call logs to iCloud with no option to disable it, and iCloud backups keep their decryption keys alongside the encrypted data, so anyone who gets into the account can decrypt them.

The middle of the talk focuses on the keychain, where passwords, Wi-Fi credentials and card details are kept. Items marked as device-only cannot be restored to another device. Local encrypted backups were relatively easy to brute-force until iOS 10 introduced a weaker derivation that was rolled back after it was exposed, and the speaker reports very slow cracking speeds on current versions. iCloud Keychain syncs through a circle of trust and an escrow service protected by a security code, using the SRP protocol. The speaker walks through the escrow commands and the recovery data they expose, such as trusted devices and protection settings.

The closing takeaway is that with two-factor authentication enabled, an authentication token taken from a previously signed-in computer or device can reach the account and its escrowed keychain data, although the owner receives a notification of the access. Without two-factor authentication and a security code, the speaker says the synced keychain data cannot be decrypted. Practitioners should check how an account's security is configured and treat cloud-synced data as a distinct acquisition target.

talks.teaser: Presents a musical keynote covering passwords, Unix root access, storage clusters and cyber warfare through original songs.
talks.summary:
This closing keynote at a Hack In The Box Singapore event was delivered as a full musical performance rather than a slide-based talk. The speaker, a hardware hacker and reverse engineer, opened with a song on password hygiene aimed at friends outside security, urging listeners to use a unique password for every account and to generate those passwords carefully so they stay random.

The middle of the set moved through several hacking stories set to music. One song drew on the GTFO journal, whose release was a polyglot file that was also a zip archive and a playable audio track. Another was inspired by a Twitter account that documented owners of a Pineapple hacking tool being compromised and greeted with mocking splash screens. A third covered on-call life in a data center and praised Ceph, a storage system that runs on mixed hardware and fails gracefully. A later song reflected on cyber warfare, citing Stuxnet and the Snowden revelations.

The set ended with a lighter parody about a relationship and a sung cover of a well-known ballad. The practical takeaways are modest: use strong, unique passwords, prefer storage designs that degrade gracefully, and share hacker history and lessons with people who do not work in security.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2016 SG Conference Track D2 - iOS 10 Kernel Heap Revisited
talks.teaser: Walks through how the iOS kernel zone allocator changed from iOS 5 to the iOS 10 beta and what those changes mean for exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits the zone allocator behind the iOS kernel heap, a subject the speaker last covered around iOS 5. Zones hold allocations of one fixed element size, kalloc wraps them to serve variable-length requests, and malloc stores a size prefix in front of each block. The speaker recaps how early exploits abused free list pointers, size fields and heap grooming primitives such as unserialized XML objects and out-of-line Mach message data.

Mitigations arrived release by release. iOS 6 brought cookies on freed blocks and poisoning of small ones. iOS 7 randomized how often poisoning happens and moved to per-page metadata with page queues, but those double linked lists lacked safe unlinking, which made exploitation easier. iOS 8 hardened the queue macros in a late beta and scaled poisoning by block size. iOS 9 shrank the VM map copy structure, added size checks and randomized the initial free list order in 9.2.

The iOS 10 beta moves zone structures into a fixed array, gives every page external metadata and records a zone index, so frees into the wrong zone can be detected. The first free pointer is obfuscated and malloc drops its size field, opening more paths for placing attacker data on the heap. The speaker concludes that the wrong-zone attack class is closed, while application data corruption, Mach port pointers and heap grooming remain viable. Findings come from macOS research and a decompiled kernel, so later betas may differ.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2016 SG KEYNOTE 2 - Hacking The Pentagon
talks.teaser: Traces how Microsoft and the Pentagon moved from criminalizing hackers to paying them for vulnerability reports.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how US policy treated hackers after the film WarGames, when hacking was criminalized rather than put to use. The speaker then traces her own path from finding one bug at a time to shaping how vendors and governments handle outside reports. At Microsoft she describes ending a long refusal to pay hackers, using a time-limited bounty during Internet Explorer beta testing to move the flow of reports earlier, and an ongoing six-figure bounty for mitigation bypass techniques that helped the company plan longer-term fixes.

The middle section covers the Pentagon effort. A small Digital Defense Service inside the department helped run a 21-day pilot, the first federal bug bounty. Over 1,400 hackers pre-registered, and about 13 minutes into the program the first report arrived. The pilot produced 138 vulnerabilities for a total of $70,000. She also contrasts defensive vulnerability brokers with offensive markets that buy exclusivity to keep bugs secret.

She closes by arguing that most organizations are not ready to receive outside reports. Citing data from a former company, she notes that 94 percent of Forbes 2000 companies had no published way to receive a vulnerability report. Her takeaway is that organizations learn about their weaknesses only through pen testing, friendly outsiders, or attacks, so they should prepare to hear from hackers before they are attacked.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2016 SG CommSec Track D2 - Fake President Fraud Defrauded
talks.teaser: Explains business email compromise tactics and defenses, then runs a callback-document demo that traces a scammer.
talks.summary:
The talk covers fake president fraud, also known as business email compromise and fake CEO scams, in which attackers impersonate senior executives to get staff in payment roles to send unauthorised wire transfers. The speaker explains the social engineering behind it, including borrowed authority, manufactured urgency, requests for secrecy, flattery and pressure that shifts blame onto the victim. Reported case figures and examples from several companies and a bank show that the scam hits organisations of any size and industry.

Defences are grouped into organisational and technical measures. Staff awareness and two-person or two-factor checks on unusual or new-recipient transfers come first, followed by limiting public information about the company and enforcing business email addresses. On the technical side, the speaker recommends blocking external mail that spoofs internal domains, signing and encrypting email, tagging external senders, requiring strong authentication for webmail, and watching for look-alike domains.

The talk ends with a live demonstration of a callback document sent to a fake CEO. When opened, it reveals the attacker's IP address and a password hash, which the demo cracks to reach a mail account. The speaker notes the IP address points only to an ISP, so the attacker's username can link to other services and help build a case for law enforcement. The speaker stresses that such techniques are a grey area and should be used only ethically.

talks.title: #HITBGSEC 2016 SG CommSec Track D1- Halcyon - An IDE for Faster NSE Development
talks.teaser: Shows Halcyon, a Java IDE that helps write and debug Nmap scripts with code completion, templates and a scan diff.
talks.summary:
Sanoop Thomas presents Halcyon, a Java-based integrated development environment for writing Nmap scripts. He explains that security researchers often build custom Nmap scripts to check for vulnerabilities during testing, and that a dedicated editor can automate much of the repetitive work. The tool ships as a single jar that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, detects an existing Nmap installation and its class paths, and understands both Nmap and Lua syntax.

The demo covers code completion tuned to Nmap libraries, a skeleton generator that builds a script template from chosen ports, services and categories, and bundled reusable code such as brute-force driver and engine functions and a web crawler. Errors are reported in the editor: in the demo, a run output pointed to an undeclared class and a missing library import, which were fixed before the scan was rerun. Helper features include a decoder for base64, hex and URL encodings, and a scan diff that compares two scan results to show added, deleted or modified values. The diff feature was added after feedback from script developers.

To finish, the speaker shows how a completed script is exported into the local Nmap script folder and the script database is updated, so it can be run from the command line. He closes with work in progress, a built-in help wizard that offers documentation for functions and variables while the user types, and invites feedback from script developers.
