talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for #HITB2012KUL D2T1 - Rodrigo Rubira Branco - Study of Malware Obfuscation Techniques.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T2 - Fyodor Yarochkin - Messing Up the Kids Playground
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning #HITB2012KUL D2T2 - Fyodor Yarochkin - Messing Up the Kids Playground.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T1 - Ollie Whitehouse - Finding the Weak Link in Binaries
talks.teaser: Explains how to audit compiled binaries for exploit mitigations and weak build choices without source code or symbols.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a practical question: how to tell whether a Windows executable was built with modern protections when no source code or private symbols are available. The speaker walks through the defences involved, including operating system features such as ASLR and DEP that a binary has to opt into, compiler protections such as stack cookies and SafeSEH, and developer-set options like heap termination and DEP policy. Each of these can be checked from the file's headers and metadata.

Several detection methods are explained. The compiler version used for each object can be recovered from the rich header, which lets an analyst spot older Visual Studio code inside a newer binary. Stack cookies are identified through header fields, import entries and code prologue and epilogue patterns. Other checks cover DLL planting exposure through LoadLibrary calls, unmanaged code in .NET assemblies, Windows 8 sandbox capabilities declared in manifests, and the force integrity flag. A scanner run against Adobe Reader presented its results as a pass or fail report that testers could read without deep expertise. The speaker also noted that calling VirtualLock directly means a binary does not benefit from ASLR.

The talk then turns to ELF binaries on Unix-like systems, where a RUNPATH entry can override loader settings and allow library injection. The closing point is that the same assessment helps defenders decide where to deploy extra mitigations, and helps attackers pick targets where exploitation is cheaper. Because the defences keep changing, the speaker argues the checks themselves must keep being updated.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #HITB2012KUL D2T2 - John Viega - Crypto for the Public Cloud.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T1 - Shreeraj Shah - XSS & CSRF Strike Back -- Powered by HTML5
talks.teaser: Shows how HTML5 APIs such as cross-origin XHR, web storage and web workers widen the CSRF and XSS attack surface.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how HTML5 has widened the attack surface of modern browsers and single-page web applications. Browsers now give page scripts local databases, file systems, storage, background threads and cross-origin networking, so the browser behaves more like a thick client. The speaker ties these features to familiar problems, cross-site request forgery and cross-site scripting.

The main case is cross-origin XMLHttpRequest. A request with a plain-text content type skips the preflight check, and when credentials are enabled the victim's session cookie is sent along, so a third-party page can submit forged JSON to a shop backend. If a server returns a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, an attacker page can also read the responses, which allows internal network scanning and crawling from a victim's browser. Other demonstrations covered forged multipart uploads, swapping the source of a Flash object on a single-page login to a cross-domain file, and using an iframe sandbox to keep a reflected XSS foothold that captures typed input. Tokens and data kept in local storage, WebSQL, IndexedDB, virtual file systems and global variables were shown to be readable by injected script or malware. Web workers and postMessage handlers that write untrusted data into the DOM were presented as further injection points.

Defenses discussed include server-side content type checks, anti-CSRF tokens, strict CORS origin lists, origin checks in postMessage handlers, and Content Security Policy directives such as script-src and object-src. The speaker notes that CSP has known bypasses. The closing advice is to add these HTML5 APIs to audit checklists, since browsers now expose a much larger attack surface.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Marc 'Van Hauser' Heuse
talks.teaser: Shows new IPv6 flooding, fragmentation and router alert flaws, plus ways to find and test hosts in large IPv6 networks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that IPv6 is becoming necessary as IPv4 addresses run out, yet its implementations are still poorly tested. The speaker presents new findings in three groups. Flooding issues come first: router advertisement floods that push systems into configuring huge numbers of addresses or swell routing tables until they crash, and neighbor solicitation floods that keep the kernel busy on several operating systems.

Fragmentation problems follow. Reassembled packets can exceed 64 kilobytes, a personal firewall blue-screened on fragmented traffic, and another firewall let fragmented packets bypass rules that blocked new TCP connections. A small set of fragments with large offset gaps exhausted one firewall's memory. A router alert option in a hop-by-hop header let pings pass a router's ICMP access list on some Cisco IOS versions. Scans of large companies' IPv6 space found more exposed remote administration services than on IPv4, and many backbone routers answered on telnet.

For remote testing, the speaker shows how to find live hosts in very large subnets using BGP prefix announcements, common host addresses, DNS reverse-zone walking and wordlists, then checking candidates with a live-scanning tool. He closes with deployment obstacles: DHCPv6 cannot supply gateways or routes in the same way, IPv6 security features cost more on switches and routers, and some vendors have been slow to fix reported bugs. Practitioners should test IPv6 as thoroughly as IPv4.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T3 - 'OPEN BOTTLE'
talks.teaser: Security Industry Panel Discussion explores #HITB2012KUL D2T3 - 'OPEN BOTTLE'.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T1 - Paul Vixie - Silo Busting in Information Security: The ISC SIE Approach
talks.teaser: Explains why exclusive security data silos hurt defenders and how an open passive DNS exchange tries to share that data.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that the security industry has built large market value over two decades without making the internet safer. Companies win customers by gaining exclusive access to network telemetry, such as a DNS resolver feed, a spam trap or a span port inside an operator's network. Because each exclusive arrangement keeps data from competitors, defenders rarely get to correlate what they see, which he calls information silos.

As an alternative, the Internet Systems Consortium runs an open exchange that accepts batches of sensor data, including passive DNS, darknet traffic and spam traps. Vetted subscribers, such as researchers, firms and agencies, receive the feed on a private switch with about a minute of delay, and a deduplication stage keeps only new records. A separate filter diverts noise, such as streaming-service DNS checks and DNS tunneling, into its own channel. The resulting passive DNS database answers historical questions, so an investigator can list the names that once pointed to an address or the domains that used a given name server. The live demo showed these pivots on a network block and on a name server.

The speaker warns that reverse-indexed history makes privacy harder to protect than single lookups do, even though the underlying records are public. He urges operators to run sensors and send their data, and invites organisations to pay for or request access. He also outlines a planned channel for WHOIS query data, which could help reveal new botnets as they start up.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D2T3 - Stefano Zanero
talks.teaser: Presents research on matching malware code across samples and tracking how families change between versions.
talks.summary:
Stefano Zanero of Politecnico di Milano argues that malware now varies constantly and is delivered stealthily, so signature lists miss much of it. He showed antivirus detection rates that rarely passed 90 percent, and noted that manual static analysis cannot keep up with the volume of samples. Pure dynamic analysis has its own gap, because parts of a sample stay dormant until specific conditions trigger them.

The first tool, Reanimator, turns code reuse into an advantage. It runs a sample in an instrumented sandbox, flags behaviors of interest, and slices out the code responsible for each one. That slice is filtered against clean executions, completed into a control flow subgraph, and matched against a database of other samples. On 208 bots with known source code, checked against the MOSS plagiarism tool, the method had few false negatives and no false positives, and it revealed behaviors that were implemented in many samples but never executed. It tolerated recompilation and obfuscation but not a different compiler, and it requires unpacked code. The second tool, Beagle, ran a malware family's updates over time, grouped system-level activity into behaviors, and compared functions across versions. In Zeus-type families, each version added roughly 5 to 10 percent new code, and some redesigns were estimated at around 9,000 lines.

The talk closed with family naming, where antivirus labels for the same samples could not be mapped onto each other. The speaker proposed combining structural and dynamic features to cluster families more reliably. His takeaway was that static analysis alone is too slow and dynamic analysis alone misses code, so using both supports triage of new samples, detection of dormant behavior, and tracking of changes between versions.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T1 - Lucas Adamski - Mozilla Apps, Firefox OS and You
talks.teaser: Explains how Firefox OS isolates apps, gates permissions at use time, and protects the system from compromised apps.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out Firefox OS goals: shield the device from malicious apps, isolate apps from each other, and share private data only with user consent. It walks the stack from gonk, a Linux base, through Gecko, the runtime shared with Firefox, up to Gaia, the HTML and JavaScript interface. Apps range from plain web content to manifest-declared sites, privileged packaged apps, and a few certified system apps.

Privileged apps get a stricter Content Security Policy that blocks dynamic code, so the reviewed code is the code that runs. That justifies persistent access to riskier APIs. Permissions are declared in the manifest and requested at time of use. Each app has its own data store, runs in a low-rights process, and cannot launch another app. A mozbrowser frame gives browser-style apps a separate data jar.

Web activities let one app hand a task, like taking a photo, to another handler without holding that permission. Privileged apps pass a manual review, and the speaker argued that brand control keeps unwanted carrier software removable. The takeaway is a manifest-driven, reviewed and isolated model that trades some web convenience, such as shared single sign-on, for privacy.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning #HITB2012KUL D1T3 - John Captain Crunch Draper - A Historical Look at the Phreaking Scene.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Wes Brown
talks.teaser: Explains how a malware sandbox correlates behavior, network and file artifacts across repeated runs at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how ThreatGRID built a malware intelligence service that does not deduplicate submissions. Instead, it reruns the same samples over long periods and records how their behaviour, files and network activity change over time. Wes Brown explains that this approach, which covers roughly a million samples a day, drove the design of an in-house cluster with petabyte-scale storage and a 40gbps interconnect.

The sandbox relies on an in-house kernel debugger and hypervisor-level hooks that malware has difficulty detecting, along with block-level disk analysis that records file system changes even when a kernel monitor is evaded. Each session keeps VM snapshots, memory dumps, network captures and a JSON analysis file. Artifacts are linked across samples through shared IP addresses, domains, registry keys, PE sections and fuzzy hashes. Brown gives examples: one IRC-controlled dropper that produced different artifacts on almost every day of a year, and a single IP address that tied together 30 malware variants that looked unrelated as binaries.

He closes by arguing that antivirus hash verdicts can change over time, so behavioural correlation is more reliable than a single good or bad label. He also suggests analysts should spend their effort on intelligence rather than reverse engineering each sample, and says Android support would need extra engineering time but reuse the same approach.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Meder Kydyraliev
talks.teaser: Defibrilating Web Security examines #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Meder Kydyraliev.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T3 - The Grugq - OPSEC: Because Jail is for wuftpd
talks.teaser: Shows how operational security failures led to hacker arrests and how personas, anonymity tools and disciplined habits reduce risk.
talks.summary:
The Grugq argues that anyone running anonymous online operations has to plan for the fact that one mistake can be fatal, and that most failures are non-technical: saying too much, trusting co-conspirators, and mixing personal life with operations. He presents a methodology built on creating cover identities and their backstories before using them, keeping each persona isolated from the others and from the speaker's real identity, and retiring personas before they attract attention.

Using several arrested hackers as examples, the talk shows how investigators linked identities. One suspect reused a handle tied to his real first name across aliases and later confirmed his identity to an informant in chat. Another used a personal Facebook account to send defacement code and connected to a compromised account from his home network. Investigators combined Wi-Fi triangulation, hardware details mentioned in chat, and the timing of online activity against physical surveillance. A leaked photo carrying GPS metadata exposed another person's location. The speaker also lists profiling risks such as weather talk, daily routines and keyboard layout.

On tooling, the speaker separates privacy from anonymity, arguing that Tor should be used before any VPN and that Bitcoin is anonymous but not private. He describes a small router that sends all traffic through Tor and fails closed, paired with an operational laptop that has no radios or battery. He closes by noting that Tor can be deanonymized by an adversary controlling many relays, so target selection matters, and that the core lesson is to say less and practice the persona until it becomes second nature.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T1 - P. Langlois & E. Gadaix - Why Telcos Keep Getting Hacked
talks.teaser: Traces decades of telecom security failures, from phreaking to SS7 and mobile core attacks, and why operators keep getting breached.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a history of telecom hacking, from in-band signalling tricks and payphone tone abuse to remote maintenance terminals with default logins that remain reachable from the internet. It explains why operators long assumed their networks were closed and trusted. The speakers then describe SS7 as the signalling layer that replaced those early systems, noting that it still lacks strong authentication, access control and perimeter filtering in many networks.

Several case studies follow. Spoofed subscriber-data and location messages can move users between networks or switch prepaid accounts to postpaid, and flooding can cause denial of service. A mobile money platform was shown to leak PINs through sniffed USSD traffic over SS7, despite vendor claims of end-to-end encryption. Other examples include femtocells compromised through firmware weaknesses, exposed Oracle and Solaris systems, GTP tunnel abuse that enabled fake charging, and a police location-tracking network reachable from a standard phone.

The talk also covers lawful interception platforms and the metadata they collect, and argues that operator security programmes focus on fraud and revenue rather than protocol security. The takeaway is that telecom operators need protocol-level security testing, filtering at network boundaries and openness to independent research, since attacks have shifted from internal fraud to external intrusion.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Don Bailey - Hackers the Movie: A Retrospective
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Don Bailey - Hackers the Movie: A Retrospective.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T2 - Haroon Meer - You and Your Research
talks.teaser: Argues that good security research needs drive and important problems, illustrated with examples from well-known researchers.
talks.summary:
Haroon Meer builds this talk around a well-known essay on research by Hamming, asking what separates great work from ordinary work. He starts with his own projects, including a Chrome plugin for GPG encryption and a study of whether Black Hat tweets are about talks or parties, then argues that great work comes less from luck or raw brains than from independent thinking, courage and sustained drive.

Using security examples, he shows how early small projects can grow into major contributions. Johnny Long's Google hacking talk started modestly, Tavis's bugs led to early iPhone and PSP jailbreaks, and HD Moore's Metasploit grew from exploit tooling that others could build on. He warns against resting on early recognition, chasing small wins and giving yourself comfortable excuses. He suggests working on important problems, sharing work so others can extend it, and marketing your research.

In questions, he said balance is rarely even for people doing serious research, and that newcomers should start doing work because skill comes from practice. For researchers whose write-ups go unnoticed, he advised persistence, recalling that cross-site scripting was once dismissed before its impact became clear. The takeaway is to keep choosing hard problems and let the work prove itself over time.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T1 - Chris Wysopal - Data Mining a Mountain of Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #HITB2012KUL D1T1 - Chris Wysopal - Data Mining a Mountain of Vulnerabilities.

talks.title: #HITB2012KUL D1T1 - A. Barisani & D. Bianco
talks.teaser: Shows how to find debug ports, dump firmware and patch the Apple SMC microcontroller in a laptop.
talks.summary:
The talk covers practical ways to get into embedded systems, which are single-purpose devices such as routers, printers and laptop controllers. It starts with finding a serial console by logic-analysing exposed pins and converting voltage levels. It then covers locating JTAG pins by using a probe resistor to identify power and ground, scanning them with a microcontroller, and dumping SPI flash by desoldering the chip or bridging it through a microcontroller.

Next, the speakers look at firmware checksums. Most devices use CRC variants, but identifying the polynomial is not enough, because some flavours cannot be described by standard Rocksoft parameters. One draft POSIX CRC, for instance, special-cases zero indexes. Checksums can also be matched by crafting collisions in four controllable bytes. Where no development toolkit is available, they wrap kernel functions by redirecting a function pointer and calling the original, which lets them log or change arguments without breaking behaviour.

As a worked example, they analyse the firmware update for an Apple System Management Controller. Its data blocks use nested sum-based checks, which only guard against corruption rather than tampering. Identifying the chip as a Renesas H8S-family microcontroller from its datasheet let them map code offsets to data and alter the SMC key table. The talk ends with a video of a modified firmware being flashed from the EFI shell.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS CLOSING KEYNOTE - Ms jaya Baloo
talks.teaser: Identity details #HITB2012AMS CLOSING KEYNOTE - Ms jaya Baloo.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D2T2 - Steven Seeley - Ghost in the Windows 7 Allocator
talks.teaser: Explains Windows 7 low fragmentation heap internals, a new free entry offset attack, and Windows 8 heap randomization.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why heap memory corruption is becoming a more valuable target as simpler stack bugs disappear from mature software. It walks through how the Windows 7 low fragmentation heap (LFH) allocator is organised, covering the front-end structures, the back-end bin and block handling, and the free entry offset that predicts where the next allocation will come from.

The middle section reviews two earlier published techniques for turning allocator metadata into an arbitrary free or an arbitrary allocation. The speaker then presents a new Windows 7 variant built on a double free that leaves a chunk header in a state the allocator accepts, so repeated allocations return the same address and a new object can overlap a function pointer. A debugger demo shows the overlap and the resulting pointer overwrite. The talk then covers Windows 8 changes, including randomized chunk selection, a busy bitmap, and a guard page on the user blocks structure. It proposes a sequential overflow into the user blocks header that can yield an arbitrary allocation without an information leak, although reliability depends on how many chunks sit between the overflowing chunk and the target.

The closing part stresses that reliability remains the main obstacle and that randomization does not remove heap exploitation. In questions, the speaker discussed whether Microsoft might add cookies to heap chunks, noting that encoding already protects part of the header, and suggested that guard pages could be applied to user blocks earlier in their lifetime.

talks.summary: The speakers describe how they jailbroke iOS 5.0.1 on A5 devices without a boot-level exploit. They explain how VPN settings and a web clip triggered code execution through raccoon, how crash reports supplied address information to work around ASLR, and how a ptrace flaw let them escape the sandbox and launch the kernel exploit. The talk also announces their untethered jailbreak for iOS 5.1.1.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D2T1 - Georgia Weidman - Bypassing the Android Permission Model
talks.teaser: Shows how Android apps abuse granted permissions, world-readable storage and exported components to steal data without exploits.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Georgia Weidman demonstrates that Android's permission model is so fundamentally flawed that malware developers don't need to bypass it at all—they can simply request excessive permissions that users readily accept. Rather than exploit the system, attackers can abuse the legitimate permission model, gain root access through vulnerable exploits, or craft clever attacks against app interfaces.

## Permission Model Failures
Weidman begins by examining Facebook for Android, which requests an extensive set of permissions (contacts, SMS, location, accounts, storage, calls, IMEI access, etc.) despite not needing them all. She builds a simple app called "hello Android" requesting only three permissions: read contacts, read IMEI, and send SMS. This app silently steals the device's IMEI and transmits it via SMS without any user notification or entry in the sent folder, proving that users willingly grant permissions they don't understand and that apps can abuse them invisibly.

## Rooting and Droid Dream Malware
Weidman discusses rooting tools (Super One Click, Z4 mod) and their legitimate use, then contrasts them with Droid Dream—the first known malware discovered in Google Play Store. Droid Dream appeared as innocent apps (bowling games, adult content) but contained copied legitimate apps while silently deploying root exploits ("Rage Against the Cage" is specifically mentioned) in the background. It asked for only four permissions, which didn't raise suspicion. Once rooted, the device's permission model completely collapses; system-level apps bypass all permission restrictions and gain complete control.

## Kernel-Level SMS Interception
Weidman demonstrates kernel-level SMS hijacking using three rooted G1 phones. After gaining root, malware can install shims at the kernel/modem driver level to intercept all SMS traffic before it reaches the application layer. GSM messages are unencrypted by the time they reach the phone (only encrypted in transit via session keys), so malware can decode, analyze, and redirect messages without keys. The demo shows an attacker sending a command SMS that the victim receives, then retransmitting that message to a contact—demonstrating how to silently add devices to botnets.

## Insecure Data Storage and Reversing
Weidman presents "bad file save" and "bad SMS file" apps. "Bad file save" stores the IMEI on the world-readable SD card; "bad SMS file" (with no storage permissions) reads and exfiltrates it via SMS. She demonstrates reversing Android apps using Dex2Jar and JD-GUI, showing how attackers can extract Java source code from APKs, discover exactly what data is stored where, and locate file names and function signatures in minutes.

## Intent Exploitation
Weidman's final attack shows an unprivileged app (SMS intent, zero permissions) calling components in a privileged app (SMS broadcaster, send SMS permission) by constructing a malicious intent. By reverse-engineering the target app to discover its package name, component names, and parameter keys, the attacker can invoke dangerous functions without owning the required permissions.

## Mitigations
Developers must: secure storage (encrypt, keep off SD card, don't make world-readable), protect dangerous interfaces with user confirmation dialogs, and use the "require permission" tag in Android manifest files. Users must update phones—but update delays from carriers mean devices remain vulnerable for months or years. Weidman notes developers often ignore security guidance because they prioritize features over safety and rarely consult Android's security documentation.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D2T1 - A. Bazhanyuk and N. Tarakanov - Automatically Searching for Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Explains taint analysis with BitBlaze to automatically find vulnerabilities, and the pitfalls of applying it to Windows kernel drivers.
talks.summary:
The talk covers automating vulnerability discovery with taint analysis, using the BitBlaze platform as the main example. Mutation fuzzing often gets nowhere against undocumented formats protected by checksums or cryptography, and manual reverse engineering of those formats is slow. Taint analysis tracks how input data flows through each instruction. BitBlaze combines a static stage, where IDA plugins flag risky spots such as copy routines, allocators and indirect calls, with a dynamic stage: an emulator that records execution, and Vine, which converts traces into an intermediate language and uses a constraint solver to produce inputs that take other branches. Repeating this loop explores new paths toward a crash.

The open-source release needed heavy custom work. Performance is the main drawback. One Microsoft Office case produced a trace of about 30 GB and took roughly 40 minutes, so the approach suits kernel drivers, where code is smaller, better than large user-mode programs. Pitfalls include lost taint through string handling and pointer-based accesses, checks on system state, and driver defenses that crash under instrumentation.

Applied to Windows kernel drivers, the approach found several issues. One routine reachable from user mode allowed an arbitrary memory decrement that could lead to instruction pointer control, fixed in a later version. A third-party engine DLL in kernel land exposed about fifty functions taking unchecked pointers, affecting several security products. The closing message is that automated tracing finds simple but serious driver bugs, while turning them into reliable exploits stays hard because of mitigations and randomization.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D2T2 - Rahul Sasi - CXML VXML IVR Pentesting for Auditors
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #HITB2012AMS D2T2 - Rahul Sasi - CXML VXML IVR Pentesting for Auditors.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Rahul Sasi, a security researcher at iGAT Partners, presents a comprehensive guide on attacking and auditing Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems using CXML and VXML languages. The talk covers practical exploitation techniques against phone banking and customer service applications, demonstrating that IVR systems widely trusted by financial institutions lack adequate security controls.

## What Are IVR Systems

IVR systems are automated telephone applications that respond to user input via Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency (DTMF) keypresses or voice commands. Common implementations include phone banking, customer support lines, and medical inquiry systems. The architecture consists of: a telephone network, TCP/IP network connecting the vxml server (which hosts the CXML/VXML application), and web application servers that perform actual authentication and data processing.

## Key Vulnerabilities Demonstrated

### Brute Force Attacks
Sasi showed a real-world phone banking vulnerability where a 4-digit PIN combined with account numbers created exploitable conditions. The bank's system only blocked accounts after 3 failed attempts and reset them at midnight daily. Using an automated Python program with AT commands, an attacker could attempt multiple PIN combinations against many account numbers within each reset window, dramatically increasing success chances.

### SQL Injection via DTMF
Despite DTMF limitations (only 0-9, *, #), SQL injection is possible using mathematical operations. The speaker demonstrated "true injection" (e.g., PIN*1*1 = PIN, evaluated as true) and "false injection" (e.g., PIN*1*0 = 0, evaluated as false). These payloads work because they're mathematically valid on MySQL and can be entered via phone keypads. Live demonstrations showed authentication bypass using payloads like "31337*1*1" (successful login) versus "31337*1*0" (no match found).

### Buffer Overflow and Error Disclosure
IVR applications often reveal internal errors as voice messages, enabling fingerprinting and exploitation. Sending long DTMF sequences to vulnerable CGI applications caused stack overflows, resulting in HTTP 500 errors that the system read aloud: "error starting voice XML application failed fetch with code 500 server error... internal error." This disclosed URLs, session IDs, and backend information.

### Alpha-Numeric Input and Voice Payloads
Applications accepting alpha-numeric voice input (common in banks using non-numeric user IDs) introduce additional attack surface. Using grammar files that map voice words to characters, attackers can construct URL-encoded payloads by spelling characters—for example, saying "percentage 27" translates to a single quote (%), enabling more sophisticated SQL injection via voice.

## Technical Demonstrations

The speaker provided live examples:
- Automated phone banking login bypass successfully extracting balance information
- DTMF processing demo showing the system recognizing "5" and speech recognition recognizing "red"
- SQL injection testing showing different responses for valid vs. invalid payloads
- Buffer overflow triggering internal server errors
- Alpha-numeric input processing demonstrating payload construction via voice

## Audit Approach for IVR Systems

Unlike web application testing (which reveals HTML error pages), IVR auditing relies on triggering internal errors that the system reads aloud as voice output. By identifying application logic flows and sending malicious payloads, auditors can extract system information and exploit vulnerabilities through audio responses.

## Real-World Impact

Sasi confirmed finding vulnerabilities in an actual Indian bank's IVR system, highlighting the critical risk that attackers could crash phone banking applications remotely using only a phone, disrupting customer access and operations.

## Future Research

Ongoing work focuses on DTMF detection algorithms (particularly the Goertzel algorithm) embedded in PBX systems and vxml servers, with the goal of fuzzing different frequencies to remotely crash multiple phone banking applications.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D2T1 - Andrei Costin - PostScript - Danger Ahead - Hacking MFPs, PCs and Beyond
talks.teaser: Shows how PostScript streams can turn networked printers and MFPs into attack platforms, dumping memory and leaking credentials.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Andrei Costin explores the security risks associated with PostScript and how it can be weaponized against multi-function printers (MFPs), client PCs, and network infrastructure. Drawing on research conducted between 2010 and 2012, Costin highlights that network printers are inherently trusted, often expose sensitive internal credentials (LDAP, SNMP), and frequently lack robust vulnerability and patch management. Furthermore, thousands of enterprise MFPs were discovered directly exposed to the public internet, creating severe security exposures.

### Key Topics
- **Nature of PostScript**: Unlike static document formats, PostScript is a dynamically typed, concatenative, stack-based, and Turing-complete programming language introduced by Adobe. Because it is Turing-complete, general-purpose computation (such as cryptographic cracking or network exploitation) can be implemented directly within print streams.
- **Obfuscation and Detection Evasion**: PostScript programs can build and execute code on the fly by concatenating strings and converting them to executable procedures at runtime. As a result, static signature-based security controls (traditional antivirus, IDS/IPS) fail to detect malicious PostScript streams.
- **Widespread Interpreter Attack Surface**: Interpreters are embedded across multiple ecosystems—including client software (Ghostscript, Microsoft Office via Access Softek), print servers (CUPS), cloud/web services processing document conversions (including Google services), and embedded print engines from various vendors.
- **Exploitation via Environment Detection**: PostScript files can query their environment using operators like `product` (e.g., detecting GPL Ghostscript). Attackers can trigger different behavior depending on execution context, such as displaying a social engineering error on a PC while delivering malicious exploitation routines when processed by an MFP.

### Technical Details
- **Client and Denial of Service Attacks**: The speaker demonstrates that a trivial recursive loop or infinite loop in PostScript or Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) can freeze Microsoft Office or crash interpreters, requiring application termination or hardware resets.
- **Decompilation of Xerox Firmware Updates**: Analyzing Xerox firmware update files (which were distributed with `.PS` extensions) revealed proprietary PostScript API extensions. These exposed powerful internal features, including VxWorks operating system hooks, QA/debugging hooks, socket controls, and direct memory/RAM interfaces.
- **PostScript Memory Dumping**: Costin wrote a memory dumper in PostScript targeting port 9100. Despite web administrative passwords, memory dumping bypassed authentication restrictions entirely.
- **Credential and Document Extraction**: Cleartext administrator passwords from HTTP GET requests, Base64-encoded basic authentication headers, private SSL keys, user PINs (such as `pjL SET HOLD KEY`), and full document print streams were recovered directly from RAM because buffers were freed without being cleared.
- **Network Reconnaissance and Pivoting**: Printers running discovery protocols (like UPnP) retain local network topology in memory. The dumper extracted IP addresses and software versions of surrounding network devices (e.g., a Linux router running miniupnpd and other network printers). Costin noted that with Turing completeness, BSD-like socket support, and raw RAM access, PostScript payloads can be weaponized to launch exploits against other internal hosts or even spread as a self-propagating worm.

### Takeaways
Costin emphasizes that printers and MFPs suffer from severe architectural shortcomings: a lack of privilege separation between print jobs and administrative interfaces, improper memory wiping, and unprotected super-APIs. Because static inspection cannot evaluate dynamic PostScript code, defensive tooling must shift toward dynamic sandboxing environments that trace interpreter operations. Organizations need stronger network segmentation and rigorous embedded security evaluations, while developers must avoid passing sensitive data in URL GET parameters or leaving cryptographic keys and sensitive print jobs uncleared in device memory.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS DAY 1 SPECIAL CLOSING
talks.teaser: Argues that security teams should stop trusting surveillance as a fix and refuse to sell zero-days to intelligence agencies.
talks.summary:
The closing session argues that organisations and governments gamble on weak security while society absorbs the cost. The speaker cites banks that still use magnetic stripes that were shown to be easy to copy decades ago, and public transport chip cards that were insecure from the start. He argues that answering these failures with more cameras and recording is a mistake, since a rewind capability does not supply the missing security and does not reduce cybercrime.

The middle of the talk turns to governments. Zero-day vulnerabilities, once sold mainly to criminal groups, are now bought by nation states and intelligence agencies, and the speaker links this to Stuxnet and to Windows flaws that were not disclosed promptly. He describes weapons payloads escaping their targets and making attribution unclear, and he urges researchers to disclose responsibly rather than sell to intelligence bureaucracies. The audience discussion covered whether researchers should help their own countries, and how to reach the public and decision makers. On the latter, he recalled how a hands-on break of Dutch voting machines in 2006 changed a debate that theoretical arguments had not moved.

He closes by saying computer security is still far from finished and that systems should not be trusted beyond what they can demonstrate. He argues that industry incentives reward complexity and billable hours, and that people tend to act only when a system is shown to be broken. Practitioners should keep making that case with evidence.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D1T1 - Roberto Suggi Liverani and Scott Bell
talks.teaser: Covers browser bugs in Firefox, Maxthon, Avant and Opera, from a use-after-free to injections into privileged browser zones.
talks.summary:
The talk presents browser bugs found across several popular browsers, starting with Firefox. The Firefox use-after-free was found by fuzzing with a modified CrossFuzz tool, and minimising the crash took months. The final proof of concept relied on a race: closing a child window while a file open dialog was showing triggered the crash inside a Windows API. Code execution was demonstrated with DEP disabled.

The middle section focuses on injection bugs rather than memory corruption. In Maxthon, content injected into the about:history page, RSS feed fields and bookmark entries ran in privileged browser zones, and an internet-hosted page could reach internal browser objects through its trusted domain. Avant browser had a same-origin policy bypass in its browser home page via an undocumented function. A Firefox add-on relied on a sanitising function that left event-handler attributes intact, and bookmarked JavaScript URIs were shown running in privileged contexts such as the Opera configuration page.

The talk closes by arguing that injection into a trusted zone can lead to code execution without any memory corruption. It also points to slow or absent responses from several vendors as a recurring problem for researchers.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D1T1 - Juan Pablo Echtegoyen - Attacking the SAP Solution Manager
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker moves from one weak SAP system through the Solution Manager and into other systems.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at attacking SAP landscapes through the Solution Manager, the central administration system that most SAP installations connect to. The speaker argues that SAP systems hold payroll, customer, banking and product data, so the impact of compromise goes beyond root shells and should be assessed at the business level. Pen tests described in the talk began with nothing more than a list of IP addresses, and in those engagements roughly 95 percent of systems were compromised.

The walkthrough starts with weak non-production systems that still use default standard users and passwords, which a brute-force module can detect. From a compromised satellite system, the speaker inspects RFC destinations in SM59, where stored credentials and trusted links to the Solution Manager allow a move up to it and then back down into other systems. Further cases cover Gateway attacks, an unauthenticated command execution flaw in the CCMS monitoring agent that runs as the system's admin user, and the Diagnostics agent's P4 interface, which can be abused to deploy a custom application that runs commands.

The closing advice is to treat the Solution Manager as a production-grade asset and keep it off the internet, while segmenting SAP networks from end-user networks. Teams should inventory every RFC connection, including ones created by developers, and remove stored or overly permissive credentials. Patching and a separate Solution Manager for production are also advised, since non-productive systems remain a route into the rest of the landscape.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D1T2 - MuscleNerd - Evolution of iPhone Baseband and Unlocks
talks.teaser: Traces the history of iPhone baseband exploits, from leaked change logs and AT command flaws to SIM tricks and activation tickets.
talks.summary:
A member of the iPhone dev team opens with why baseband work is hard. The cellular processor can crash at any moment and drop its USB link, and its crash logs hold little beyond registers and a stack dump. Parts of the firmware run directly from flash, and early basebands leaked detailed change logs in their embedded comments. The talk also covers hidden diagnostic commands gated by a single flag, and an AT command bitmask that disabled hundreds of commands. Clearing that mask re-enabled them for testing.

The middle section walks through unlock methods. Ultrasn0w intercepted messages passed between baseband tasks and altered a security comparison, which short-circuited the unlock check. Later firmware checked for tampered messages, and that check was bypassed. Turbo SIM answered early IMSI queries with a faked carrier until the firmware was fixed. Activation tickets, which are signed ASN.1 structures listing permitted IMSIs, were studied in detail. A server bug exploited by the SAM tool produced a ticket tied to a single SIM card. On the 3G, a bootloader check accepted arbitrary lengths and addresses, and a borrowed signature satisfied the other check.

The closing section turns to newer hardware. The iPhone 4S has no baseband flash, so its image must be fed to the chip on every boot, which makes boot-stage experiments easier. Baseband tickets carry a nonce check, and Qualcomm's move to the Hexagon DSP was flagged as a likely source of new bugs. The speaker encourages researchers to buy an iPhone 4S and look for baseband vulnerabilities.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS D1T1 - Arnauld Mascret - Whistling Over the Wire
talks.teaser: Shows how URL shorteners on Twitter can be used to single out and profile one target through browser behavior.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at how a team that runs intrusion missions for companies could use Twitter and its link shorteners to reach one specific person rather than a broad audience. The speaker argues that a single targeted delivery is harder to detect than a mass spread, and notes that earlier work covered LinkedIn and Facebook while this one focuses on Twitter.

The method starts with profiling a target from public account data, such as followers, tweets, shared links, hashtags and the client application used to post, gathered from pages that look like normal browsing. The speaker then describes creating supporting accounts, using email tricks to obtain many addresses, and the CAPTCHA on the mobile sign-up form, which the speaker tried to read with a custom OCR, a difficult route. The talk compares how shorteners forward visitors through HTTP redirects, meta refresh and JavaScript, and how user agent and plugin details reveal what a visitor's browser can do.

The core technique checks whether the target has visited a chosen site, using CSS visited-link styling and a timing test on cached images, which the speaker put at around 50 URLs per second. A live demo showed a JavaScript-based redirect finishing faster than a meta refresh. The closing takeaway is that a platform built for sharing links and clicks gives attackers a dependable way to deliver code, and that the tools needed already exist. Audience questions covered how many accounts were needed and whether Twitter is more trusted than Facebook.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS KEYNOTE 2 - Bruce Schneier
talks.teaser: Explains how morals, reputation, laws and security sustain trust in society, and why technology keeps upsetting that balance.
talks.summary:
Schneier opens by noting how much daily life rests on trust in strangers, from hotel staff and taxi drivers to the systems behind an ATM withdrawal. He frames the talk as a look at how society induces cooperation, drawing on his book Liars and Outliers. Cooperative systems, he argues, attract parasitic defectors, and the prisoners dilemma captures the tension between individual and group interest.

He describes four societal pressures that keep defection at a manageable level: morals, reputation, laws and institutions, and security systems. Reputation is especially strong, and he cites a coffee-machine experiment in which a pair of eyes on a sign raised payment compared with a picture of flowers. Technology lets these pressures scale, as credit scores and eBay feedback do, yet each new technology upsets the balance. Attackers tend to exploit innovation faster than defenders can respond, leaving a widening security gap. He suggests reacting quickly rather than trying to close that gap.

Questions covered lobbying by the security industry, whether the four pressures can be separated, cultural differences in norms, and privacy norms shaped by companies with financial interests. He ends by saying defectors are needed because they drive social change, and that the realistic goal is to reduce defection to a manageable rate rather than eliminate it.

talks.title: #HITB2012AMS - KEYNOTE 1 - Andy Ellis - Getting Ahead of the Security Poverty Line
talks.teaser: Shows how under-resourced security teams can measure their value and cut risk through small, sustained changes.
talks.summary:
Andy Ellis opens by defining the security poverty line, a term coined by Wendy Nather for organizations that lack resources for even baseline controls. He frames security value as resources multiplied by capabilities, where capabilities combine skill, effort and effectiveness. Environment matters: when five staff focused on corporate security were moved under the CIO, the group became roughly twice as effective without losing anyone.

Ellis then turns to how people react to risk. Drawing on Sam Peltzman's work on seat belts and NASCAR, and on Amsterdam bicycles without hand brakes, he argues that people hold a set point of perceived risk and will absorb or push back against change. Long-lived risk tends to get rationalized away, so he recommends removing risk in small, routine steps that a business can digest. He also separates good assessors, who help improve controls, from auditors working checklists, and warns that late vendor reviews rarely change anything.

His case studies show the approach in practice. After a past breach exposed an SSH trojan, his team turned login gateways into VPN-like pass-throughs and replaced a widely shared root key with per-user access grants, cutting access by more than 99.9 percent. Annual awareness training became a single policy page with an acknowledgment log, and a 10-petabyte customer cloud was scanned for malware with a lightweight HTML-focused check instead of antivirus. He closes by urging leaders to grow capability each year and track deferred work in a simple spreadsheet.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - Day 2 - Track 1 - Air Travel Hacking Understanding and (Ab) Using the ....
talks.teaser: Reveals GDS fare mechanics, routing-rule gaps, and fuel dumping tactics that cut transatlantic fares far below retail quotes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames commercial air travel as a stack of marketing booking classes, inventory counters, and global distribution systems that grew from airline-owned tools into outsourced platforms such as Amadeus and Galileo. It distinguishes physical cabin classes from single-letter booking codes, codeshares, plating carriers, and ticket stock, then shows how experts expose the same fare data consumer sites hide.

The middle walks through fare bases, routing rules, add-ons, end-to-end combinations, and point-of-sale differences, including tools like ExpertFlyer and ITA Software for mining rules before booking. The speaker describes typo fares, permissive routing mistakes, client-side price manipulation on a multi-country travel site, Perl-based scraping across aggregators, and automated cents-per-mile hunting. The centerpiece is fuel dumping: adding a cheap third segment so the issuing carrier fails to collect YQ surcharge, with worked examples driving transatlantic totals down sharply.

Practitioners should treat these as fragile, often short-lived gaps in complex tariffs rather than guaranteed discounts, favor large agencies over small agents, avoid broadcasting working combinations, and watch faster airline fare updates closing mistakes within hours. The close notes parallel pricing errors in hotels and cruises, community disclosure norms, and brief comments on upgrades, bumps, and inventory-based tactics.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - Day2 - Track 1- Femtocells - Kevin Redon & Nico Golde - A Poisonous Needle in the..
talks.teaser: Shows how a consumer femtocell can be rooted and abused to intercept, inject and redirect mobile operator traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at femtocells, small home base stations that mobile operators sell to customers and connect to the carrier network over the internet. The speakers first outline the 3G UMTS architecture and where femtocell components such as the home node B gateway, security gateway and management system sit. They then bought a consumer femtocell from a French operator and studied its recovery process, which downloads configuration and firmware over a mix of HTTPS and plain HTTP.

They reported several flaws in that process, including a server certificate the device never checked, which let them serve their own configuration and firmware. A hidden vendor web interface allowed changing the operator identity and access mode, turning the device into an IMSI catcher. Through a proxy for the generic access network protocol, they modified and injected SMS messages, and used forged paging and authentication exchanges to act as a subscriber. They also detached a phone from the network with an unauthenticated IMSI detach message. A stack overflow in the embedded web server, which runs as root, let them compromise other femtocells remotely.

Further findings included web pages that leaked IMSI and MSISDN values across about five thousand devices, neighbor-cell data that revealed device locations, and an operator performance server reachable with shared credentials. Using a SIM card and laptop, they reached the operator's core side and sent HLR queries. The speakers argued that the architecture relies on trusting devices placed in customers' homes, and that the split of responsibility between vendor and operator leaves gaps. The takeaway is that home equipment should not be trusted by default.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - Day2 - Track1 - Marc Blanchou & Mathew Solnik
talks.teaser: BlackBox Android Breaking En details HITB2011KUL - Day2 - Track1 - Marc Blanchou & Mathew Solnik.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - Day2 - Track 1 - Stefan Esser -IPhone Exploitation. One ROPe to Bind Them All
talks.teaser: Shows how multi-environment ROP and automated gadget analysis raise success rates against many iOS 4 targets without prior leaks.
talks.summary:
The presentation tackles iPhone exploitation when the attacker has a stack buffer overflow but no information leak, and must succeed across many iOS 4 device and build combinations. It catalogs how Apple’s protections force pure return-oriented programming: non-executable stack and heap, code signing, libraries consolidated in the shared cache with per-firmware load-order variation, and evolving mitigations split into pre-4.3 and 4.3.x eras with partial ASLR that still leaves many third-party apps and the dynamic linker weakly randomized.

To beat long odds—roughly tens of thousands of possible gadget locations in the cage versus far fewer for dyld—the speaker builds multi-environment ROP chains whose meaning only becomes clear in a specific target. A lightweight Python ARM/Thumb emulator scans thirteen dynamic linker binaries, intersects gadgets at shared offsets, and wires “switcher” sequences that infer environment from which stack slot supplies the next program counter. Small per-linker copy stubs advance the stack and preserve payload data so one front half can vibrate phones, steal files, or phone home with dyld slide and cache fingerprints for a precise second stage.

With ASLR, clustering gadgets by page offset can improve dyld hit rates modestly (for example one in 64 versus one in 256), while analogous shared-cache collision work balloons shellcode size for marginal gain. The closing argument: without ASLR, one rope can bind post-4.2.1 targets; with ASLR, gains exist but remain limited until richer emulation expands the gadget set.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - D1T2 - Alexander Polyakov, Dimitry Chastuhin
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed SAP Java engines can be breached from the internet, then used for post-exploitation and credential theft.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the Java engine of SAP systems, which the speakers say gets less research attention than the ABAP side despite linking many business applications. They start with exposed services: default ports carry unencrypted traffic, and the password sent to the administration tool is only obfuscated. Decompiling the Java code showed the scheme depends on a mask value shared by all installations, which made a decryptor possible. Internet-facing systems come next, with hundreds of default web applications, information disclosure flaws, a page that could scan internal networks, and an SMB relay issue affecting clustered Windows nodes.

The middle section covers access control. A CSRF protection was bypassed through an identity management web service, and web.xml role restrictions fell to the invoker servlet, which calls servlets by class name. A HEAD verb-tampering flaw skipped method restrictions, and chaining these let the speakers create a user on a vulnerable server without logging in. For post-exploitation, they showed reading stored RFC destination credentials, reading ABAP tables from the Java side, and planting a backdoor class, then outlined a worm concept that spreads through trusted connections.

The talk closes with a free web.xml checker covering nine categories of misconfiguration, with a commercial version also available. Suggested defenses include patching, disabling unused web applications, firewalling the identity management interfaces, and running regular security assessments. Some details were withheld until vendor fixes shipped.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - D1T2 - Jim Geovedi - Satellite Telephony Security - What Is and What Will Never Be
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding HITB2011KUL - D1T2 - Jim Geovedi - Satellite Telephony Security - What Is and What Will Never Be.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at HITB2011KUL, speaker Jim Geovedi explores the security architecture and interception vulnerabilities associated with satellite telephony systems. Geovedi reviews the history of satellite hacking research and outlines the operational structure of satellite communication networks, comparing terrestrial cellular architectures to satellite radio interfaces. He demonstrates how satellite communications—particularly those adhering to GEO Mobile Radio (GMR) standards derived from GSM—can be monitored and intercepted via tactical and strategic approaches.

### Key Topics
- **History of Satellite Research**: Evolution of satellite security research from early discussions in 1996 and 1998, to DVB satellite hacking by researchers like "Warmenh" (Warman) and Adam Laurie in 2009, leading up to GMR satellite phone systems.
- **Satellite Orbits & Operators**: The technical differences and operational tradeoffs among Low Earth Orbit (LEO, 500–2,000 km, e.g., Iridium, Globalstar), Medium Earth Orbit (MEO, 8,000–20,000 km), and Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO, ~35,000 km, e.g., Inmarsat, Thuraya, ACeS).
- **Network Architecture & Standards**: GMR-1 and GMR-2 specifications based on GSM standards; multiplexing approaches including TDMA and CDMA; spot beam coverage dynamics compared to terrestrial GSM cells; and network gateway routing connecting to terrestrial networks (PSTN/PLMN).
- **Monitoring & Interception Techniques**: Distinction between tactical mobile ground interception (line-of-sight L-band signals at ~1.5–1.6 GHz) and strategic passive gateway monitoring (intercepting satellite C-band downlinks at 3–6 GHz using 7–9 meter dishes).

### Technical Details
- **Frequency Bands & Channels**: Handsets communicate with satellites over L-band frequencies (~1.6 GHz uplink, ~1.5 GHz downlink). Primary gateway Earth stations link with satellites using C-band frequencies (~6 GHz uplink, ~3 GHz downlink) and coordinate telemetry, tracking, and spot beam configurations.
- **Encryption & Protocol Vulnerabilities**: GMR-1 and GMR-2 inherit cryptographic and signaling mechanisms from terrestrial GSM. Encryption protocols discussed include A5/1 (noted as crackable in seconds, and used for protecting initial signaling/location update/IMSI attach) and A5/2 for payload/data traffic. The talk highlights that because cellular and GMR protocol stacks have historically been proprietary and closed, auditing has lagged behind standard networks.
- **Location Tracking & Intercept Capabilities**: Handsets provide GPS positions back to gateways for spot beam management, though documented accuracy is deliberately limited to roughly 100 meters. Geovedi showcases passive monitoring data capture, recovering call analysis metrics including spot beam IDs, timestamps, call durations, dialed numbers, caller IDs, partial IMSI/TMSI, IMEI, and Arabic SMS messages.
- **Tooling & Projects**: The presentation references the open-source Osmocom project—notably Osmocom-GMR and Karsten Nohl and Sylvain Munaut's work with OsmocomBB—as enabling researchers to analyze satellite mobile packets and construct software-defined packet sniffers.

### Takeaways
Geovedi emphasizes that satellite telephony systems rely on legacy GSM foundations and weak encryption schemes, making both tactical and strategic eavesdropping viable. With newer hybrid smartphones (such as Windows Mobile satellite devices) entering the market and open-source projects like Osmocom-GMR emerging, satellite systems represent a critical, yet frequently overlooked, attack surface that requires closer community scrutiny.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - D1T1 - Mahmud Ab Rahman
talks.teaser: Reverse Engineering Android Malware investigates HITB2011KUL - D1T1 - Mahmud Ab Rahman.
talks.summary:
The talk covers reverse engineering Android malware, from packaging basics to hands-on case studies. It explains that an APK is a zip archive holding DEX bytecode, and how malware spreads through repackaged legitimate apps, fake removal tools, exploit-laden pages and remote installs abusing a compromised Google account. A toolchain for disassembling, decompiling and reassembling DEX code is introduced.

The manifest is treated as a starting map: receivers, services, activities and permissions that do not fit an app's purpose point to suspicious code, alongside searches for telling strings and SMS or network API calls. An SMS stealer disguised as a movie player, supplied without a manifest, was analysed from its onCreate method; it stole messages and sent only a handful of premium-rate texts per run to avoid drawing attention. A DroidDream variant bundled into repackaged games used two root exploits to copy its payload into the system partition, then sent device details to a command server using decoded, encrypted URLs. A mobile banking sample linked to the Zeus family intercepted incoming SMS and forwarded it, while a SpyEye-linked fake security app was pushed through injected web pages.

Challenges covered include anti-emulator checks, obfuscation, keys embedded in samples, and optimized bytecode that breaks decompilers. The speaker argues Android malware remains relatively simple but will grow more complex, and closes with the difficulty of spotting malicious apps in stores and the abuse of remote install and uninstall.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - D1T1 - Riley Hassell - Hacking Androids for Profit
talks.teaser: Shows how Android apps can be abused for phishing, impersonation and data theft, and what consumers can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the risks Android users face when they install apps. The speaker argues that the marketplace performs little vetting, so almost anyone can publish an app under a familiar name, and that permission prompts use wording ordinary consumers cannot interpret. Trojans that ride popular trends, impersonating apps, and third-party markets with more malware are presented as the main threats.

The middle of the talk covers specific attack classes. An overlay demo shows a fake login screen placed over a real app, capturing credentials typed into Skype. Other cases include apps requesting permissions unrelated to their purpose, exported activities that other apps can launch without checks, and SQL and XML injection in app code. Package-name squatting can hide an app from task killers. In one demo, a logged-in browser session was reused to trigger a remote app install on a phone.

The closing advice focuses on consumer habits. Users should check how long an app has been listed, weigh ratings for unusual uniformity, and question permissions that do not fit an app's job. Automatic Wi-Fi connection should be turned off, the remember option should be unticked when granting root to a jailbreak tool, and a mobile security app is still worth installing. The speaker concludes that marketplace operators should validate apps before publication and that permission descriptions need to be written for non-experts.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - D1T1 - Andrea Barisani & Daniele Bianco
talks.teaser: Shows how a hidden skimmer in a payment terminal can capture chip card data and PINs despite EMV protections.
talks.summary:
This talk examines EMV, the chip standard behind chip-and-PIN cards, and argues that moving away from magnetic stripes has not removed card skimming. The speakers focus on a hidden skimmer built into the card slot of a point-of-sale terminal, where the chip interface is reachable by design and hard to notice. They examined several popular European terminal models and found that their tamper sensors often did not cover the card interface. In one model, the display could reportedly be lifted in minutes to expose the chip contacts without triggering an alarm.

The skimmer can log the data a terminal reads from the card, including names, expiry dates and track data, and capture the PIN. Cloned chip data could once produce a working magnetic stripe copy, but newer cards carry a different CVV on the chip, and some websites still accept purchases without a security code. The most serious result was a downgrade: by altering the card's verification method list and action codes, the skimmer forces plaintext PIN entry, so the PIN reaches the device in clear text. A sample transaction log showed the PIN captured alongside a normal online transaction. Offline data authentication was also weak, with static SDA cards easy to copy.

The speakers argue that the protocol is too complex to patch reliably and that PIN-based liability rules shift fraud losses onto cardholders. They report that a Dutch operator reportedly disabled plaintext PIN checks for domestic cards through a firmware update. Their practical advice is to disable plaintext PIN verification, move authorization online where possible, and treat payment terminals as untrusted devices.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - KEYNOTE 2 - Jennifer Granick
talks.teaser: Traces how technology reshaped personal privacy and government secrecy, and how the law has struggled to keep up.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that technology has removed much of the privacy and secrecy people once took for granted. A phone call, a letter or a television habit once left little or no record, while today cameras, cell phone location pings, e-books and social networks create searchable trails. The speaker contrasts the Pentagon Papers, which needed a photocopier, a truck and a newspaper willing to publish, with the WikiLeaks cables, which could be copied onto a thumb drive and posted in full.

Through a series of cases, the talk shows how the law has been used to control information. A Sprint employee disclosed that an automated law enforcement site had received 8 million location requests over 13 months. Diebold used copyright takedowns to suppress internal emails about its voting machines, and Cisco and an employer sued over router vulnerabilities presented at Black Hat in 2005. The state secrets doctrine has ended lawsuits, and a Seattle man used police video logs obtained in discovery to publish a record of when officers had recorded their encounters with people.

The speaker is skeptical that statutes such as the Electronic Communications Privacy Act and class action privacy suits reliably protect users. The takeaway is that hackers and activists who creatively combine technology and the law can shed more light on government and protect privacy, as Twitter did when it challenged secret orders in court.

talks.title: HITB2011KUL - KEYNOTE 1 - Kenneth Geers - Is The Pen Still Mightier Than The Sword
talks.teaser: A keynote contrasts mass disclosure with targeted industrial attacks, drawing lessons from WikiLeaks, Stuxnet, and alliance cyber planning.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a long tradition of treating words as stronger than weapons, then argues that computers and global connectivity have amplified that idea while also enabling new forms of harm that reach across borders as easily as ideas do. Syria’s uprising is contrasted with the hidden massacre in Hama in 1982 to show how recording and sharing events online changes accountability, alongside examples such as suspected cyber support for air strikes, Anonymous defacements, and NATO’s slow shift from ignoring networks to naming cyber attacks among top alliance threats.

The middle of the talk pairs two 2010 watersheds. WikiLeaks is framed as pushing forbidden stories to a worldwide audience, raising questions of trust, over-classification, insider access, and real harm when sources are exposed. Stuxnet is described as the opposite model: highly targeted code that manipulated centrifuge speeds while misleading operators, exploited unpatched industrial environments and removable media to cross air gaps, and reportedly destroyed large numbers of machines with strategic effect and less obvious kinetic fallout.

The close returns to whether information still outranks force. The speaker cites counter-proliferation impact, warnings that critical infrastructure may need to be subverted long before conflict, and Michael Hayden’s point that hacking unlike bombing requires peacetime preparation. Practitioners hear that deterrence and arms-control thinking from the nuclear era may need cyber equivalents, that no one inherits perfect security from complex software, and that disclosure activism and precision network attacks both belong in strategic planning for governments and critical sectors.

talks.title: HITB2010KUL Keynote 2 - Taking Back the DNS Part 3
talks.teaser: Shows how recursive DNS policies help enterprises block rotating malware domains without perpetual registry blacklists.
talks.summary:
The segment frames DNS as a mandatory touchpoint for nearly all network activity, including malware and spam that hide behind constantly changing domain names. When malicious infrastructure rotates through large numbers of names across several top-level domains, pushing removal upstream becomes either unbounded operational work or a policy that operators abandon under pressure. Enterprises doing risk management cannot assume unrelated registry or ISP parties will block those names forever, especially when insurance and contracts need clear accountability.

The presenter describes response policy mechanisms that let recursive resolver operators publish policy content keyed not only on domain names but also on patterns such as name server addresses, so protection does not require enumerating every possible authoritative server IP. A high-volume case involving malware that emits many unique names per day illustrates why local resolver policy scales better than hoping five TLD registries will sustain perpetual blocks. Subscription-based DNS reputation services are positioned as contractable controls insurers can understand, compared with informal reliance on third parties.

Implementation is discussed in the context of dominant open-source resolver market share, deliberately shipping capability outside a long standards debate while acknowledging censorship and abuse objections and offering a limited free policy feed for time-generated threat names. A short incident-oriented policy window compensates for unreliable client clocks. Material on aggregating global sensor feeds into shared security information is deferred to a later segment; closing discussion covers supported resolver release lines and plans to land the feature in an upcoming point release.

talks.title: HITB2010KUL Keynote 2 - Taking Back the DNS Part 5
talks.teaser: Describes a non-commercial exchange where security analysts share sensor data and malware metadata over VLAN channels.
talks.summary:
The keynote presents a non-commercial exchange fabric that works like an internet exchange, except that security analysts, commercial or not, trade security-relevant data instead of customer traffic. Sensor operators feed their traffic into a private switching fabric, and researchers watch it in real time. Because the data is already there, starting a new analysis project no longer requires building a sensor network; a researcher only connects a computer to the Ethernet switch. The speaker urges operators of recursive name servers to run sensors and share their data, and gives preference to people who publish their results for the community.

For malware, the exchange uses VLANs as separate channels, one of them dedicated to malware. Someone who obtains a sample posts a small metadata record covering its hash, strings, the domains it looked up, and the addresses it tried to reach, along with a URL for the binary. Others who have not seen that hash can contact the sender and fetch the file. The speaker argues this is still reactive, but it removes the long delay of sharing samples only at the end of the day.

In the question round, the speaker says passive DNS is useful for mapping criminal enterprises and bringing local police into investigations, not only for building response zones. Membership of the exchange is not public; sensor operators see a limited view. The speaker described a paid premium private channel whose sponsor controls who joins, and a default-empty private channel that admits people case by case. Fees are charged, but the speaker says no one has been turned away for being unable to pay.
